docs.title: Welcome to XenoCore
docs.text:
All · 5 min · No code

The sample party fighting Gaur Plain's Unique monster: auto-attacks, an Art from the palette, a Topple.

XenoCore is a framework for party-based, real-time RPG combat and menus, built as a Game Feature plugin on Epic's Lyra sample for Unreal Engine 5.8. You control one member of a party of up to seven while the others fight beside you. Characters auto-attack, you choose Arts from a palette, and Arts chain enemies through Break, Topple and Daze. Around the combat sits the rest of an RPG: equipment, loot, levelling, NPCs, quests, shops and saving.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
Area Included Party A roster of members, a party of up to seven (a setting; the sample starts with two and recruits five more), reserves, leader swapping in and out of battle, party tactics, follow and combat AI, downed members revived with the Party Gauge Combat Auto-attack, target lock, weapon draw and sheathe, hit reactions, damage numbers, hit feedback Arts Data-driven Arts and Talent Arts, cooldowns, the combat palette, the Arts menu Reactions and statuses The Break, Topple, Daze chain, and status effects with icons and popups Stats and progression Strength, Ether, Agility, defences, weight; experience per character, reserve experience, level-ups, skill trees Equipment and items Six equipment slots per character, a shared party bag, weapon types with their own animation sets, gems in sockets, Common / Rare / Legendary rarity, sortable lists Enemies An enemy base with its own StateTree AI, sight/sound/ether detection, squads on respawning spawners, arts, experience rewards and drop tables, and seven sample enemy types Loot Treasure chests that persist and roll their contents when opened, drop tables per enemy family with level bands, and a Take All / Take None panel World interaction NPCs, conversations with a framing camera, recruiting party members by talking, a quest system with offers, log, HUD tracker and rewards, shops and trades World A day/night clock, per-area weather, area music slots, a minimap with the time and weather on it Front end Boot screens, title screen, save slots, autosave and save points, tutorial cards Menus and HUD A full CommonUI menu suite and HUD, with gamepad and keyboard prompts Sample content Seven VRoid party members, seven enemy types, weapons, armour, gems, the Gaur Plain sample map with seven quests, and a test gym

Nearly everything a designer does is data: make a child of a XenoCore base Blueprint (or duplicate a sample data asset), change its settings, press Play. The recipes walk through the common tasks, and Child or duplicate? says which to use when.

docs.title: What it isn't
docs.text:
• Not a finished game. There is no story, and the sample numbers (enemy stats, prices, rewards) are placeholders to tune, not a balanced game.
  • Single-player only. Nothing is built for networking or replication.
  • Built on Lyra, and needs it. XenoCore is a Lyra Game Feature plugin; it does not run in a project without Lyra. You bring a Lyra Starter Game project (free) and drop the plugin into it. The sample party also needs the free VRM4U plugin; see Install.
  • Delivered as C++ source. The first time you open the project, Unreal compiles XenoCore, so you need Visual Studio 2022 installed (Lyra is a C++ project too). After that, most work needs no code at all.
  • No music in the box. The sample map's music slots are empty; add your own tracks (see Area music).

The full list is on Known limitations, and common questions are answered in the FAQ.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text: Follow Getting Started in order. It takes under two hours and ends with your own Art and your own enemy in the game.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text:
All · reference · No code

Every XenoCore release, newest first. Versions follow Semantic Versioning: a major release may break your content, saves or the C++ and Blueprint API, and says what to re-check; a minor release adds features; a patch release only fixes bugs. See Compatibility for how to take an update.

docs.title: Unreleased
docs.text: Changes merged since the last release; they ship in the next version. Nothing yet.

docs.title: 1.0.0 (initial release)
docs.text:
Engine: Unreal Engine 5.8, Win64, with Lyra Starter Game 5.8 and VRM4U for 5.8. Save-data version: 5.

The first public release. It includes:

  • Party: up to seven active members (the sample starts with two and recruits five), reserves, leader switching in and out of battle, companion AI that uses the same Arts and cooldowns as the player, Party Tactics, the Party Gauge, downed members and revives.
  • Combat: auto-attack, target lock and cycling, weapon draw and sheathe, Arts and Talent Arts with cooldowns and a combat palette, area-of-effect Arts, the Break, Topple and Daze chain, status effects, block, evade and critical hits, aggro, hit feedback and damage numbers.
  • Progression: per-character statlines and experience curves, level-ups, skill trees with branches and traits.
  • Items: a shared party bag, six equipment slots per character, weapon types per character, gems, Common / Rare / Legendary rarity, sortable item lists, treasure chests with drop tables (Take All or Take None).
  • Enemies: an enemy base with StateTree AI and Arts, four detection types, squads on respawning spawners with linked aggro, level labels, seven sample enemy types.
  • World and story: NPCs and conversations with a framing camera, recruiting by talking, quests with offers, a log, a HUD tracker and rewards, shops and trades, a day/night clock, per-area weather, area and battle music slots (no tracks included), a minimap, surface footsteps.
  • Front end: boot and title screens, three save slots plus autosave and save points, tutorial cards, a full CommonUI menu suite and HUD with gamepad and keyboard prompts.
  • Editor: a one-click project setup (Tools › XenoCore › Apply XenoCore Project Settings) and save-time checks on XenoCore's data assets, including item definitions.
  • Sample content: the Gaur Plain sample map with seven quests, a front-end map and a test gym, seven VRoid party members with AI-generated battle voices, weapons, armour and gems.

Known gaps are listed on Known limitations.

docs.text: The C++ source, Blueprints, data assets, maps, materials, procedural icons and the synthesized sounds (victory chime, rain, thunder) are XenoCore's own, covered by your Fab licence for XenoCore.

docs.text:
These are included for use in your project, in games you build with Unreal Engine, under your Fab licence for XenoCore and the terms of their original sources. They are not for standalone redistribution or resale as assets: do not extract them and sell, share or list them on their own or inside another asset pack. Shipping them inside your game is fine.

docs.title: AI-generated voices
docs.text: The sample party's battle voice lines (about 1,149 sound waves in Audio/Voice) were generated with ElevenLabs text-to-speech from scripts written for XenoCore. The Fab listing is marked Created with AI for this reason. See Battle voices to replace them.

docs.title: Not included
docs.text: VRM4U (required) By ruyo, MIT licence, github.com/ruyo/VRM4U. Download it separately; its licence and its bundled third-party licences come with it. Lyra Starter Game (required) Epic Games, free on Fab. XenoCore uses Lyra's code and some of its content (the UE5 Mannequin, its animations, Lyra's fonts) from the Lyra project you create. NVIDIA DLSS (optional) NVIDIA's own plugin, under NVIDIA's licence. See Turn on NVIDIA DLSS. Music None ships. See Give a map its music.

docs.title: FAQ
docs.text: Evaluator · 5 min · No code

docs.title: Does it support multiplayer?
docs.text: No. XenoCore is single-player only. Party members are AI-controlled characters on one machine, and nothing is replicated. Adding multiplayer would mean replicating the party, targeting, Arts, inventory and saves: treat that as a new project built on XenoCore's ideas. See Compatibility.

docs.title: Can I add it to a project that is not based on Lyra?
docs.text: No. XenoCore is a Lyra Game Feature plugin: its C++ is built on Lyra's game module, and its maps run a Lyra Experience. Start from a Lyra Starter Game 5.8 project (free on Fab) and add XenoCore to it. See Install and first launch.

docs.title: Do I need to know C++?
docs.text: No. Almost everything is data: Blueprints, data assets and Data Tables. You do need Visual Studio 2022 installed, because XenoCore is delivered as source and compiles the first time the project opens. See Requirements.

docs.title: Which platforms and engine versions?
docs.text: Windows 64-bit and Unreal Engine 5.8 only. No Mac, Linux, console or mobile support. When a new engine version comes out, XenoCore is re-tested and a new upload is published for it. See Compatibility.

docs.title: Why do I need VRM4U?
docs.text: The seven sample party members are VRoid characters, and their skeletons, faces, toon materials and hair physics run on VRM4U, a free plugin by ruyo (MIT licence). XenoCore cannot include it, so you download it once; see Install. Your own characters do not have to be VRoid characters: see Add a party member.

docs.title: Is NVIDIA DLSS required?
docs.text: No. DLSS is optional. If you install NVIDIA's own DLSS plugin, DLSS, Frame Generation and Reflex appear in the game's video settings; without it they are simply not shown. See Turn on NVIDIA DLSS and Frame Generation.

docs.title: Is there music?
docs.text: The music system ships (a field track, a battle track that fades in when a fight starts, a night track and fallbacks), but no music tracks are included, so the sample is silent. Add your own tracks to the map's Area Music actor or to the project-wide fallbacks: see Give a map its music.

docs.title: Are the voices AI-generated?
docs.text: Yes. The sample party's battle voice lines were generated with ElevenLabs text-to-speech from scripts written for XenoCore, and the Fab listing is marked Created with AI. You can replace any line with your own recording: see Battle voices.

docs.title: Can I remove the sample content?
docs.text: Yes. Build your own characters, gear, enemies and map first, then follow Replace the sample content to remove the samples without leaving missing references.

docs.title: Can I use the included content in my game?
docs.text: Yes, inside games you make. Some content comes from other sources (Epic's samples, Megascans, a stylized grass kit, Mixamo and Paragon-derived animations, pixiv's VRoid sample models): it is included for use in your project, but not for resale as assets on its own. See Credits and licences.

docs.title: Where do I get help?
docs.text: Open an issue at github.com/baremetalrt/xenocore-dist/issues. Reporting a bug says what to include.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
All · 5 min · No code

What XenoCore 1.0.0 does not do, so you can plan around it before you build on it. Each line links to where the topic is covered.

docs.title: Platform and project
docs.text:
• Unreal Engine 5.8 only. Other engine versions are not supported; a new engine version gets a new upload after it has been re-tested. See Compatibility.
  • Windows 64-bit only. Both C++ modules are built for Win64; macOS, Linux, consoles and mobile are not supported.
  • Lyra only. XenoCore is a Game Feature plugin built on Lyra's C++ and does not run in a project that is not based on Lyra Starter Game 5.8.
  • Compiled from source on first open. You need Visual Studio 2022; see Requirements.
  • Needs VRM4U. The sample party runs on the free VRM4U plugin, which you download separately.

docs.title: Game type
docs.text:
• Single-player only. Nothing is replicated or predicted for networking, and some systems rely on that. Multiplayer is not a setting you can turn on; see Compatibility.
  • A framework, not a finished game. There is no story, and the sample numbers (enemy stats, prices, rewards) are a starting point to tune.

docs.title: Sample content
docs.text:
• One sample region. Gaur Plain is the only field map, plus the title-screen map and a small test gym.
  • Gaur Plain is not a World Partition map. It loads as one level. Build your own large maps with World Partition: see Build a world-partition map.
  • No music included. The area and battle music system works, but every track slot is empty, so the game is silent until you add your own tracks. See Give a map its music.
  • The sample voices are AI-generated. See Battle voices to replace them with your own recordings.

docs.title: Not built yet
docs.text:
• Taking some items from a chest. The loot panel offers Take All or Take None; choosing individual items is not built. See Loot.
  • Some skills are stand-ins. 63 of the 100 sample skills do a simpler thing than their name suggests, because the system they need (tension, visions, chain attacks, counters, gem crafting and others) does not exist yet. See Skills.
  • Skill Links. The setting exists but nothing reads it. See Skills.
  • Some Party Gauge fill reasons. The fill table prices Burst Affinity, very high Tension and Chain Attack kills, but none of those mechanics exist yet. See Party Gauge, downed and revive.
  • Time of day extras. Night-only enemies, time-gated collectables and NPC schedules, wet surfaces and a distant rain curtain. See Time of day and weather.
  • Minimap options. Rotation and hiding are console commands only; there is no options-menu entry. See Minimap.

docs.title: Animation
docs.text:
All · 15 min read

What the player sees: characters walk and run with smooth blending, turn their upper body toward a locked enemy while their legs keep running, switch to a sword stance when a battle starts, fidget when left standing, flinch without dropping their swing, and (on VRoid characters) blink, pull faces and turn their heads toward whoever they are looking at.

Every party character shares one host Animation Blueprint, Characters/Player/ABP_XenoCore_Base, which holds the state machine (Idle, Move, the jump states). Which clips each state plays come from a linked animation layer: a small Animation Blueprint chosen by what the character holds and by its masculine or feminine style. The host is shared and never edited per character; a new weapon or stance is a new layer child that only swaps clips, set in its Asset Override editor with no graph editing.

docs.title: What you can change
docs.text:
• Masculine or feminine movement for a character: Choose an animation style.
  • A new weapon stance: Add a weapon (see Extending it).
  • One character's own flinch, topple, dodge, death or victory pose: Give a character its own combat animations.
  • One character's idle fidgets and resting faces: Give a character its own idle breaks and faces.
  • Stride, turn and head-look limits: settings on the host Animation Blueprint (Settings).

docs.title: How it fits together
docs.text: Piece Class / sample asset Job Anim instance (C++ parent of every XenoCore Animation Blueprint) XenoCoreAnimInstance Works out ground speed, direction, stride scale, battle stance, target twist, head turn and idle breaks, so no Blueprint graph has to Host ABP Characters/Player/ABP_XenoCore_Base Locomotion state machine, montage slots, inertialization, stride warping, spine twist, head and neck turn Layer interface Characters/Player/AnimLayers/ALI_XenoCore_AnimLayers The layer functions: FullBody_Idle, FullBody_Move, FullBody_Jump, FullBody_Apex, FullBody_Falling, FullBody_Land, FullBody_SkeletalControls Layer base AnimLayers/ABP_XenoCore_ItemLayersBase The layer graphs, written once Layer children ABP_XenoCore_UnarmedAnimLayers, ABP_XenoCore_UnarmedAnimLayers_Feminine, ABP_XenoCore_GreatSwordAnimLayers Override clips and blend spaces only Blend spaces Characters/Player/BlendSpaces/BS_XenoCore_Unarmed_Locomotion, _Feminine, BS_XenoCore_GreatSword_Combat_Locomotion Direction × speed Style parts Characters/Core/Cosmetics/B_XenoCore_Cosmetic_Masculine, _Feminine Carry Cosmetic.AnimationStyle.Masculine / .Feminine Weapon instance Weapons/B_WeaponInstance_Base, GreatSword/B_WeaponInstance_GreatSword Picks and links the layer when the weapon is drawn or stowed Face (VRoid only) Characters/VRoid/<Name>/Animation/ABP_XenoCore_VRoidRetarget_* Blinks, expressions and mouth on a VRoid body Expression table Characters/Core/Face/DT_XenoCore_FaceExpressions Named faces (Happy, Laugh, Smug…) as mixes of face curves Anim profile Characters/VRoid/<Name>/DA_XenoCore_AnimProfile_VRoid_* One character's own reaction, death and victory clips, idle breaks and resting faces Enemy ABP Characters/Enemies/Minion/ABP_XenoCore_Minion_Melee Built on the same C++ parent, not on the host ABP. Moves on a 2D blend space, Minion/Animations/BS_XenoCore_Minion_Locomotion2D (direction × speed), so a minion circling sideways in a fight plays side and back jogs

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
Every frame. The C++ parent works out these values, which the graphs read (you can see them in the Animation Blueprint's Variables list):

  • Ground Speed (horizontal only) and a smoothed copy; Is Moving above Moving Speed Threshold (20).
  • Direction, −180 to 180 against the actor's facing. Out of battle the character faces where it runs, so this stays near 0.
  • Stride Scale = Ground Speed ÷ Authored Clip Speed (400), floored at Min Stride Scale (1.0), so warping only ever lengthens the stride above the fastest clip.
  • In Battle, from Status.XenoCore.InBattle on the character's ability system.
  • Target Yaw Delta, the damped, clamped angle to the locked target. It turns the upper body toward the target while the legs keep running (look traversal), up to Max Target Twist (70°).
  • Look Bone Rotation 0–2, the head and neck turn toward what a companion is looking at (see The head turn).
  • Wants Idle Break (see below).

The state machine. The host moves between Idle and Move on ground speed with a short blend, and through jump states (Jump, Apex, Falling, Land) when airborne. Each state calls its layer function, such as FullBody_Move, which plays a 2D blend space: direction on one axis, speed on the other, with walk clips at 200 and jog at 400, so both walking and running blend continuously.

Choosing the layer. The weapon instance Blueprint holds two sets, Equipped Anim Set and Uneuipped Anim Set (Lyra's spelling), each a list of layer classes with the tags that select them. When the weapon is drawn or stowed, the set for that state is searched for the layer whose tags best match the character's style tags (so a feminine character gets the feminine unarmed layer), that layer is linked, and the change of stance blends over Anim Layer Blend Time instead of popping.

If nothing is linked, each layer node falls back to ABP_XenoCore_UnarmedAnimLayers.

Masculine and feminine. A party pawn's Cosmetic Part (on B_XenoCore_PartyMember_Base) adds a style part carrying Cosmetic.AnimationStyle.Masculine or .Feminine. The same tag picks the body mesh through the pawn's Body Meshes rules (SKM_Manny or SKM_Quinn) and the unarmed layer. The feminine layer uses Lyra's MF_ clips (MM_ is Lyra's masculine set).

Idle breaks. After Idle Break Delay (8 s) plus a random Idle Break Jitter (up to 6 s) of standing still, Wants Idle Break turns true for exactly the length of the chosen clip, and the idle layer blends to that clip and back. Each character rolls its own timing, so a party does not fidget in unison.

Which clip plays comes from two places:

  1. The character's Anim Profile, if it has one: Idle Breaks out of battle, Armed Idle Breaks with the weapon drawn. One is picked at random each time, never the same one twice running.
  2. Otherwise, the stance's own Idle Break Anim on its layer child. The shipped ones: MM_Unarmed_IdleBreak_Fidget (unarmed), MF_Unarmed_Idle_Break (feminine), AS_Kwang_IdleBreak_Laugh (greatsword). An empty Idle Break Anim means that stance never fidgets, unless the profile gives it a list.

Each shipped VRoid member has four breaks in its profile, drawn from Lyra's three and nine bare-handed clips in Characters/Core/Animations/IdleBreaks (Stretch, Waiting, Sneeze, Greeting and others). Their Armed Idle Breaks are empty, so with the sword out they use the stance's own break. See Give a character its own idle breaks and faces.

Montages. Attacks, Arts, hit reactions and the draw and sheathe play as montages on top of the state machine. Attacks and Arts use the slots of the default slot group (DefaultGroup): the party's play on FullBody, the minion's on DefaultSlot; Topple, Daze, guards, recoils and victory emotes also use FullBody; the draw and sheathe use UpperBody. A flinch plays additively on the AdditiveHitReact slot, which sits in its own group, AdditiveGroup: it is layered on top of whatever the body is doing, so a hit reads while the character walks or swings, and it never stops the swing. A character does not flinch while drawing or sheathing.

A miss plays a duck or a dodge, picked at random from the evade ability's Random Montages (GA_XenoCore_Evade), on the Defence slot. In battle the arms are taken back from the stance under that slot, so the body ducks while the hands stay on the sword; unarmed, the clip's own arms play.

While a hit's knockback is pushing the body, the anim instance reads its velocity as zero, so a character sliding backwards from a blow does not break into a forward jog.

Fails silently: a flinch that never shows, or that cancels the swing

A flinch montage must be on the AdditiveHitReact slot, its clips must be Additive Anim Type Local Space (base pose: the clip's own first frame), the anim Blueprint must apply that slot additively, and the slot must be in its own slot group on the skeleton. Montages in one group stop each other, and compiling an anim Blueprint puts a new slot in DefaultGroup, so a flinch there cuts the attack short and the next swing cuts the flinch off. Check it in the skeleton's Anim Slot Manager: AdditiveHitReact belongs under AdditiveGroup, as on SK_Mannequin.

Per-character combat clips. Reaction and death montages come from the reaction ability and the pawn by default, shared by everyone who has them. A character's Anim Profile (a data asset, set on the pawn under XenoCore › Animation) overrides them for that character only, slot by slot: an empty slot keeps the shared clip. Each reaction ability names the profile row it reads with its Profile Key (Anim.XenoCore.Reaction.Flinch, .Topple, .Daze, .Guard, .Evade, .Recoil). Walking, running and idles are not in the profile; they come from the style and the weapon, as above. See Give a character its own combat animations.

Stride warping happens once, in the host ABP, driven by Stride Scale.

VRoid faces. A VRoid party member runs the Mannequin animation on an invisible body; its VRoid mesh copies the pose, and its retarget Animation Blueprint (ABP_XenoCore_VRoidRetarget_*) drives the face:

  • a random blink, timed per character;
  • an expression chosen from the character's gameplay tags by Expression Rules, first matching rule wins. The shipped order: downed looks pained, dead closes the eyes, Topple and Break look surprised, Daze sad, a victory celebration laughs, casting an art and being in battle look angry, a conversation looks relaxed;
  • a mouth flap while Talking Tag is held, or lip sync for a voice line;
  • Play Expression for scripted moments, which wins over the rules for its duration.

An expression is named by a row of the face's Expression Table, which defaults to Characters/Core/Face/DT_XenoCore_FaceExpressions. It ships 19 rows: Happy, Smile, Laugh, Giggle, Wink, Smug, Annoyed, Angry, Determined, Sad, Worried, Surprised, Shocked, Relaxed, Bored, Sleepy, Yawn, Thinking and Pained. Each row is a Curves map of face curve to weight, built from the VRM presets (happy, angry, sad, relaxed, surprised, aa, ih, ou, ee, oh, blink, blinkLeft, blinkRight). Suppress Blink stops the blink while it shows, and Pulse Curve, Pulse Weight and Pulse Rate add an oscillating curve on top, such as a laugh's opening and closing mouth. A name that is not a row is played as one curve at full weight, so a rule that says angry still works.

To play a face from any Blueprint, call Play Expression On Actor with the pawn (or its cosmetic part), a row name, a weight and a duration. It returns false, and does nothing, on a character without a face, such as a Mannequin-bodied member or an enemy.

docs.title: The head turn
docs.text:
Companions turn their head and neck toward whatever their gaze is on: the leader, another member, the view, the battle target. What they look at is chosen by the party StateTree (see Companion AI); this is the part that moves the bones.

ABP_XenoCore_Base adds Look Bone Rotation 0, 1 and 2 to neck_01, neck_02 and head, after the chest twist. The head carries about half the turn and moves fastest, and the neck trails it, so the turn reads as a head leading rather than one stiff hinge. When the chest is already twisted toward a battle target, that twist is taken off first, so the head does not turn twice.

The head returns forward while the character holds any of Look Blocked By Tags (downed, celebrating, toppled, dazed by default), because a clip is driving the head then. A player-controlled body has no gaze and always looks straight ahead.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:

A style tag with no rule gives the default body

The character-parts component always applies a body mesh from Body Meshes. A style part whose tags match no rule, or whose class is empty, resolves to Default Mesh. Every shipped pawn has one, and XenoCore's party and player characters fall back to their spawn mesh (with a warning) if a Default Mesh is missing, so the result is the wrong body rather than none. A pawn outside XenoCore's character classes still disappears. A party pawn that sets no Cosmetic Part must not add a part at all. See Characters.

For programmers. Fails silently: an anim property without Blueprint Read Only

If you add a C++ property to an anim instance and drive an anim graph pin from it, it must be Blueprint Read Only (or Read Write). Otherwise the Animation Blueprint fails to compile with no message anywhere, and Play in Editor just says a Blueprint failed to compile.

Fails silently: a face curve the mesh does not have

An expression row that names a curve the VRoid model's face does not have shows nothing, and nothing is logged. A typo in a row name looks the same, because a name that is not a row is tried as a single curve. Rows built from the VRM presets listed above are known to work; check any row that uses a raw Fcl_* morph curve in Play before relying on it.

Fails silently: the idle break branches wired backwards

In Blend Poses by bool, the first pose pin is the True pose. Wired the other way round, the fidget becomes the idle and the real idle plays as an occasional interruption.

Fails silently: a second Stride Warping node

Stride warping already runs in the host. Adding it in a layer too applies it twice and the feet slide. A Stride Warping node with no thigh bones set does nothing at all, which hides the mistake until someone fills them in.

Fails silently: a montage on the wrong slot group

The layer-swap blend is requested on DefaultGroup. A montage on another group blends wrongly when the stance changes, with no error.

docs.title: Extending it
docs.text:
• A new weapon stance: duplicate ABP_XenoCore_GreatSwordAnimLayers into your own folder, set its clip and blend-space overrides and its Idle Break Anim, then point your weapon instance's Equipped Anim Set at it. No graph editing is needed. See Add a weapon.
  • Changing a character's animation style: see Animation style.
  • One character's own topple, flinch, block, dodge or death: fill in its Anim Profile; see Give a character its own combat animations. No ability needs duplicating.
  • Never recreate ABP_XenoCore_UnarmedAnimLayers. The host's layer nodes use it as their fallback class; a new asset under the same name orphans them. Duplicate it instead.
  • Do not reparent an Animation Blueprint to another Animation Blueprint to share logic: a child Animation Blueprint loses its own graph. Use override-only layer children as above; logic shared by every Animation Blueprint belongs in the C++ parent, which is a programmer's job.
  • Keep gameplay-tag-driven variables on the host Animation Blueprint; on a linked layer they stop updating after the layer is linked.
For programmers: classes and calls

The C++ parent is UXenoCoreAnimInstance: it captures velocity and rotation on the game thread and computes the values above in the thread-safe update. The face is UXenoCoreFaceAnimInstance, the profile UXenoCoreCharacterAnimProfile, an expression row FXenoCoreFaceExpressionRow. On a draw or stow, the weapon instance's SetDrawn collects the cosmetic tags, calls Lyra's PickBestAnimLayer, then LinkAnimClassLayers, then RequestSlotGroupInertialization("DefaultGroup", AnimLayerBlendTime). The flinch ability refuses while Status.XenoCore.Arming is held.

docs.title: Why it's built this way
docs.text:
For programmers
  • Own host, not Lyra's. Lyra's locomotion enters Start/Stop states on input and commits to them for up to a second, which feels unresponsive for this style of game; its state machine lives in Lyra's own asset and cannot be owned. XenoCore's Idle ↔ Move machine with a 2D blend space is snappier and blends walk and run continuously.
  • Lyra's layer mechanism, kept. Per-state linked layers, PickBestAnimLayer from the weapon on draw, and an inertialization request (Lyra delivers the same request through a transition). Links are made once on an event, never per frame, and never unlink-then-link, which would drop every node to its fallback for an instant.
  • Not derived from ULyraAnimInstance, because it has no export macro and cannot be derived from outside Lyra's module; UXenoCoreAnimInstance reproduces the part it needs and pulls the ability system itself.
  • Idle breaks in the anim stack, where Lyra keeps its own, because the graph already knows whether the Idle state is active; an ability polling for it was heavier and less exact.

docs.title: Architecture overview
docs.text:
Programmer · 20 min read · No code

XenoCore is one Game Feature plugin that sits on top of Epic's Lyra sample. Lyra supplies the framework: game mode, Experiences, the ability system plumbing, CommonUI menus and the character base classes. XenoCore adds everything RPG by subclassing Lyra's classes and adding components to Lyra's actors, never by editing Lyra. The one idea that makes the rest make sense: party-wide state lives on the player controller, per-character state lives on each pawn, and presentation lives in subsystems. Every system page in this section is one row of that split.

If you are new to the Lyra vocabulary, read the Glossary entries for Experience, Game Feature plugin and Pawn data first.

Designers: what you need from this page

This page is written for programmers. As a designer you need three things from it: the ownership map (which asset holds which setting), the rule that your changes go in your own copies, and the extension points. Everything else is background.

docs.title: How it fits together
docs.text:
The plugin is Plugins/GameFeatures/XenoCore. It has two C++ modules and one content root:

Part What it is Source/XenoCoreRuntime All gameplay C++. Loaded in game and editor. Source/XenoCoreEditor Editor-only tools (animation-layer, camera, map and Niagara helpers). Never ships in a packaged game. Content/ Every XenoCore asset. Appears in the Content Browser as XenoCore Content. Config/Tags/XenoCoreTags.ini Gameplay tags that only data uses. Tags that C++ names are declared in XenoCoreGameplayTags.h.

The plugin starts in the Registered state (XenoCore.uplugin, BuiltInInitialFeatureState) and is switched on by an Experience, exactly like Lyra's own ShooterCore.

docs.title: The Game Feature Data asset
docs.text:
Content/XenoCore (the asset named after the plugin) is the plugin's Game Feature Data. It runs while the feature is active and holds three actions:

Action What it adds Add Components On every LyraPlayerController: BP_XenoCore_Party (the party), XenoCoreQuestComponent (quests) and XenoCorePartyGaugeComponent (the Party Gauge). On every Controller: BP_XenoCore_Progression (levels, EXP, gold) and LyraInventoryManagerComponent (the shared bag). On every PlayerController, client side only: LyraIndicatorManagerComponent (world indicators). Add Input Context Mapping IMC_Default (Lyra's) at priority 1 and IMC_XenoCore (XenoCore's inputs) at priority 2. Add Gameplay Cue Path Registers the plugin's GameplayCues folder (the action's default path, /GameplayCues, relative to the plugin), so GCN_XenoCore_Hit, GCN_XenoCore_Swing and GCN_XenoCore_HealNumber can be found.

It also tells the Asset Manager to scan /XenoCore/Experiences, /XenoCore/Maps and /XenoCore/System/Playlists, which is how the plugin's Experiences become discoverable without you editing the host project's config.

Fails silently: a new cue folder is never searched

Only the plugin's GameplayCues folder is registered. A Gameplay Cue Notify you save anywhere else in XenoCore Content (for example under Battle/GameplayCues) is never found: the cue fires, nothing plays, nothing is logged. Keep cue notifies in GameplayCues, or add a second path to the action.

docs.title: The Experiences
docs.text: Experience Used by What it does Experiences/B_XenoCore_Experience The sample world and L_XenoCore_Gym Sets Default Pawn Data to Game/PawnData_XenoCore_Player; adds the LAS_XenoCore_HUD action set (the HUD layout W_XenoCore_HUDLayout and the number-pop component); grants AbilitySet_XenoCore_Interact to LyraPlayerState (whose ability system XenoCore does not use, so this grant does nothing; the party's Leader Only Ability Set is the grant that works); adds B_XenoCore_TeamSetup (a team creation component) to LyraGameState; enables the XenoCore Game Feature. Experiences/B_XenoCore_FrontEnd_Experience L_XenoCore_FrontEnd Adds BP_XenoCore_TitleState to the game state, which pushes the boot screens and the title screen.

docs.title: The ownership map
docs.text:
This is the table to come back to. When you want to know where something is stored, who changes it and who is told about it, find its row.

State Lives on Class (Blueprint) Why there Roster, active party, leader slot Player controller UXenoCorePartyComponent (Characters/Party/BP_XenoCore_Party) Party-wide, and must survive switching which character you drive. Levels, EXP, Art Points, learned arts, palettes, skill progress, gold Player controller UXenoCoreProgressionComponent (Game/BP_XenoCore_Progression) Keyed by member definition, so a benched character with no body still has a level. The bag (all items) Player controller ULyraInventoryManagerComponent Party-wide; Lyra's own item-cost code looks for it on the controller. Quest records Player controller UXenoCoreQuestComponent Party-wide and save-shaped. Party Gauge Player controller UXenoCorePartyGaugeComponent Party-wide battle state; not saved. See Party Gauge, downed and revive. Menu pause, ability-input pump Player controller AXenoCorePlayerController Pumps the pawn's ability system, not the player state's. Ability system, attributes, active effects Each pawn ULyraAbilitySystemComponent on AXenoCoreCombatantCharacter (party) or AXenoCoreEnemyCharacter (enemies, a separate branch from Lyra's ALyraCharacterWithAbilities) Each character is its own identity; switching leader never moves stats. Health and death, revive Each pawn UXenoCoreHealthComponent Swapped in for Lyra's health component on every combatant. Worn equipment Each pawn UXenoCoreEquipmentComponent Equipment spawns meshes, which are per body. Input binding and camera for the driven body Each playable pawn UXenoCoreHeroComponent Binds the pawn's own ability system; re-binds input when a body is taken back. Party AI behaviour Each companion's controller AXenoCorePartyMemberController + StateTree ST_XenoCore_PartyMember Carries the team; behaviour is data. Enemy AI behaviour Each enemy's controller AXenoCoreEnemyController + an enemy StateTree Carries the team, aggro and leash. Current target The target-mode ability instance UXenoCoreGameplayAbility_TargetMode (GA_XenoCore_TargetMode) One instance per pawn, so the lock and its target share one lifetime. Dialogue box and line sequencing World UXenoCoreDialogueSubsystem One conversation at a time, driven from the NPC's graph. "What am I standing next to" and the A prompt World UXenoCoreInteractionSubsystem One owner for one button and one screen corner. Damage-taken and heal numbers World UXenoCoreDamageNumberSubsystem Listens to Lyra's damage message; draws what Lyra does not. Battle text (MISS, CRITICAL HIT!, BREAK...) World UXenoCoreBattleNotifySubsystem Can annotate any actor, widget or not. Loot popup World UXenoCoreLootPopupSubsystem Reacts to a chest being opened. Party join/leave banner World UXenoCorePartyNoticeSubsystem Waits until the game is unpaused before announcing. "The battle was won", fanfare and victory emotes World UXenoCoreBattleVictorySubsystem The one place that tells a win from a retreat. Battle voice lines and banter World UXenoCoreBattleVoiceSubsystem One speaker at a time across the party. See Battle voices. Map markers World UXenoCoreMapMarkerSubsystem What the minimap draws. See Minimap. Holding the loading screen until the world is ready World UXenoCoreWorldReadySubsystem Lifts only once bodies are posed and shaders have settled. Save slots, load order, autosave Game instance UXenoCoreSaveSubsystem Must outlive a map change. Time of day, weather, tutorial cards seen Game instance UXenoCoreTimeOfDaySubsystem, UXenoCoreWeatherSubsystem, UXenoCoreTutorialSubsystem Survive travel; each is a save participant. See Time of day and weather. Your own saved state Wherever it lives, as a save participant IXenoCoreSaveParticipant, UXenoCoreSaveParticipantComponent Stored in the save under its own key; XenoCore never needs to know what it is. See Make a system save. Which widgets and assets C++ opens Project settings UXenoCoreUISettings, UXenoCoreContentSettings A subsystem has no asset of its own to point at a widget. See UI shell and HUD. Title screen Game state (front end only) UXenoCoreTitleStateComponent (UserInterface/BP_XenoCore_TitleState) Lyra's own front-end shape.

Single-player by design

Several resolvers answer "the party" by taking player controller 0. That assumption is written down in one function per system (UXenoCorePartyComponent::GetPartyComponent, UXenoCoreProgressionComponent::GetPartyProgression, UXenoCoreInventoryStatics::GetPartyInventory). XenoCore does not support multiplayer or split-screen.

docs.title: One resolver per question
docs.text:
Every "where is X?" question has exactly one function that answers it, and everything else calls that function. Use these from Blueprint rather than searching for components yourself:

Question Ask Where is the party? Get Party Component Where are levels, EXP and gold? Get Party Progression Where is the bag? Get Party Inventory What is this pawn locked onto? Get Current Target (UXenoCoreTargetingStatics)

Fails silently: asking a companion's own controller

A companion is possessed by an AI controller that has none of the party components. A graph that does Get Controller → Get Component by Class on a companion gets nothing and carries on with empty data. Always use the resolvers above.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
1. The map loads its Experience. The Experience enables the XenoCore Game Feature, whose Game Feature Data adds the controller components and input contexts.
  2. Lyra's game mode spawns the bootstrap pawn from Default Pawn Data (B_XenoCore_Player). Its hero component binds its ability system and grants its ability sets.
  3. UXenoCorePartyComponent::BeginPlay either restores a save or adds each Starting Roster member, then spawns bodies for the active members around the player and hands the leader's body to the player. See Party.
  4. Each spawned body initialises its own ability system, grants its pawn data's ability sets and applies its statline at its level. See Characters.
  5. Subsystems register their message listeners at world begin play and react from then on.

docs.title: Change signals are messages
docs.text:
Lyra's own inventory and equipment change messages are sent only from replication callbacks, so in a single-player game they never fire. XenoCore broadcasts its own on the Gameplay Message Subsystem. Each has exactly one broadcaster, and every change goes through that broadcaster. The one safety net is the inventory watcher, which announces bag changes made around the statics.

Channel Sent by Carries XenoCore.Party.Message.Changed Party component "Something changed" plus the active count. Re-read the component. XenoCore.Progression.Message.Changed Progression component Levelled count and the EXP just awarded. XenoCore.Progression.Message.LevelUp Progression component Every member who levelled, with before and after levels. XenoCore.Inventory.Message.Changed UXenoCoreInventoryStatics (and UXenoCoreInventoryWatchSubsystem for changes made around it) Bag changed. XenoCore.Equipment.Message.SlotChanged Equipment component A slot changed. XenoCore.Targeting.Message.TargetChanged Target-mode ability Old and new target. XenoCore.Battle.Message.Notification Battle notify subsystem Text, colour and target for a battle line. XenoCore.Enemy.Message.Defeated Enemy character An enemy died. XenoCore.Battle.Message.Won Battle victory subsystem A battle was won (not fled). XenoCore.Party.Message.TacticChanged Party component A party tactic changed. XenoCore.Loot.Message.ChestOpened Treasure chest A chest was opened. XenoCore.Quest.Message.Changed, .TurnedIn Quest component Quest state; turn-in carries the payout.

The full list and payloads are in Events you can listen to.

Changing the bag directly

Every bag change goes through UXenoCoreInventoryStatics. A change made by calling Lyra's inventory component yourself is caught by UXenoCoreInventoryWatchSubsystem, which sends XenoCore.Inventory.Message.Changed for it a frame later, so menus stay current. It cannot undo one, though: Lyra's Remove Item Instance will remove an item a character is wearing, and the save then loses it. See Items and inventory.

docs.title: Extending it
docs.text:
The rule: never edit Lyra. Subclass it, add a component, or add a row of data. Lyra's files are the host; if you change them, a Lyra update overwrites your work, and XenoCore's behaviour may change under you.

  • To change a XenoCore system's numbers, edit the Blueprint subclass that holds them (BP_XenoCore_Party, BP_XenoCore_Progression, BP_XenoCoreDamageExecution) or, better, make a child Blueprint of it in Content/MyGame/ and point the Game Feature Data at your child.
  • To change behaviour in C++, subclass the XenoCore class and override its virtuals. See Subclass a mechanic.
  • To add a new system, give it the same shape: party-wide state on a controller component with a static resolver, per-character state on the pawn's ability system, presentation in a world subsystem that listens to a message.

Every public class and struct in XenoCoreRuntime is exported (XENOCORERUNTIME_API), so a C++ subclass in your own module links, including the characters, both AI controllers, the stat set, the damage execution and the equipment component. Only some of Lyra's classes are not exported; see Subclass a mechanic.

docs.title: Extension points
docs.text:
These are the places built for your additions. Each needs no edit to a XenoCore asset or source file.

To add Use Recipe A menu entry, or a different menu button Menu Entries or a XenoCoreMenuEntrySet in Project Settings › Game › XenoCore UI Add a menu screen A replacement for a screen or HUD widget C++ opens The matching XenoCore UI or XenoCore Content setting Restyle the menus A widget on the HUD An Add Widgets action on a HUD.Slot.XenoCore.* slot Add a HUD element Something the player presses A on A Blueprint child of AXenoCoreInteractableActor Add an interactable object Saved state for your own system A XenoCore Save Participant component, or the interface Make a system save A yes/no question in a screen The Ask Confirm node Add a confirmation popup An input action for every playable character One row in Game/AbilitySet_XenoCore_Input Add an input action with a prompt An equipment stat One modifier row on Inventory/GE_XenoCore_EquipmentStats Add an equipment stat New behaviour in C++ A subclass in your own module Subclass a mechanic

XenoCore needs no edits to Lyra

Where XenoCore needs Lyra content to behave differently, it ships its own copy instead of changing Lyra's: the damage-number cue is GameplayCues/GCNL_XenoCore_DamageTaken (fired by GE_XenoCore_Damage; Lyra's GCNL_Character_DamageTaken is untouched), and keyboard key icons are added at startup from Project Settings › Game › XenoCore UI › HUD › Keyboard Key Icons. A fresh download of Lyra therefore needs nothing re-applied.

docs.title: Why it's built this way
docs.text:
• Pawn-hosted ability systems. Lyra keeps a player's ability system on the player state, which would mean every party member shares one identity or needs its own player state. XenoCore uses Lyra's own ALyraCharacterWithAbilities shape (the one Epic's damageable test dummy uses), so a character's stats, arts and effects travel with its body. Switching leader is only possession.
  • Controller components for the party. The same place Lyra's quick bar and item-cost code look. It survives pawn changes and is reachable from anything with a world.
  • Subsystems for presentation. A notification is about the battle, not a pawn, so it has no business being a component on every character.
  • Own messages. Lyra's change messages rely on replication. XenoCore's fire in standalone play, and each has one sender, so a listener never has to guess which of several paths changed something.

docs.title: Arts
docs.text:
All · 15 min read · No code

The Arts screen: a character's Arts, their levels and details.

An Art is a special move a character picks from the combat palette. Every Art is described by one data asset, an Art definition (UXenoCoreArtDefinition), and runs as a shared Gameplay Ability (UXenoCoreGameplayAbility_Art) that reads everything it needs from that asset. Which Arts a character knows, which ones sit on their palette and how far each is levelled are stored per character on the party's progression component. The one idea that makes the rest make sense: an Art is data. A standard Art needs no Blueprint and no code; you only write a Blueprint when an Art needs behaviour the shared ability does not have.

See the Glossary for Art, Talent Art, palette and Break.

At a glance

In play: each character has a bar of Arts beside the Talent Art in the centre; pick one with the D-pad, it plays, lands its damage and effects, and greys out for its cooldown.

What you can change, no code:

  • A new Art: Your first art, Create an attack art, Create a healing or support art
  • What it inflicts: Make an art inflict reactions
  • Who learns it, when, and where it sits on the bar: Palette slots
  • A Talent Art: Create a Talent Art
  • When companions and enemies use it: Tune companion AI
  • Every setting: What you can change

docs.title: How it fits together
docs.text:
Piece Class / sample asset Job Art definition UXenoCoreArtDefinition · Battle/Arts/DA_XenoCore_AirSlash Name, power, cooldown, range, area, effects, montage, palette look Talent Art definition UXenoCoreTalentArtDefinition · Battle/Arts/DA_XenoCore_TurnStrike An Art definition plus a Gauge Cost Shared Art ability UXenoCoreGameplayAbility_Art · Battle/Arts/GA_XenoCore_Art_Base Range check, montage, impact timing, effects, cooldown, movement lock Talent Art ability UXenoCoreGameplayAbility_TalentArt · Battle/Arts/GA_XenoCore_TurnStrike Same, but paid from the Talent gauge instead of a cooldown Per-Art ability (optional) GA_XenoCore_BackSlash, GA_XenoCore_LightHeal Children of GA_XenoCore_Art_Base, carrying only their Art Data and their Ability.XenoCore.Art.* tag. Only for Arts that need their own ability; everything else runs as the base Shared effects GE_XenoCore_ArtCooldown, GE_XenoCore_ArtEffect, GE_XenoCore_Heal One cooldown effect and one damage/heal carrier for every Art Learnset table A DataTable of FXenoCoreArtUnlock rows · Characters/Party/Learnsets/DT_XenoCore_ArtLearnset_Default, set as Art Learn Table on the character's pawn Blueprint (AXenoCoreCombatantCharacter) Which Arts a character learns, at what level, in which starting slot Loadout and levels UXenoCoreProgressionComponent · Game/BP_XenoCore_Progression Known Arts, palette slots, Art levels, Art Points (AP) Palette (HUD) UXenoCoreArtsPaletteBase · UserInterface/HUD/W_XenoCore_ArtSlot Draws the Arts, greys unusable ones, shows cooldown rings and the Talent gauge Palette input GA_XenoCore_PaletteUp/Down/Left/Right/Confirm (UXenoCoreGameplayAbility_PaletteCycle) Move the selection, confirm the selected Art Arts menu UXenoCoreArtsScreenBase · UserInterface/Arts/W_XenoCore_ArtsScreen Arrange the palette (Setting tab) and spend AP (Level Up tab), switched with ZL / ZR

The player's palette and the companion AI fire an Art the same way, so a companion's Art obeys exactly the player's range, cooldown and costs.

For programmers: how a press becomes a hit
  • The palette input abilities never activate an Art themselves. They move or confirm the selection, and the target-mode ability turns the selected entry into an activation.
  • The palette and the companion AI both fire an Art through one function, Fire Art (UXenoCoreGameplayAbility_Art::FireArt).
  • The progression component grants each palette Art to the pawn as an ability spec whose source object is the Art definition. That is how many Arts share one ability class and are still told apart.
  • The ability class used is, in order: the definition's Ability Class, else whatever class is already granting that Art, else the progression component's Default Art Ability Class (GA_XenoCore_Art_Base).

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
Learning. Each character's pawn Blueprint points at a learnset: a DataTable whose rows are FXenoCoreArtUnlock, set as Art Learn Table. When a character's record is created, and again when they level up, every row at or below their level is learned. Rows are read sorted by Unlock Level, so their order in the table does not matter. The first time, each row's Default Slot places it on the palette; -1 means learned but not placed. An unset or empty Art Learn Table means "keep whatever the character's ability sets grant", which is how enemies and unauthored pawns behave.

A row's Art is a soft reference: reading the table does not load the Arts in it. An Art (its montage, effects and VFX) loads when the character learns it, at spawn or level-up, so Arts a character is still levels away from cost nothing. See Loading and ticking.

A character gets their own list by pointing at a different table. The shipped tables are in Characters/Party/Learnsets/:

Table Used by Arts (level learnt) DT_XenoCore_ArtLearnset_Default B_XenoCore_PartyMember_Base and the colour variants that do not set their own Back Slash, Light Heal, Air Slash (1) DT_XenoCore_ArtLearnset_Kael Kael (B_XenoCore_Party_VRoid_L) Back Slash, Light Heal, Air Slash, Stream Edge (1); War Swing (2) DT_XenoCore_ArtLearnset_Mira Mira (B_XenoCore_Party_VRoid_K), B_XenoCore_Party_Maroon Back Slash, Light Heal, Air Slash, Shield Bash, Wild Down (1) DT_XenoCore_ArtLearnset_Nia Nia (B_XenoCore_Party_VRoid_S), B_XenoCore_Party_Cyan Back Slash, Light Heal, Air Slash (1) DT_XenoCore_ArtLearnset_Dorran Dorran (B_XenoCore_Party_VRoid_C), B_XenoCore_Party_Lime Back Slash, Light Heal, Air Slash (1) DT_XenoCore_ArtLearnset_Isolde Isolde (B_XenoCore_Party_VRoid_M), B_XenoCore_Party_Purple Ember Ring, Ether Ward, Frost Lance (1); Mind Sap (3) DT_XenoCore_ArtLearnset_Sabine Sabine (B_XenoCore_Party_VRoid_Q), B_XenoCore_Party_Yellow Bellow, Hamstring, Venom Edge (1); Wild Down (2) DT_XenoCore_ArtLearnset_Tamsin Tamsin (B_XenoCore_Party_VRoid_Y), B_XenoCore_Party_Pink Bolster, Light Heal, Mending Wave (1); Slit Edge (2); Renewal (3)

Open a table to see each row's Default Slot. Which character learns what, and when, is your project's call; the shipped tables are a starting point.

When a level-up teaches an Art, the level-up banner (W_XenoCore_LevelUp) adds a line New Art indented under the character who learned it, benched characters included. Arts get no floating text over heads: the whole party levels at once, so it would be noise. (A learnt skill does float.) The data rides on the level-up message as FXenoCoreLevelUpEntry's Arts Learned.

One example member gets Arts another way

The colour example PartyMember_Blue (not in the sample cast) uses B_XenoCore_Player as its pawn, which is not built on the party base and has no Art Learn Table. Its Arts come from AbilitySet_XenoCore_Hero.

Slotting. Slots are numbered in unlock order, not screen position, and the bar fills from the centre out: slot 0 sits immediately left of the Talent Art, slot 1 immediately right, slot 2 next left, slot 3 next right, and so on outward. The Arts menu strip and the battle palette both draw it this way. Default Slot and Art Slot Unlock Levels both count in this order, so the further a slot is from the centre, the later it opens. The Arts menu shows no slot numbers: a list row reads Equipped for an Art on the bar, an empty strip slot is Empty Slot, and a locked one is Locked Slot, whose detail line says This slot opens at level N.

Setting a palette slot (from the Arts menu, or the XenoSetArt console command) re-grants the live pawn's Arts at once, so the HUD changes with no extra wiring. The Talent Art is never on the palette row: it is granted by the equipped weapon's ability set (each sample member's sword has its own set, for example Weapons/GreatSword/AbilitySet_XenoCore_JunkSword grants GA_XenoCore_TurnStrike; the per-sword Talent Arts are children of Battle/Arts/GA_XenoCore_TalentArt_Base) and sits in the palette's centre slot during battle. The centre slot shows whichever Talent Art the character was granted, with that Art's own name, description and icon; the entry authored on the palette widget is only a fallback for a character with none.

Activation. When an Art is used, the shared ability:

  1. Refuses if the target is outside the Art's Distance. This is a backstop: when the player picks an Art out of reach, target mode first runs the character in and uses it on arrival, so range never greys an Art on the palette.
  2. Commits, which puts the Art on cooldown. An Art that is interrupted or misses still cools down.
  3. Cancels the auto-attack, so the Art cuts into the swing instead of queueing behind it. This happens only once the commit succeeds, so an Art that cannot be paid for leaves the swing alone. After the Art the auto-attack starts again from its first swing.
  4. Plays the definition's Montage at Montage Play Rate, first turning the character to face the target over a short time.
  5. At Impact Fraction of the montage's length, applies the Art: its power as damage or healing, then each Effects entry whose condition is met. A damage Art aimed at enemies first makes the same contact roll as the auto-attack, for each hit and each target: it can miss (no damage, no effects on that target) or be blocked. A blocked Art does no Topple, and the attacker's recoil ends the Art, so its remaining hits never land. Ether Arts can miss well-levelled enemies but are never blocked. See Blocks and dodges.
  6. Ends when the montage completes, is interrupted or is cancelled. A failsafe ends it shortly after the montage's expected length if nothing else does.

While an Art runs, the character carries Status.XenoCore.ArtExecuting (every other Art is blocked and shows as disabled on the palette) and Gameplay.MovementStopped (the character cannot walk or turn). Both are removed on every way the Art can end.

Cooldown. One shared effect, GE_XenoCore_ArtCooldown, is applied with the Art's own Cooldown Duration and its own Cooldown Tag. The palette ring reads that tag. The effect comes from the art ability's Default Cooldown Effect Class (ships as GE_XenoCore_ArtCooldown), used whenever the ability's own Cooldown Gameplay Effect Class is unset, so data-only Arts and Blueprint Arts both cool down with nothing to set.

Talent Arts. A Talent Art has a Cooldown Duration of 0 and costs gauge instead. The gauge (TalentGauge, 0 to 100) fills by the character's TalentChargePerHit each time an auto-attack lands, through GE_XenoCore_TalentCharge. The centre slot lights once the gauge covers the Art's Gauge Cost, the same test the ability uses. The gauge is spent when the Art activates, so a Talent Art that misses still costs its gauge. Nothing resets the gauge after a fight, but it lives on the character's body, so a benched member or a party wipe starts again from empty.

Levelling. Each character banks Art Points from kills (Art Points Base + Art Points Per Enemy Level × the enemy's level, times the level-difference reward multiplier; quests pay none). See Progression. Spending AP raises an Art one level, up to its cap. Every Power, Cooldown Duration and Effects curve reads the Art's level. Talent Arts cannot be levelled.

Default 100

Every effect field takes a Niagara system or an older Cascade particle system, so effects from Epic's sample projects and Paragon work as they are. An empty field keeps the shared look every Art has: the damage sparks and number, the montage's own trail, the shared hit shake.

See an area as you tune it

Type XenoCore.Arts.DrawArea 1 in the console during play. Each Art draws its circle or cone at the moment it lands, puts a green sphere on every enemy it reached, and labels the count. XenoCore.Arts.DrawArea 0 turns it off; it is off by default and never appears in a shipped build. XenoCore.Arts.DrawAreaSeconds sets how long each drawing stays.

Fails silently: a looping effect in an Art's FX field

An Art spawns a new effect every use and never destroys it, so a looping system piles up for the rest of the session. Use one-shot (burst) systems in Cast FX, Impact FX and Area FX.

Fails silently: a custom Hit Camera Shake has no rumble

Hit Camera Shake replaces the shared hit cue, and the controller rumble lives on that cue. An Art with its own shake does not rumble.

Impact Event Tag on a montage without the notify

The Art still lands one hit, when the montage ends, and the Output Log warns that the montage never sent the event. Add an XenoCore Gameplay Event notify with that tag on the contact frame.

Statuses (the Effects list), and User or Whole party entries, land on the first hit of a multi-hit Art only; damage, numbers and impact effects land on every hit. If an enemy blocks a hit, the attacker recoils and the Art ends there, so its remaining hits never land.

For a montage that should always slow time wherever it plays, put the XenoCore Time Dilation notify state on it instead of setting Time Dilation on each Art. Arts often share a montage, so a notify there slows every Art that uses it.

Each Effects entry has Effect (a GE_XenoCore_Status_* or GE_XenoCore_Reaction_*), Chance (0 to 1), Duration and Magnitude (curves keyed by Art level, sent to the status), Condition (Always, In the art's position, From the side, From behind, From the front, Target is Broken, Target is Toppled, Target is Dazed), Recipient (Each target, User, Whole party) and Announce Chance. Conditions are judged on the target as it was before this hit, so one Art cannot Break and then Topple with the same press.

Two Arts sharing a Cooldown Tag share one cooldown

Using either Art puts both on cooldown. An Art with a cooldown but no Cooldown Tag cools down invisibly: the palette shows it ready while it refuses to fire. The editor checks both when you save an Art definition (or run Validate Assets): a missing tag on an Art that cools down at any level is an error, and a tag another Art definition also uses is an error naming the other Arts. The shared-tag check runs in the editor only, so an Art never saved or validated there can still slip through.

Fails silently: Power or a status Duration left at 0

Power multiplies its curve, so a Value of 0 deals nothing whatever the curve says. A status whose duration comes from the Art lasts zero seconds if the entry's Duration is 0. Data validation reports the second case on save.

What saving an Art definition checks

Problem Reported as Empty Display Name Error A cooldown at any level, but no Cooldown Tag Error A Cooldown Tag another Art definition also uses Error (editor validator) A status entry whose duration comes from the Art, with Duration 0 Error No Montage: the Art plays no animation, its effect lands at once and it ends Warning No Palette Glyph Warning A heal aimed at an Enemy Warning

Fails silently: a montage on the wrong slot

An Art montage must play on a slot in the DefaultGroup slot group. On another group it blends wrongly with no error.

docs.title: On the character
docs.text:
Art Learn Table (Class Defaults › XenoCore › Arts) on the pawn Blueprint, beside Skill Tree: a DataTable whose row structure is XenoCoreArtUnlock (the picker offers no other kind). Each row has Art (loads when learnt), Unlock Level (1 or more) and Default Slot (0 to 7 in unlock order, or -1 for learned but unslotted). The row name is free text; Lv01_BackSlash is the convention because it sorts in the editor. Learnsets can be CSV-imported like any DataTable.

To give a character their own list, create a DataTable with row structure XenoCoreArtUnlock, or duplicate DT_XenoCore_ArtLearnset_Default (a table, not a concrete Art, so duplicating it is fine), then set that character's Art Learn Table.

docs.title: On the Talent Art ability
docs.text: Talent Gauge Effect (XenoCore › Talent). Slow motion is no longer set here: it is the Time Dilation group on the Art definition, so any Art can use it.

docs.title: Extending it
docs.text:
• A new standard Art: create it blank in your own folder (Content/MyGame/Arts): right-click › Data › Data Asset › XenoCoreArtDefinition. Fill in the fields, give it its own Cooldown Tag, and add a row for it to a character's learnset. Do not duplicate a concrete Art such as DA_XenoCore_AirSlash: the copy brings Air Slash's Break and side-Slow effects with it. DA_XenoCore_SlitEdge, DA_XenoCore_StreamEdge and DA_XenoCore_WarSwing are examples built this way. Kael learns Stream Edge (a cone) at level 1 and War Swing (a circle around him) at level 2; Tamsin learns Slit Edge at level 2. See Your first art and the recipes Attack art, Support art and Palette slots.
  • An Art with custom behaviour: create a Blueprint child of GA_XenoCore_Art_Base and point the definition's Ability Class at it. Do not override Activation Owned Tags on it: an override replaces the base's container rather than adding to it, and silently drops the lock-out and movement-stop tags.
  • A new Talent Art: create a blank XenoCoreTalentArtDefinition, make a child Blueprint of GA_XenoCore_TalentArt_Base and point its Art Data at the new definition, and grant the ability from the weapon's ability set. See Talent art.
  • Reactions and statuses an Art applies: see Reactions and statuses.
  • Never edit GA_XenoCore_Art_Base, GE_XenoCore_ArtCooldown or GE_XenoCore_ArtEffect in place: every Art in the game uses them.

docs.title: Why it's built this way
docs.text:
For programmers: the design reasons
  • One asset per Art. Arts are granted as ability specs with the definition as source object, so any number share one ability class. A per-Art Blueprint and unique ability tag is no longer needed.
  • Cooldown from the definition. The ability overrides GetCooldownTags and applies one shared effect with a SetByCaller duration and the Art's tag as a dynamic granted tag, so no per-Art cooldown asset can drift. It commits in C++, so no Art Blueprint can forget to.
  • Tags for lifetimes. The lock-out and movement stop are ActivationOwnedTags, removed by GAS on every end path, and the shared ability binds every montage end delegate (bAllowInterruptAfterBlendOut true) so an interrupted Art can never leave the character frozen.
  • Levels on the progression component, keyed by the member definition, because a benched character has no pawn and the Arts menu still has to edit them.

docs.title: Battle voices and banter
docs.text:
Designer · 12 min read · No code · Last tested: 2026-10-02

Party members speak. They shout their arts by name, call out when a fight starts, name the ally they are reviving, groan when hit, cheer a win and chat while the party travels. That is Xenoblade's pattern. With AI companions it is also a gameplay signal: you hear "Wild Down!" and know a Topple is coming without looking.

Everything here is set in the editor. The lines are rows in a Data Table, the pacing is a second Data Table, and the global feel is one Data Asset. There is no C++ per line, per character or per category.

What you can change, no code

  • What a character says, and when: Writing a character's lines
  • How often anyone speaks: Pacing: the rules table
  • Talking to a companion out of battle: Talking to an ally
  • A line for your own moment (a boss phase, a quest beat): Adding a category of your own
  • Your own recordings: Recording lines

Status, 2026-10-03

All seven characters are voiced (470 lines, two takes each, with lip-sync keys and an expression per line) and the gameplay triggers are wired: art calls, battle start, hits, downed and revive, victory, Talent ready, the Party Gauge, level up, switching leader and talking to an ally. Faces lip-sync and change expression with each line.

docs.text: Piece What it is Where it lives A character's lines Data Table, row type Xeno Core Voice Line Row One per character, e.g. Audio/Voice/Kael/DT_XenoCore_Voice_Kael, chosen in the member definition's Voice Table Pacing Data Table, row type Xeno Core Voice Rule Row Audio/Voice/DT_XenoCore_VoiceRules Global feel Data Asset Xeno Core Battle Voice Config Audio/Voice/DA_XenoCore_BattleVoiceConfig, chosen in Project Settings > XenoCore Content > Voice Volume Sound class SC_XenoCore_Dialogue Follows Lyra's Dialogue volume slider, mixed through Lyra's VoiceSubmix Left / right Attenuation ATT_XenoCore_Voice The voice is attached to the speaker's head and pans by where they stand. It stays at full volume out to 25 m, so a fight never gets quieter The player UXenoCoreBattleVoiceSubsystem Asked to Speak; decides whether the line is heard

docs.title: Writing a character's lines
docs.text:
A row is one thing a character can say:

Field Meaning Category When it is said, a XenoCore.Voice.* tag (table below) Art Only for this art. Leave empty for any art Addressee Only when speaking to this ally (revives, exchanges). Leave empty for anyone Reply After this line, the Addressee answers with a line of this category, spoken back to this character. This is how a two-person exchange is written, with no graph Takes The recordings, each with its lip-sync keys. One is picked each time, and none repeats until all have played Expression, Expression Weight The face held while the line plays: a face curve such as angry, happy, sad Subtitle What is said, shown only if subtitles are on Direction How it was recorded, e.g. [shouts]. Reference only

Which row plays. Rows with the requested category are the candidates. A row naming an Art or an Addressee only matches that art or ally, and the most specific match wins. So write one generic Art row as a fallback, then one row per art the character can use.

Arts are shared, lines are not

Light Heal is on five characters, so its call-out cannot live on the art. Each character's table has its own Art = Light Heal row in their own voice. When a character learns a new art, add a row to their table.

docs.title: Talking to an ally
docs.text:
Out of battle, stop beside a companion and the prompt reads A - Talk. They answer with a line from their Field.Talk rows, voiced and shown in the dialogue box over their head. Nothing is held: you keep walking, the camera stays yours, and the box closes itself.

Setting Where The prompt's word, or empty to make a character untalkable Talk Verb on the party member's Blueprint (Class Defaults › XenoCore › Interaction) How close to stand Interact Range, same category (110 cm, the revive range), the same field an NPC has Only when still Talk Max Leader Speed, same category (50 cm/s): the party walks bunched, so Talk is offered only once you stop What they say Field.Talk rows in their voice table; the box shows the row's Subtitle Which categories also show the box Show In Dialogue Box on the config (shipped: Field.Talk) How long the box lingers after the voice Dialogue Box Linger on the config

In battle the prompt is not offered; a downed ally offers Revive instead.

docs.title: The face
docs.text:
While a line plays, the speaker's face lip-syncs to it and shows the row's Expression. The mouth follows the take's keys (baked from the recording, so nothing is guessed at runtime) and closes the moment the voice stops, including when a more important line cuts in.

Setting Where Which expression and how strongly Expression and Expression Weight on the voice row (a VRM name: happy, angry, sad, relaxed, surprised) Lip sync on or off; mouth size; snappiness Lip Sync, Lip Sync Weight Scale and Lip Sync Blend Speed on the character's face anim Blueprint (ABP_XenoCore_VRoidRetarget_*, parent XenoCoreFaceAnimInstance)

A recording with no keys falls back to a generic mouth flap.

It also makes the next win Close Revive The reviver names the ally, then the ally answers Party Gauge A bar filling; the gauge full. The leader speaks Enemy last One engaged enemy left. The leader speaks Victory The win, after Victory Line Delay. One speaker per win, taking turns. Close if anyone was downed, or the leader is below Close Victory Health Fraction Level up Once per level-up burst Take control Switching leader Field idle, scenery, travel Every Field Banter Interval, out of battle, never during a conversation: travel while the leader moves, otherwise idle or (Field Scenery Chance) scenery Field exchange and reply On a banter tick, Field Exchange Chance of the time: one character opens to a named ally and that ally answers.
