An empty entry means no reaction from that side. These are the shared defaults; a character's Anim Profile can override any slot Profile Key Any reaction ability › XenoCore › Reaction Which row of a character's Anim Profile this reaction reads (Anim.XenoCore.Reaction.*). Empty means it always plays its own montages. Every shipped reaction has one Front Back Half Angle Any reaction ability › XenoCore › Reaction Width of the front and back sectors. Default 45 Hold Until Montage Ends, Follow Up Montage Any reaction ability › XenoCore › Reaction Keep the ability open for the montage, then crossfade into a get-up. The knock-down classes turn the hold on for you Hold While Trigger Tag Present Knock-down ability › XenoCore › Reaction Needs Hold Until Montage Ends. Hold the knock-down for as long as the triggering reaction tag lasts, not for the montage's length. On for the minion's reactions, off for the player's Flinch On Hit Hit-react ability › XenoCore › HitReact Play the flinch clip when hit. Off: no clip, the knockback still applies Flinch Suppressed By Tags Hit-react ability › XenoCore › HitReact A flinch does not play while the character holds any of these. Default: Topple, Daze Push Distance, Push Time, Push Strength Over Time Hit-react ability › XenoCore › HitReact › Push How far and how fast a hit at Force Multiplier 1 knocks this body back. Defaults 60 cm over 0.12 s. Push Distance 0 = never pushed Force Multiplier Art definition › Art › Hits, or auto-attack ability › XenoCore › Attack How hard that Art or swing knocks its target back. 0 = no knockback Incapacitated Tags Auto-attack or enemy Art ability › XenoCore › AutoAttack The attacker cannot swing or use Arts while it holds any of these. Default: Topple, Daze Status Icon Size, Status Refresh Interval Party member plate widget › XenoCore › Party › Status HUD icon size and poll rate

Fails silently: a Follow Up Montage's blend time lives on the montage

The crossfade from knock-down to get-up uses the follow-up montage asset's own Blend In time. There is no blend setting on the ability.

Fails silently: Hold Until Montage Ends off on a knock-down

Without it the ability ends on the frame it starts, so its movement lock is added and removed at once: you get a popup and no animation. The knock-down, guard, recoil and dodge classes turn it on in C++, so this only bites if a Blueprint copy turns it off, or a new reaction class forgets it. A flinch needs it off, or one hit waits on the last one's animation.

Fails silently: a knock-down cut short or left standing

With Hold While Trigger Tag Present on, the reaction ends early and without its get-up if something else takes the animation slot, such as a death montage or a Daze landing on a Topple. That is intended. It also refuses to start on a dead or dying character, so a reaction landing on the killing blow plays nothing.

Fails silently: restating Activation Blocked Tags on a hit-react child

The hit-react base blocks on ArtExecuting and Arming. A Blueprint child that sets its own Activation Blocked Tags replaces that list rather than adding to it. If you override it, list every tag, including the two from the base. GA_XenoCore_Player_HitReact does exactly this and lists all four. The same applies to Flinch Suppressed By Tags and Incapacitated Tags: setting either on a Blueprint child replaces the default Topple and Daze, and an empty list turns the rule off for that ability.

docs.title: Extending it
docs.text:
• A new status: create a Blueprint child of UXenoCoreStatusEffect in your own folder, set its duration to SetByCaller XenoCore.Status.Duration if Arts should choose the duration, add its modifiers and the four display fields. It then pops up and shows on the HUD with no registration. See Status effect.
  • Making an Art react: add a GE_XenoCore_Reaction_* entry to the Art's Effects list. See Art reactions.
  • Different clips for one character: do not duplicate the reaction ability. Fill in that character's Anim Profile instead; see Give a character its own combat animations.
  • A knock-down for a new character type: a Blueprint child of UXenoCoreGameplayAbility_ToppleReact (or _DazeReact). The trigger, the hold and the movement lock are already set; you only add clips. For an enemy, copy GA_XenoCore_Minion_Topple (and _Daze), swap its Directional Montages, and grant both in the enemy's ability set. Without them the enemy still cannot act while Toppled, but it stands still instead of falling.
  • A new kind of knock-down (for example XC1's Launch), programmers: a C++ child of UXenoCoreGameplayAbility_KnockdownReact whose constructor calls Set Trigger Tag with the new reaction tag. Never put that tag in Activation Blocked Tags: the tag is already present when the ability starts, so it would refuse itself.
  • Do not add a new reaction by applying a loose tag instead of an effect. A loose tag never expires and skips the chain requirement.

docs.title: Testing tools
docs.text:
• XenoCore.Reaction 1 / 2 / 3 applies Break, Topple or Daze to the player alone, for that effect's authored duration; XenoCore.Reaction 0 clears them. It applies the tag directly, so it deliberately skips the chain requirement to let you test each reaction on its own.
  • XenoCore.Anim.Describe (add enemy or part of a pawn's name) lists every reaction clip a character plays and whether it comes from its profile or the shared default. XenoCore.Anim.Play Topple front previews the clip alone.
  • Add enemy (XenoCore.Reaction 2 enemy) to apply it to your locked-on target instead, or to the nearest living enemy when nothing is locked. Use it to check an enemy's knock-down without waiting for the Art chain.

docs.title: Why it's built this way
docs.text:
For programmers: the design reasons
  • An effect, not a tag. A reaction applied as an effect gets a real duration and its prerequisite for free from the effect's tag-requirement component; a loose tag was permanent and let Daze land on a target that had never been Broken.
  • Watch the tag, not the source. The popups, the player's reactions and the face all listen for the tag appearing on an ASC, so an Art, a status, a script or the console command all behave the same and nothing can apply a reaction silently.
  • Status presentation on the effect. UXenoCoreStatusEffect adds only the four fields a Gameplay Effect has no home for, so there is no separate list of statuses to keep in step.
  • The victim decides the flinch. The attacker only sends an event; direction is computed from the victim's facing, and the victim's own blocked tags decide whether it reacts.

docs.title: Save and front end
docs.text:
All · 15 min read · No code

What the player sees: boot cards, then a title screen with Continue, New Game, Load Game, Settings and Quit. In game, the menu's Save and Load open a list of four slots (an autosave and three manual slots), each with a thumbnail, the leader, the party's portraits, the place and the play time. Glowing save points autosave when the leader steps on them, and a load brings the party back exactly as it was, where it was.

A save captures the party, the bag, gold, quests, the leader's position, every unopened treasure chest on every map visited, and the records of any save participants (your own systems that store their state). The idea that makes the rest make sense: a load always starts a fresh world. XenoCore never undoes the current world in place; it opens the map again and restores the party into it.

docs.title: What you can change
docs.text:
• Make your own Blueprint remember something (a door that stays open): Make a system save.
  • Where New Game starts, and the boot cards: the title screen and BP_XenoCore_TitleState (see Settings).
  • Where save points are: place Game/BP_XenoCore_SavePoint in a level.
  • The place name a save shows for your map: Location Names in Project Settings › Game › XenoCore Save (do this for every new map; see the warning below).
  • How the save screen looks: duplicate it and point XenoCore UI › Save Screen at your copy.

docs.title: How it fits together
docs.text: Piece Kind Job Save system Built in, alive from launch to quit (title screen included) Slots, writing, loading, autosave, play time, the slot thumbnail. Reach it in a Blueprint with Get Game Instance Subsystem › Xeno Core Save Subsystem Game/BP_XenoCore_SavePoint Actor A pad that autosaves when the player stands on it UserInterface/W_XenoCore_SaveScreen Screen, set by XenoCore UI › Save Screen The slot list, in Save or Load mode XenoCore Save Participant Blueprint interface and actor component (same name in the editor) Let any actor, component or object store its own record in the save, under its own key UserInterface/W_XenoCore_SaveRow Row widget One slot: thumbnail, leader, portraits, location, play time, date UserInterface/HUD/W_XenoCore_AutosaveBadge HUD plate "Autosaving..." while an autosave writes Maps/L_XenoCore_FrontEnd Map The front end. The project's default map and the editor's startup map Experiences/B_XenoCore_FrontEnd_Experience Experience Adds BP_XenoCore_TitleState to the game state UserInterface/BP_XenoCore_TitleState Game state component Plays the boot screens, then pushes the title screen UserInterface/Boot/W_XenoCore_Boot_Studio, _Unreal, _Autosave, _Shaders Boot cards The pre-title sequence UserInterface/W_XenoCore_TitleScreen Screen Continue, New Game, Load Game, Settings, Quit UserInterface/Boot/W_XenoCore_LoadingScreen Widget The loading screen, set in Project Settings › Common Loading Screen

docs.title: What is saved
docs.text:
Saved Details Gold The party's purse The bag One entry per item, as the item definition's class path, with the gems in its sockets (each gem by path, with its rolled strength) Every character, active or reserve Level, experience toward next level, active slot, health as a fraction of max, equipment by slot, known Arts with level and cap, the Arts palette, Art Points, skill-tree progress (selected branch, and per branch: unlocked, skills learnt, SP into the next). See Skills Party shape The leader's slot and the maximum active party size Party tactics The party's orders and each member's own orders, by name. See Party tactics Quests Each quest's status, objective counts and recorded requester, and the tracked quest Position The leader's transform. The party re-forms around the leader Treasure chests For every map visited: each unopened enemy-dropped chest (class, position, drop table, tier), each hand-placed chest that has been emptied, and any chest still holding items the bag had no room for. See Loot Slot header Leader name and level, active members, location and chapter text, play time, save time, map, thumbnail Time, weather, tutorials The clock, the weather roll and which tutorial cards have been seen. These are XenoCore's own save participants Save participants One record per participant key: that participant's SaveGame-flagged variables (or whatever its C++ writes), plus its own data version. Records whose participant is absent this session are carried over, not dropped

Not saved: the rest of the world. Collectable orbs and enemies are back as the map authors them after every load, because a load reopens the map. Chests are the one exception: they are respawned from the file when their map begins play. Per-item state is not saved, apart from gem sockets; items are rebuilt from their definitions, which is exact today because nothing else changes an item after it is created. See the warning under Settings.

Every reference in the file is a path, and every enum is stored by name, not by number. An asset that no longer exists is skipped with a warning rather than crashing the load.

Older save files keep loading after a template update. A file written before a feature existed simply lacks its data: no participant records reads as "nothing saved yet", no tactics loads the Default Tactics, and no gems leaves every socket empty.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
Boot. The project opens L_XenoCore_FrontEnd. Its Experience adds BP_XenoCore_TitleState, which waits for Lyra's loading screen to lift, then shows each boot card in its Boot Screens list: fade in, hold, fade out. A, B, Escape or a click skips a card (it still fades). The shader card only appears if shaders are still compiling. The sequence plays once per launch; returning to the title goes straight to the title. The world behind stays black and silent until the title appears.

Title screen.

  • Continue loads the newest loadable file, autosave included. It is disabled when there are no saves.
  • New Game tells the subsystem a new game is starting, then opens New Game Map (L_XenoCore_GaurPlain).
  • Load Game opens the save screen in Load mode.
  • Settings pushes Lyra's settings screen.
  • Quit quits.

The title screen keeps the world running behind it, so the scene animates.

Saving. From the in-game menu, Save opens the save screen in Save mode. The autosave row is listed but cannot be saved over. Saving is refused while any enemy is engaged in a fight: picking a slot then shows Lyra's message box, Save / You cannot save right now., with an OK button. Writes are asynchronous; the screen's "do not turn off the power" notice lasts exactly as long as the write.

Autosave. A save point autosaves when the player (not a following party member) steps on it. If a fight refuses the save, it keeps retrying every Retry Interval while the player stands there. The HUD's autosave badge shows while the write runs. Save points are the only autosave trigger in the template.

Loading. The save system keeps the file, travels to its map (even the current one), and restores in a fixed order as the world comes up: levels and experience first (so members spawn at their saved level), then quests, then the bag, then the roster. Each character's equipment and health are restored as that character's body is created. While restoring, the usual new-game seeding (starting roster, starting items, starting equipment) stands down, or the party would arrive holding two of everything. The leader is placed once the leader's final body exists.

The loading screen stays up until the world is fit to be seen, not just loaded: the party's bodies exist and are posed, the save is restored, and the world has gone quiet (no shaders, assets or grass still being built) for a few rendered frames. That is what stops T-posed characters and pop-in on the first frame. It holds the first reveal of a map only; after it lifts, nothing brings it back until the next map. If the world never goes quiet it gives up after a timeout and logs a warning. The timings have no Project Settings page; see the last rows of Settings.

Save participants restore last, after all of the above, so a participant that reads the party or the bag sees the loaded state. The save system then fires On Save Loaded with the slot index (Get Loaded Slot Index returns it afterwards). A participant that registers later (an actor streaming in) gets its record the moment it registers, and one that unregisters (streams out, or its level is left) has its current state recorded first, so it comes back as it was.

Which participants are saved. Without registering: the player controller, the player state, the game state, and every component on them, if they implement the interface. Anything else: actors with a XenoCore Save Participant component, and objects passed to Register Save Participant. Each is stored under a key: its own Save Key or Get Save Participant Key if set; otherwise map plus actor name for a placed actor, or the class name for anything else.

Deleting. On the Load screen, a slot that holds a file offers Delete in the footer. It asks for confirmation in a popup over the screen before the file goes. The autosave can be deleted this way too.

Leaving. Return to Title and Quit in the in-game menu ask for confirmation only when something has been played since the last save, autosave or load. Return to Title opens the project's default map.

The slot thumbnail is captured when the in-game menu opens, before the menu is drawn. A save written later uses that picture.

The slot's location and chapter. A save row names the map it was written on, from Location Names in Project Settings › Game › XenoCore Save, and prints Default Story Text as its chapter line. A map with no entry prints no location, and the row draws cleanly without it. Calling Set Location Text on the save system overrides the name for the current map only (for a region inside a large map); the override lapses once the party is on another map. Set Story Text replaces the chapter line until it is called again with an empty string.

Respawn after defeat. Stepping on a save point also records it as the party's respawn point, which a party wipe returns to. This happens on every visit, even when the pad does not save again.

Console commands (development builds): XenoSave <slot>, XenoLoad <slot>, XenoSaveDump, and XenoCore.Boot.ForceShaderScreen 1 to preview the shader card. The command-line switch -XenoCoreSkipBoot skips the boot cards. See Console commands.

Fails silently: your map's saves show no location

Location Names only lists the sample maps. A save written on a map of yours prints an empty location until you add an entry for it in Project Settings › Game › XenoCore Save. Nothing is logged. Add the entry when you create the map.

Adding per-item state breaks saving

If you give items state of their own (durability, charges), the save does not know about it and loaded items come back fresh. Items are not save participants: saving that state needs a programmer to extend the save file.

Fails silently: two participants on one key

Every copy of a spawned actor gets the same derived key (its class). Only one is saved; the rest log an error (duplicate save participant key). Give each copy its own Save Key.

A save key is forever

Records are matched by key. Renaming a key, or re-placing a level actor whose key comes from its name, leaves old saves holding a record nobody claims, and the actor starts with its defaults.

Never renumber the save version

This is for whoever extends the save file in C++. Save format versions (EXenoCoreSaveVersion) are appended, never renumbered: a shipped version number is sitting in a player's save file. A participant's own Get Save Data Version follows the same rule.

docs.title: Extending it
docs.text:
• More or different boot cards: duplicate a card from UserInterface/Boot/ into your folder, change it, and add it to Boot Screens. A movie card takes a Movie.
  • A different first map: set New Game Map on your copy of the title screen and point Title Screen Class at it.
  • More save points: place BP_XenoCore_SavePoint. Set its mesh on a child Blueprint to restyle it.
  • Saving your own data (for example a door that stays open): tick SaveGame on the variables and add a XenoCore Save Participant component, or implement the interface on a controller component. No C++, and no change to XenoCore's file version: each participant carries its own Get Save Data Version and migrates in On Save Data Restored. See Make a system save.
  • React to any load: bind On Save Loaded on the save system. It fires once the whole load, participants included, is applied.
  • A different save screen: duplicate W_XenoCore_SaveScreen and set XenoCore UI › Save Screen. The menu's Save and Load entries and the title screen open whatever it names.
  • Save from a Blueprint: call Save To Slot or Request Autosave on the save system. Both return false when saving is refused.
For programmers: classes

UXenoCoreSaveSubsystem (game-instance subsystem) owns slots, writes and loads. The file is UXenoCoreSaveGame (a ULocalPlayerSaveGame) with a header and a body; its format version is EXenoCoreSaveVersion (InitialRelease = 1, WorldChests = 2, ParticipantData = 3, PartyTactics = 4, Gems = 5). Participants implement IXenoCoreSaveParticipant or carry UXenoCoreSaveParticipantComponent; C++ may override CaptureSaveData / RestoreSaveData. Screens and widgets derive from UXenoCoreSaveScreenBase, UXenoCoreSaveRowBase, UXenoCoreAutosaveBadgeBase, UXenoCoreTitleScreenBase, UXenoCoreBootScreenBase and UXenoCoreLoadingScreenBase; the front end's state is UXenoCoreTitleStateComponent; save points are AXenoCoreSavePoint. The loading-screen hold is UXenoCoreWorldReadySubsystem.

docs.title: Why it's built this way
docs.text:
For programmers
  • A game-instance subsystem. Loading travels to a map, and a world subsystem would be destroyed halfway through its own job. It is also alive on the title screen, which is what lets Continue and Load work there.
  • Epic's ULocalPlayerSaveGame. It brings the data version, pre-save and post-load hooks, and async writes. It writes the version at save time, which avoids a known sample bug where a version set in a constructor is never serialized.
  • Header and body split. The save list loads every file it shows. A body that fails to migrate still leaves a row the player can see and overwrite, instead of an empty list that looks like lost saves. A file from a newer build shows its row but refuses to load.
  • Participants rather than a list. XenoCore's own systems are captured by name, in a fixed order. A buyer's system is not in that list and should not have to be: it writes an opaque, versioned record under its own key, so the file format never changes when a system is added.
  • A fresh world on load. Resetting every orb and enemy for free means no code has to undo world state in place. Chests are the exception because unopened chests are meant to wait for the player; the save stores what each chest will roll from, never its items, so a reload does not let the player see a chest's contents in advance.
  • Health as a fraction. Max health depends on level and gear, both restored after health is read, so saved points could exceed the new maximum.
  • The front end is Lyra's pattern. Lyra's own front end puts a state component on the game state through its Experience; XenoCore's does the same with its own component, so the title map itself stays empty.

Next: UI shell and HUD · Events you can listen to

docs.title: Shops and trade
docs.text:
All · 12 min read · No code

There are two ways to get items from an NPC. A shop sells for gold and buys almost anything back. A trade is a barter: the NPC hands over one item for one of yours that is worth at least as much. Each is a data asset (a shop table or trade table) set on a placed NPC, opened by a node in that NPC's On Interact graph. Neither has any state of its own: stock never runs out, so the party bag and the party's gold are the only things that change. The idea that makes the rest make sense: every price comes from one number on the item, its Sell Value, and each system applies its own multiplier to it.

docs.title: What you can change
docs.text:
• A shopkeeper and what they sell: Open a shop.
  • A trader and what they offer: Set up a trade.
  • An item's price: its Sell Value (on the item), or Price Override on one row of a table.
  • The screens' wording and look: their Blueprints' class defaults (see Settings).

docs.title: How it fits together
docs.text:
Piece Kind Job Shop/DA_XenoCore_Shop_Colony9 Shop table (data asset) The Gym sample shop's stock: seven pieces of equipment Shop/DA_XenoCore_Shop_KamosOutpost Shop table The Gaur Plain shop at Kamos Outpost, which also sells rank I gems Trade/DA_XenoCore_Trade_Colony9 Trade table (data asset) The sample trader's offers and overtrade bonus Open Shop Blueprint node Opens the shop, continues on Transacted or Nothing Changed Open Trade Blueprint node Opens the barter screen, continues on Traded or Cancelled UserInterface/HUD/W_XenoCore_ShopScreen Screen Buy / Sell / Quit, lists, quantity confirm, "equip now?" UserInterface/HUD/W_XenoCore_TradeScreen Screen Their item, your item, confirm UserInterface/W_XenoCore_TradeRow Row widget One list row on either screen Shop and trade nodes Blueprint nodes (XenoCore › Shop, XenoCore › Trade) Prices, what may be bought, sold or offered, and the buy and sell actions

Both screens are pushed onto the menu layer, so the world pauses while they are open. The NPCs using the Colony 9 tables are placed in Maps/L_XenoCore_Gym; the Kamos Outpost shopkeeper is in Maps/L_XenoCore_GaurPlain.

Stock loads when the screen opens. Every Item in a shop or trade table (offers and the overtrade bonus) is a soft reference, so a placed shopkeeper does not load its stock, with its weapon meshes and abilities, along with the map. The shop and trade screens load the table's items as they open. See Loading and ticking.

Where gold lives. The party's gold is held by the progression component (Game/BP_XenoCore_Progression, on the player controller). See Progression.

docs.title: A shop
docs.text:
A shopkeeper talks first. There is no "Shop" verb on the prompt. The NPC's On Interact graph plays its dialogue, then checks Can Shop, and if the NPC has a Shop Table it runs Open Shop with Get Shop Table and the NPC itself:

  1. The player chooses Buy, Sell or Quit.
  2. Buy lists the table's items in tabs (equipment split by slot). Choosing one opens a quantity confirm showing the total and the player's gold. The most you can buy is the smallest of: what your gold covers, the room left under the item's Max Carried, and 99.
  3. Buying takes the gold first, then adds the items. Anything that did not fit is refunded.
  4. After buying equipment, the shop asks whether to equip it now, on a character you pick.
  5. Sell lists your bag. Worn copies cannot be sold ("You cannot sell weapons that are in use"). Key items never appear.
  6. The list stays open after each purchase or sale, with the numbers updated in place.
  7. Leaving fires Transacted if anything was bought or sold, otherwise Nothing Changed.

docs.title: A trade
docs.text:
A trader is any NPC with Trade Offers set. That adds a Trade verb on X to the prompt. The NPC's graph checks Is Trade Verb and runs Open Trade with Get Trade Offers:

  1. The player picks what they want from the NPC's list first.
  2. Then what they give from their own bag. Only Materials and Collectables can be offered.
  3. The trade clears when the offered item's value is at least the wanted item's price. If it is also at least the price plus the table's bonus value, the NPC throws in the Overtrade Bonus item too, and the screen says so before you confirm.
  4. One item for one item. The NPC never runs out; a second copy is a second trade.
  5. Leaving fires Traded if at least one exchange happened, otherwise Cancelled.

Both nodes hide the interaction prompt and the dialogue box while the screen is up and restore them afterwards. Neither closes the conversation: the graph usually has a line to say after.

docs.title: Prices
docs.text:
Price Rule Shop buy price Sell Value × 10, or the row's Price Override Shop sell price Sell Value × 1, rounded down once Trade value of Materials Sell Value × 1 Trade value of everything else Sell Value × 10 A trade row's price the item's trade value, or the row's Price Override The overtrade threshold row price + the bonus item's trade value (or its Value Override)

Sell Value and Max Carried are on the item's XenoCoreFragment_ItemCategory fragment. See Items and inventory.

Materials cannot be bought from a shop, and Key items cannot be sold. The shop table's data validation refuses stocking either.

Rarity does not change any price. Xenoblade 3 makes value independent of rarity. The sort cycle (Y) adds Rarity, which lists the rarest first and then A–Z, beside Most Recent, Name and Value. Names are drawn in their rarity colour; see Set and style item rarity.

Trading at ten times a collectable's sell value is deliberate: it makes items picked up while exploring worth more in barter than in the shop.

The multipliers are fixed

The ×10 buy price, the ×1 and ×10 trade values and the 99-per-purchase limit are fixed in C++. To price one item differently, use Price Override on its row; to make a whole shop dearer or cheaper, a programmer has to change the multiplier.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Where it lives What it does Offers › Item Shop table › XenoCore › Shop An item the shop sells, in list order Offers › Price Override Shop table › XenoCore › Shop Its price. 0 means "use the item's buy price", not free Resolved Price Shop table (read only) The price that 0 resolves to, so you can see it Offers › Item, Price Override Trade table › XenoCore › Trade › Offers An item the NPC will part with, and its price (0 = its trade value) Resolved Price, Overtrade At Trade table (read only) The actual price, and what earns the bonus Overtrade Bonus › Item Trade table › XenoCore › Trade › Overtrade Bonus The bonus item. Empty means this NPC never gives one Overtrade Bonus › Value Override same Extra value needed on top of the price. 0 = the bonus item's own trade value Shop Table, Trade Offers Placed NPC › XenoCore › NPC Which tables this NPC uses Complete Heading W_XenoCore_TradeScreen › XenoCore › Trade › Completion The heading of the banner after a trade Celebrate On Trade same Confetti and fanfare after a trade. Off by default Tab Button Class, Row Class, Stat Row Class, Icon Set, icon sizes Both screens › XenoCore › Merchant Which widgets and icons the lists use Texts under XenoCore › Shop › Text W_XenoCore_ShopScreen The shop's panel wording

Set Shop Table and Trade Offers on the placed NPC, never on the Blueprint

Set on B_XenoCore_Npc's class defaults, every NPC in the game becomes a shopkeeper or a trader, including your quest givers. These are per-instance settings.

Fails silently: an item with no category fragment

An item without a XenoCoreFragment_ItemCategory, or with Sell Value 0, has no price. In a shop it cannot be bought; in a trade table it is priced 0 and trades for anything. Right-click your tables in the Content Browser and choose Asset Actions › Validate Assets: both report such rows as errors.

Price Override 0 means derive, never free

There is no way to give an item away through a shop or a trade. A gift belongs in a quest reward.

docs.title: Extending it
docs.text:
• A new shop or trader: duplicate the sample table into Content/MyGame/, change its rows, and set it on a placed NPC. See Open a shop and Set up a trade.
  • Different wording after a shop or trade: add Show Dialogue nodes on the node's output pins in the NPC's graph.
  • Stock that changes over time is a different table swapped in by your own logic (for example on quest state, through Get Party Quests). Tables have no stock count or conditions.
  • Skill bonuses to prices and a third screen of this kind (a crafting bench, say) need a programmer; see the note below.

Never edit the sample tables in place if you want to keep them as reference; they are overwritten by template updates.

For programmers: classes and extension points

Tables are UXenoCoreShopTable and UXenoCoreTradeTable; the nodes are the latent actions UXenoCoreOpenShop and UXenoCoreOpenTrade; the screens derive from UXenoCoreShopScreenBase / UXenoCoreTradeScreenBase, both on UXenoCoreMerchantScreenBase, with rows on UXenoCoreTradeRowBase. Prices are in UXenoCoreShopStatics and UXenoCoreTradeStatics (BuyMultiplier, MaterialMultiplier, StandardMultiplier, MaxPerTransaction). GetSellPriceMultiplier and GetOfferValueMultiplier are the single place a skill bonus would go; both return 1.0 today. A third merchant-style screen derives from UXenoCoreMerchantScreenBase, which supplies the Menu input mode, back handling, the finish callback, rows, tabs, focus restore and the details card.

docs.title: Why it's built this way
docs.text:
For programmers
  • One base for the shared mechanics. The trade screen came first; the shop is the second screen of the kind, which is the point at which the shared parts moved into a base. Neither child duplicates the focus, tab and pooling fixes.
  • One number per item. Baking a multiplier into the item would be wrong for the other two consumers, so the item carries Sell Value and each system applies its own rule.
  • One resolver per price. Rows, the confirm total and the actual transaction all read the same GetPrice, so nothing can be shown at one price and charged at another. The read-only Resolved Price fields in the editor are a display of that same function.
  • Every bag change goes through UXenoCoreInventoryStatics, and every gold change through the progression component, so the change messages fire and open screens stay current. See Events you can listen to.

  • The finish pin always fires. The NPC graph is suspended on the node. If the screen were torn down without answering, the conversation could never finish, so the answer is delivered when the screen deactivates, however that happens.

  • CommonUI reuses screens. CommonUI's layer pools activatable widgets, so the same shop or trade screen instance is shown again on the next visit. Anything that must be fresh per visit is reset in BeginShowing, which a child's show function must call first. A latch set once at construction survives into the next visit and, for example, stops the finish callback from ever firing a second time.

docs.title: Skills
docs.text:
All · 20 min read · No code

A character's skill trees.

Skills are each character's passive upgrades. Every character has a skill tree of branches (five in XC1), each holding five skills learnt strictly top to bottom. Characters earn skill points (SP) from kills; the SP flows into the one branch the player has selected, and the selected branch also grants that branch's trait, a stat bonus that grows as the branch fills. Progress is owned by the same component that owns levels, Game/BP_XenoCore_Progression (UXenoCoreProgressionComponent), and is stored per character, keyed by the member definition. The one idea: a tree is a Data Table and a save only ever stores counts. "Branch row X, 3 skills learnt, 240 SP into the fourth" is the whole record, so you can rewrite, rename or rebalance skills without breaking saves, and every stat a skill gives is re-derived from that record whenever anything changes.

At a glance

In play: the Skills screen (main menu › Skills) shows each character's branches; pick one, and the SP from every kill fills its skills top to bottom.

What you can change, no code:

  • A character's tree, a new branch or a new skill: Add a skill or a skill tree
  • SP costs, trait ladders and SP per kill: the three shared tables in Battle/Skills
  • How fast SP comes in overall: Skill Point Reward Scale on Game/BP_XenoCore_Progression
  • Every setting: What you can change

63 shipped skills are stand-ins

Every one of the 100 shipped skills, and every branch trait, does something. But 63 of the skills keep their Xenoblade Chronicles name, shape, colour, scope and cost while doing a different, simpler thing, because the system their original effect needs is not built yet (tension, visions, chain attacks, counters, equipment weight classes, gem crafting), or is built without the hook the skill needs (aggro modifiers on arts, Party Gauge fill and revive bonuses). Stand-in skills lists each one, what it does, and what it waits on.

docs.title: How it fits together
docs.text:
Piece Asset or class What it does Skill tree Battle/Skills/DT_XenoCore_SkillTree_*, rows of XenoCoreSkillBranchRow One row per branch. The row name is the branch's id; row order is the order the branches are drawn in. The character's tree Skill Tree on the character Blueprint (XenoCore › Skills) Which table this character uses. Read from the class defaults, so a benched character (no body) still has one. Cost curves Battle/Skills/DT_XenoCore_SkillCostCurves SP to learn each of a branch's five skills. Two rows: Starting (300, 700, 1,000, 2,000, 3,500) and Quest (200, 500, 800, 1,000, 1,500). Trait ladders Battle/Skills/DT_XenoCore_SkillTraitLadders A trait's value at 0, 1 ... 5 skills learnt. Six rows, for example AgilityFlat 2, 5, 8, 10, 12, 15. SP per kill Battle/Skills/DT_XenoCore_SkillPointRewards Flat SP by level difference: Trivial 1, Easy 5, Even 10, Strong 15, Dangerous 20. Stat carrier Battle/Skills/GE_XenoCore_SkillStats One infinite effect per body that carries every stat skill and the trait, one channel per stat. Skill abilities Battle/Skills/Abilities/GA_XenoCore_Skill_* Behaviour for skills that react to something (battle start, a kill, an ally falling). Blueprint children of XenoCoreSkillAbility_TimedBuff. Progression component Game/BP_XenoCore_Progression Holds every character's record, awards SP, applies skills to bodies, answers "how big is this bonus?". Skills screen UserInterface/Skills/W_XenoCore_SkillsScreen (UXenoCoreSkillsScreenBase) The menu screen, opened from the Skills entry of the main menu. Icon set UserInterface/Skills/DA_XenoCore_SkillIconSet How every skill icon is drawn. No skill has its own icon art.

The shipped trees and who uses them:

Tree Character (pawn) Branches open at start DT_XenoCore_SkillTree_Shulk Kael (B_XenoCore_Party_VRoid_L) and Blue (Game/B_XenoCore_Player) 3 of 5 DT_XenoCore_SkillTree_Reyn Mira (B_XenoCore_Party_VRoid_K) 3 of 5 DT_XenoCore_SkillTree_Dunban Nia (B_XenoCore_Party_VRoid_S) 3 of 5 DT_XenoCore_SkillTree_Fiora Dorran (B_XenoCore_Party_VRoid_C) 3 of 5 DT_XenoCore_SkillTree_Arcanist Isolde (B_XenoCore_Party_VRoid_M) 3 of 5 DT_XenoCore_SkillTree_Trickster Sabine (B_XenoCore_Party_VRoid_Q) 3 of 5 DT_XenoCore_SkillTree_Medic Tamsin (B_XenoCore_Party_VRoid_Y) 3 of 5

A tree can be shared: Kael and Blue point at the same table, but each has their own progress, because progress is keyed by the character, not by the table.

docs.title: A branch
docs.text:
Each row of a tree table is one branch:

Field What it does Display Name The branch's name on the screen. Trait Description One line shown when the branch header is focused. Trait Stat A XenoCore.Stat.* tag: the stat the trait raises. Empty means the branch has no trait. Trait Operation Add (points, or percentage points for a rate) or Scale (a percentage of the stat). Trait Ladder A row of DT_XenoCore_SkillTraitLadders. Cost Curve A row of DT_XenoCore_SkillCostCurves. Unlocked At Start Open from the start. Otherwise a quest opens it. First Skill Prelearned The first skill starts learnt, at 0 SP. Skills Exactly five skills, top to bottom.

docs.title: A skill
docs.text:
Each of a branch's five Skills is one entry. A skill does its work in up to three ways, all optional and all driven by one number, Value:

Field What it does Display Name, Description Shown on the screen. The description may contain {Value}, which is replaced with the formatted value ("Reduces equipment weight by {Value}."). Shape The icon's frame: Circle, Square, Hexagon, Star or Diamond. Only the future Skill Links feature reads it (Diamond means "this character only"). Timing Always (blue icon) or In Battle Party (orange icon): the skill works only while its owner is an active member. Scope Self, Battle Party (every active member) or Whole Party (everyone, benched included). The icon's glyph. Value The skill's strength. What Stats add, what a Bonus is worth, what an Ability reads. Duration Seconds, for a skill with an Ability that applies a timed buff. Stats Stats raised by Value while the skill reaches the body. Each entry is a Stat tag and an Operation (Add or Scale). A skill can raise several. Condition, Condition Threshold When the Stats hold: Always, Health At Or Below or Health At Or Above a percentage of max HP, or No Armour (nothing in any armour slot; the weapon does not count). Chance Percent chance that an Ability's trigger fires. 100 is always. Bonus A XenoCore.SkillBonus.* tag another system asks about (see below). Ability A skill ability class, granted to the body while the skill reaches it. SP Cost Override −1 uses the branch's cost curve. Anything else replaces it for this skill. Link Cost Reserved for Skill Links, which are not built. Read by nothing.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
Seeding. The first time anything asks about a character's skills, their record is filled in from the tree: every Unlocked At Start branch is opened, a First Skill Prelearned branch starts with one skill learnt, and the first unlocked row in table order becomes the selected branch. Seeding only ever adds: a branch you add to a table later appears for existing saves too, and progress on existing branches is never touched.

Earning SP. When an enemy dies, SP is awarded before the EXP:

  1. The party's level is worked out per Skill Point Level Basis: the active party's average (default), the leader's, the lowest active member's, or each character's own.
  2. The level difference (party level − enemy level) picks a band in the reward table. The first row whose range contains it wins.
  3. The band's SP × Skill Point Reward Scale × the enemy's Skill Point Multiplier is paid to every roster member. Benched members get Reserve Skill Point Rate of it, which the sample sets to 0, like the EXP rate, so a benched character earns nothing (XC1 pays 90%).

Quests do not pay SP. Anything else can, by calling Award Skill Points (see Extending it). After a kill, each party member's HUD plate shows the EXP, AP and SP they earned together.

Spending SP. SP flows into the character's selected branch only. It fills the next unlearnt skill; when the skill's cost is met, the skill is learnt and any remainder carries into the next. The icon on the Skills screen fills from the bottom as SP arrives. On each skill learnt:

  • "Skill Learnt" floats over the character (if they have a body), and
  • XenoCore.Skills.Message.SkillLearnt is broadcast carrying the Member, Branch (row name), Index (0 to 4) and Skill Name.

SP earned by a finished branch is thrown away

Once all five skills of the selected branch are learnt, any further SP for that character is wasted. Nothing warns the player; the screen shows ---- / ---- against the branch. This is deliberate, it is what makes choosing a branch a decision, but test it as a player would.

Selecting a branch. On the Skills screen, focus a branch header and press accept (Change Trait), or click it. Switching is free and unlimited. Learnt skills stay active whichever branch is selected; only the trait follows the selection. Selecting a locked or unknown branch is refused with a warning in LogXenoSkills.

Unlocking a branch. A quest opens a branch when it is turned in, through its reward's Skill Branches list (Member plus Branch, the row name). Blueprint can do the same with Unlock Skill Branch. The party member sees a notice over their head (Branch Unlocked Text), and the Skills screen gains a column. The quest offer screen and the turn-in banner both list branch rewards.

Applying skills to a body. Whenever something changes, the progression component re-derives every body's skills from scratch:

  1. It removes the stat effect it applied last time.
  2. For every roster member whose skills reach this body, it adds up each learnt skill's Stats (checking Condition), plus the trait of this body's own selected branch.
  3. It applies one GE_XenoCore_SkillStats carrying the totals, one channel per stat.
  4. It grants any skill Ability that newly reaches the body and removes any that no longer does. Abilities already granted are left running, so a buff counting down or a "once per battle" latch survives a refresh caused by something unrelated.
  5. It keeps HP as the same fraction of max HP, so a Max HP skill never quietly takes HP away.

This runs when a body spawns, when a skill is learnt, when a branch is selected, when the party changes, when equipment changes, after a level-up, and when a body's HP crosses a skill's condition threshold. Nothing about it is saved; it is always rebuilt from the record.

Who a skill reaches. A skill owned by one character applies to a body when:

  • the owner is that body, or the skill's Scope is Battle Party and the body is an active member, or the Scope is Whole Party; and
  • the skill's Timing is Always, or its owner is an active member.

So an orange (In Battle Party) party-wide skill buffs the active party only while its owner fights, and a blue (Always) whole-party skill works even from the bench. The same rule decides who a Bonus counts for.

Level-ups. A level-up re-applies the statline and then refreshes skills, because a Scale skill is a percentage of a stat that has just moved. A level-up still heals to full, including any extra max HP a skill adds.

docs.title: Stat skills and traits
docs.text:
Most skills are just Stats plus a Value. They arrive through GE_XenoCore_SkillStats, whose twelve channels are the list of stats a skill can raise:

XenoCore.Stat.Strength, .Ether, .Agility, .PhysicalDefence, .EtherDefence, .CriticalRate, .BlockRate, .Weight, .WeaponAttackMin, .WeaponAttackMax, .MaxHealth, .MoveSpeed.

  • Add adds Value as points. For Critical Rate and Block Rate the value is a whole percentage (15 means +15 %). Move Speed is a percentage over the character's authored walk speed.
  • Scale adds Value percent of the stat as it stands without skills (statline plus equipment), so it grows with gear. Timed buffs up at that moment, such as Strength Up, are left out of the price.
  • A negative Value lowers the stat (Weight −5). The screen labels it "Weight Down".

A skill naming a stat the effect has no channel for does nothing and logs a warning naming the skill.

docs.title: Bonuses other systems ask for
docs.text:
A Bonus skill adds nothing to a character by itself. Instead, a system asks "what is this character's total bonus for this tag?" with Get Skill Bonus and applies it. The answer is the sum of the Value of every learnt skill with that tag that reaches the character, as a percentage. Shipped systems ask with these tags:

Tag Asked by Effect XenoCore.SkillBonus.QuestExperience Quest turn-in % more EXP from quests XenoCore.SkillBonus.BattleExperience Enemy kill % more EXP from enemies XenoCore.SkillBonus.ArtPoints Enemy kill % more Art Points from enemies XenoCore.SkillBonus.HealingPower Healing arts % more HP restored by the caster XenoCore.SkillBonus.PhysicalDamageTaken Damage formula % less physical damage taken XenoCore.SkillBonus.EtherDamageTaken Damage formula % less ether damage taken XenoCore.SkillBonus.CriticalDamage Damage formula % more damage on a critical hit XenoCore.SkillBonus.FirstStrike Damage formula % more damage on the attacker's first hit of each battle

Because the answer is read from the record, a bonus works for a benched character too.

docs.title: Skills with behaviour
docs.text:
A skill that reacts ("when an ally falls", "at the start of a battle") names an Ability: a Blueprint child of UXenoCoreGameplayAbility_Skill. It is passive: granted while the skill reaches the body, active from the moment it is granted, removed when the skill stops reaching it. It can read its own skill with Get Skill, Get Skill Value and Get Skill Duration.

The shipped behaviour skills all use one ready-made class, UXenoCoreSkillAbility_TimedBuff: when this happens, apply that buff for the skill's Duration. A Blueprint child with two fields set is a new skill; there is no graph.

Setting (XenoCore › Skills) What it does Trigger Ally Incapacitated (another active member goes down), Battle Start, Battle Start Vs Higher Level (the battle is against an engaged enemy at least Level Gap levels above), On Kill, On Miss (this body's attack is evaded), On Critical. Buff The status effect to apply, a GE_XenoCore_Status_*. Additional Buffs More statuses applied at the same time, with the same strength and duration. Level Gap For Battle Start Vs Higher Level. Default 3. Battle Start Window How long after the battle starts an engaged enemy still counts as "starting a battle against it". Default 1.5 s.

The skill's Value is sent to the buff as its strength (a status that reads a percentage turns 20 into +20 %), its Duration as the buff's length, and its Chance is rolled each time the trigger fires. A battle-start trigger fires at most once per battle; a failed roll is that battle's answer. Because the buff is an ordinary status, it shows on the HUD and over the character like any art's buff.

The On Kill, On Miss and On Critical triggers listen for gameplay events on the character: XenoCore.Event.Combat.Kill (sent by a dying enemy to whoever damaged it last), XenoCore.Event.Combat.Miss and XenoCore.Event.Combat.Critical (sent by the damage formula).

Your own attacks must send the combat events

If you add an attack that does not use XenoCore's damage execution, on-miss and on-critical skills never fire for it, and nothing reports it. Send XenoCore.Event.Combat.Miss or .Critical to the attacker with Send Gameplay Event To Actor and they will.

Condition gates Stats only

Condition decides whether a skill's Stats hold. It does not gate a Bonus or an Ability. A skill with a condition and no stats does nothing more than an unconditional one; Data Validation warns about it.

docs.title: Stand-in skills
docs.text:
All 100 shipped skills have an effect. Each character's tree mixes three kinds:

  • Faithful skills (37) do what the original game's skill does.
  • Stand-ins (63) keep the original skill's name, shape, colour, scope and SP cost, and use an effect that already works in XenoCore. Each is the nearest live effect in the spirit of the name: a taunt raises defence, a tension skill gives a combat buff at a similar moment, an equipment-class skill reduces Weight.
  • Traits all work. Three branches whose original trait was counter rate (_Reyn Impatience, _Dunban Bravery, _Fiora Rashness) raise Block Rate or Critical Rate instead, on the same ladder.

A stand-in is ordinary data. To give a slot the original effect once its system exists, or any effect of your own, edit the skill's entry in its tree table (see Changing a shipped tree).
