The pre-learnt first skills are stand-ins

Each character's free first skill is an equipment-class skill (Medium or Mechonis Equipment). Until equipment weight classes exist, it reduces Weight, so every character starts with a learnt skill that works. Weight is subtracted from Agility when hits are rolled, so less of it means better evasion and accuracy (see Stats and damage).

docs.title: The Skills screen
docs.text:
The screen is opened by the main menu's Skills entry (Open Skills Screen). It shows one character at a time, starting with whoever you are controlling:

  • L / R step through the whole roster, benched members included, with a strip of portraits.
  • The card shows the character's portrait over one column per unlocked branch, in table row order; locked branches are left out, not greyed. Each column is a header over five icons.
  • An icon is composed from the skill's data: Shape is the frame, Timing the colour (blue Always, orange In Battle Party), Scope the glyph (one figure, three figures, ALL). An unlearnt skill is a dark silhouette; the one being learnt fills from the bottom.
  • The selected branch's header is drawn in the button style's Selected state (the same blue as every selected row in the project) and shows a second line, SP 200 / 700, or Complete. That line is the character's SP: there is no SP balance, only progress into the next skill.
  • The cursor is XC1's: a yellow frame with an arrow on each side, the same on a branch header and on a skill icon, so it never looks like the selection. Its colour and sizes are Cursor Colour, Cursor Frame Width, Cursor Arrow Size and Cursor Arrow Gap on the header and icon classes.
  • Focusing a branch header shows its trait, the trait's current value, Selected or Not selected, skills learnt, and SP into / cost for the next skill (or ---- / ---- when the branch is complete).
  • Focusing a skill shows its stat and value, SP cost or Learnt, Active (Always / In battle party), Affects (Self / Battle party / Whole party) and Effect Time if it has a duration.
  • Change Trait appears on the action bar only while the cursor is on a branch that is not already selected.

The screen derives from UXenoCoreCharacterMenuScreenBase, a shared base for any menu screen about one character. The Arts screen uses the same base. It owns roster cycling (benched included), the portrait strip, the bumper glyphs, an optional pair of tab triggers (ZL / ZR), and Menu input mode. A screen built on it overrides On Member Shown to paint, and always reads records by member definition, never from a pawn, because the shown character may be benched.

docs.title: What you can change
docs.text:
Setting Where it lives What it does Skill Tree Character Blueprint › XenoCore › Skills The character's tree. Empty means no skills; the screen shows "No skill tree". Skill Point Reward Table BP_XenoCore_Progression › XenoCore › Skills SP bands per kill. Skill Point Reward Scale BP_XenoCore_Progression › XenoCore › Skills One multiplier over all kill SP. 1.0 by default; raise it for a shorter game instead of editing the bands. Reserve Skill Point Rate BP_XenoCore_Progression › XenoCore › Skills Benched members' share of kill SP: 0 in the sample (the C++ default is XC1's 0.9). A separate setting from the EXP rate, so the two can differ. Skill Point Level Basis BP_XenoCore_Progression › XenoCore › Skills Whose level sets the band: Party Average (default), Leader, Lowest, Own. Skill Stats Effect BP_XenoCore_Progression › XenoCore › Skills The stat carrier, GE_XenoCore_SkillStats. Skill Learnt Text, Branch Unlocked Text, Skill Learnt Colour, Skill Feedback Scale BP_XenoCore_Progression › XenoCore › Skills › Feedback The line floated over a character. Empty text turns it off. Skill Point Multiplier Enemy Blueprint or placed enemy › XenoCore › Enemy Scales the SP this enemy pays. 1.0. Skill Branches Quest definition › Reward Branches the quest opens on turn-in. Costs, ladders, bands DT_XenoCore_SkillCostCurves, _SkillTraitLadders, _SkillPointRewards Shared by every branch that points at them. Icon Set, Icon Class, Header Class, Header Style, Accept Action, Show Skill Links Tab, sizes and colours W_XenoCore_SkillsScreen class defaults › XenoCore › Skills The screen. Header Style is the branch headers' button style, ButtonStyle_XenoCore_Menu; restyle that asset and the headers follow. Empty falls back to the header's own plate colours. Leave Show Skill Links Tab off; Skill Links are not built. Portrait Size, Unselected Portrait Opacity, Max Visible Portraits, the four actions W_XenoCore_SkillsScreen class defaults › XenoCore › Menu The character strip and bumpers, from the shared base. Shape Textures, Glyph Textures, Always Colour, In Battle Party Colour, Unlearnt Colour DA_XenoCore_SkillIconSet Every icon. Restyling all skills is a texture swap here.

Every table checks itself when saved or validated. You get a Data Validation error for a branch without exactly five skills, a branch with no Cost Curve, a trait stat with no Trait Ladder, a skill with no name or a Stats entry with no stat, a cost curve without five costs, a ladder without six values, or an SP band whose minimum is above its maximum. You get a warning for a skill with no Stats, Bonus or Ability (it does nothing) and for a Condition on a skill with no Stats.

The row name is the save's id

A save stores branches by row name. Renaming a branch row after players have saves resets that branch for them: the old progress is kept under the old name and never shown, and the new row starts fresh. Nothing is logged. Choose final row names before release, and change Display Name instead.

Reordering skills changes what a save has learnt

A save stores how many skills of a branch are learnt, not which. Swap skills 2 and 4 and every save with three learnt now has the old skill 4 instead of skill 2. That is how skills stay editable, so reorder only before release, or accept the change.

docs.title: Save
docs.text:
On load, each record is re-seeded from the current table (additively), so new branches appear. If the saved selected branch no longer exists or is locked, the first unlocked row is selected instead. Skill effects are never saved; they are rebuilt when the bodies spawn. See Save and front end.

For programmers: the saved fields

Each member's saved record carries:

Field Meaning bSkillsSaved False for a save made before skills existed; that character is seeded fresh on load. SelectedSkillBranch Row name of the selected branch. SkillBranches One entry per branch: Branch (row name), bUnlocked, SkillsLearnt (0–5), SkillPointsIntoNext.

docs.title: Console commands
docs.text:
Command Effect XenoGiveSP 2000 Pour SP into the leader's selected branch, then print the tree. SP past a complete branch is wasted, as in play. XenoSkills Print the leader's tree, selected branch, and each branch's state, learnt count and SP into the next skill.

Both are cheat-manager commands, so they work in PIE and development builds. Output is under the LogXenoSkills log category; skill abilities log under LogXenoSkillAbility.

docs.title: Extending it
docs.text:
• Give a character a tree, or add skills: see Add a skill or a skill tree.
  • Award SP from anything else (a landmark, a cutscene): call Award Skill Points on Get Party Progression with the member and amount. Tick Apply Reserve Rate to pay benched members the reserve share.
  • Open a branch from script: Unlock Skill Branch (Member, Branch row name). Safe to call twice.
  • Make your own system skill-aware: add a tag under XenoCore.SkillBonus in your own gameplay tag config, set it as a skill's Bonus, and in your system call Get Skill Bonus (member) or Get Skill Bonus For Actor (a body; returns 0 for anything that is not a party member). No skill code changes.
  • Let skills raise a new stat: add a modifier to GE_XenoCore_SkillStats for the attribute, with magnitude Set By Caller and your XenoCore.Stat.* tag as its data tag (copy an existing channel). The channel list is the effect's modifier list, and the screen labels it from the tag. This edits a shipped asset; note it for template updates.

A new percentage stat added as a channel is 100 times too strong

The conversion from a whole percentage in the data to a 0–1 fraction on the attribute is applied only to Critical Rate and Block Rate. If you add a channel for another attribute stored as a 0–1 fraction, a skill's +15 lands as +15.0, which usually clamps to 100 %. Store such a stat as a whole percentage, or ask a programmer to add it to the conversion in XenoCoreProgressionComponent_Skills.cpp (AddStat).

  • Behaviour that TimedBuff cannot express: create a Blueprint child of XenoCoreGameplayAbility_Skill. Set Evaluate Interval to poll and override On Evaluate, or listen for gameplay events in Activate Ability. Use Apply Buff To Self to apply a status with the skill's value and duration. Keep the base empty: no tags or effects of its own.
  • React to a skill being learnt: listen for XenoCore.Skills.Message.SkillLearnt. Refresh anything that shows SP or skill counts on XenoCore.Progression.Message.Changed, which is sent on every SP award and branch change. See Events you can listen to.
  • A new menu screen about one character (programmers): subclass UXenoCoreCharacterMenuScreenBase in C++ and override On Member Shown, Reset For Show and, if the screen has tabs, the tab handlers.
  • Never edit DT_XenoCore_SkillPointRewards' bands to make a demo faster; change Skill Point Reward Scale instead, so the reference numbers stay intact.

docs.title: Why it's built this way
docs.text:
For programmers: the design reasons
  • Data Tables, not one data asset per skill, because a designer sees a whole character in one asset, tables round-trip CSV and JSON in the editor, and they can be filled from script. The trade is that a row cannot hold a Blueprint graph, which is why behaviour lives in a separate ability class the row points at, the same "data pointing at behaviour" split as an art definition and its ability.
  • Saves store counts, never skill ids, because skills are learnt strictly in order. Designers can rename, rewrite and rebalance skills freely.
  • One stat effect per body, rebuilt from scratch, following GE_XenoCore_EquipmentStats: no stat name is hard-coded, the effect's channels are the list, and "remove, sum, re-apply" cannot drift the way incremental adds and removes would. It is additive on top of the statline, never an override, so it survives a level-up re-stat.
  • Bonuses are asked for, not pushed, so the damage formula, the quest turn-in and the healing art each read one number when they need it, a benched character's bonus works without a body, and a new bonus is a new tag rather than new skill code.
  • Skill abilities are diffed, not re-granted, so a refresh caused by an SP award or a gear change never restarts a buff that is counting down.
  • The record lives on the progression component, beside levels and Art Points, for the same reason those are there: progress is per character and half the roster has no body at any moment. No new component was added.
  • The Skills screen and Arts screen share a base because they were the second and first screens of the kind; the base holds only what both need.

docs.title: Stats and damage
docs.text:
All · 20 min read · No code

A character's numbers are Gameplay Ability System attributes on its own ability system. Health comes from Lyra's health set; everything else (Strength, Ether, Agility, defences, rates, weapon attack, level, talent gauge) is XenoCore's UXenoCoreStatSet. Numbers get onto a character in two layers: a statline effect that reads curve tables at the character's level, and an equipment effect that adds the stats of what it wears. Damage is calculated by one execution, UXenoCoreDamageExecution, set up as Battle/Attributes/BP_XenoCoreDamageExecution and used by Battle/Attributes/GE_XenoCore_Damage. The one idea: the formula is not symmetric. A party member hitting an enemy treats the enemy's defence as a fraction; an enemy hitting a party member subtracts the party member's defence as flat points.

At a glance

In play: the numbers over every hit, MISS, BLOCKED and CRITICAL HIT!, and the stats on the Party and Equipment screens.

What you can change, no code:

  • A character's stats at each level: Give a character its own statline
  • An enemy's: Author an enemy statline
  • Hit, block and critical chances, and how much a level gap matters: the settings on Battle/Attributes/BP_XenoCoreDamageExecution (open it, click Class Defaults, see XenoCore › Damage). Listed under What you can change.
  • A brand-new stat needs a programmer: Add a stat to the damage formula

docs.title: How it fits together
docs.text: Layer Asset What it sets Attribute set UXenoCoreStatSet (C++), granted by every character's ability set Which stats exist. Health Lyra's ULyraHealthSet, created with the pawn's ability system Health, Max Health. Statline Battle/Attributes/GE_XenoCore_BaseStats_* Base stats at a level, read from a curve table. Override modifiers. One per character (_Kael, _Mira ...) and one per enemy type. Party curves Battle/Attributes/CT_XenoCore_PartyStatlines Each character's own rows, such as Kael.Strength, one curve per stat, X = level. Each follows the XC1 character whose skill tree it uses. CT_XenoCore_BaseStats holds the older shared Shulk.* rows the colour mannequins still read. Enemy curves Battle/Attributes/CT_XenoCore_EnemyStats Rows such as Minion_Melee.Strength. Level UXenoCoreMMC_EffectLevel and the pawn's C++ Character Level is set to the level the statline was applied at. Equipment Inventory/GE_XenoCore_EquipmentStats Adds each worn item's stats through Set By Caller tags XenoCore.Stat.*. Damage GE_XenoCore_Damage → BP_XenoCoreDamageExecution Health damage per hit. Level difference Battle/Attributes/CT_XenoCore_DamageLevelDiff Rows Damage.LevelDiff.Physical and Damage.LevelDiff.Ether.

docs.title: The attributes
docs.text:
Attribute Meaning Range Strength Physical attack stat. Does nothing for ether attacks. 0 and up Ether Ether attack stat. Does nothing for physical attacks. 0 and up Agility Hit chance and evasion. 0 and up Physical Defence, Ether Defence Flat points on a party member; a fraction (0 to 0.9) on an enemy. 0 and up Critical Rate, Block Rate Chance per hit, as a fraction. 0.1 is 10%. 0 to 1 Weight Armour weight, subtracted from Agility for hit rolls only. 0 and up Weapon Attack Min, Weapon Attack Max The weapon's damage range. 0 and up Character Level The level used in every curve lookup. 1 to Max Character Level (99) Experience, Experience To Next Level Written by the progression component for display. Talent Gauge 0 to 100. Fills as auto-attacks land; spent by Talent Arts. 0 to 100 Talent Charge Per Hit Gauge percent added per landed auto-attack. Set by the statline. 0 and up Auto Attack Speed Multiplier on swing cadence; Haste and Slow change it. 0.1 to 4

A party character has no defence, block or critical chance of its own: those come only from equipment. That is intended.

Max Character Level is a config value with no editor field. To raise the cap, close the editor, open your project's Config/DefaultGame.ini in a text editor, and add:

[/Script/XenoCoreRuntime.XenoCoreStatSet]
MaxCharacterLevel=120

and extend your curve tables, and every row of DT_XenoCore_ExperienceCurves, to the new cap.

docs.title: The damage formula
docs.text:
Every hit runs these steps, in order:

  1. Team check. If the attacker may not damage the target (same team, or no team), the hit does nothing and a warning is logged under LogXenoDamage.
  2. School. Ether if the damage effect's spec carries XenoCore.Art.School.Ether, otherwise physical. The school decides which attack stat and which defence are used.
  3. Contact roll: miss, block or hit. Rolled by the attacking ability before the effect is applied (see below). A miss shows MISS over the target and nothing else happens: no damage, no reaction, no talent charge. A block shows BLOCKED and marks the hit as blocked for step 8.
  4. Weapon roll. A random value between Weapon Attack Min and Max, with Max capped at Min + 99.
  5. Art multiplier. The Set By Caller XenoCore.Art.Magnitude.Damage. Auto-attacks send none, so it is 1.
  6. Modifiers. 1, or the critical multiplier on a critical hit. Never below Minimum Modifiers.
  7. Level multiplier. The level-difference curve at (attacker level − target level).
  8. Block. If step 3 rolled a block, damage is multiplied by Block Multiplier: 0 by default, so a block takes no damage at all.
  9. The formula, then rounded down:
Attacker Damage Party member (stat + weapon) × art × (1 − defence) × modifiers × level × block, with defence capped at Max Defence Fraction Enemy max(stat − defence, 0) × art × modifiers × level × block

The side is decided by what the attacker is, not by who is driving it, so a companion under AI control and the same character under your control deal the same damage. In order:

  1. An AXenoCoreEnemyCharacter is always an enemy.
  2. A character with a Member Definition (every party member) is always party.
  3. Otherwise, the team: on the player's team is party, on any other team is enemy. This covers a player pawn with no member definition, such as the one Lyra spawns when Starting Roster is empty.
  4. Last resort, for an actor with no team: whether a player is controlling it.

If the attacker and the target come out on the same side, a warning is logged under LogXenoDamage: the target's defence is then being read in the wrong units, which means your team setup lets a side hurt itself.

Critical hits roll against the attacker's Critical Rate. The multiplier is Critical Multiplier (1.25), or Critical Multiplier Vs Reacting (1.5) against a Toppled or Dazed target. An ether attack against a Dazed target is always critical.

A critical hit shows CRITICAL HIT! over the target, draws the damage number gold and plays the heavier critical hit sound. It also adds 10 to the Party Gauge when a party member lands it. The text, its size and punch, and an optional hit-stop are under Project Settings › Game › XenoCore Content › Critical Hit; see Tune hit feedback.

Hit rolls. The chance is 1 + (attacker − target) × Agility Hit Per Point, using Agility minus Weight on both sides, plus a level-difference modifier, clamped between Hit Chance Floor (5%) and Hit Chance Cap (100%). Equal agility and equal level always hit.

  • Ether attacks ignore Agility but still take the level modifier, so they miss enemies well above you.
  • A Toppled or Dazed target cannot be missed.
  • The level modifier comes from Physical Hit By Level Gap or Ether Hit By Level Gap, indexed by the level gap (0 to 10, the last entry covering 10 or more). It is a bonus when the attacker is higher and a penalty when it is lower. The shipped numbers are XC1's: a physical attacker 3 levels below loses 24%, and at 6 or more below it loses 120% to 200%, which puts it on the 5% floor.

Block rolls. Physical hits only; ether is never blocked. The chance is the target's Block Rate plus Block Rate Per Level (5%) for each level the attacker is below the target (a penalty when it is above), capped at ± Block Level Modifier Cap (100%). A Toppled or Dazed target does not block.

  • Party members get Block Rate only from their weapon and skills.
  • Enemies have none of their own, so an enemy blocks only when it is higher-levelled than you.
  • Block Level Dead Zone (0) ignores small gaps; set it to 2 for no level effect within ±2.

XenoCore departs from XC1 on blocks

In XC1 a block halves the damage. XenoCore's Block Multiplier defaults to 0, so a block negates the hit completely. Set it to 0.5 on BP_XenoCoreDamageExecution to restore XC1.

Fails silently: a blocked opening hit does not start the fight

An enemy is drawn into a fight by losing HP. With Block Multiplier at 0, an enemy that blocks your first hit takes no damage and stays where it is. Hit it again.

Fails silently: the team gate

Damage between actors on the same team, or where either has no team, is dropped. The target still flinches, because the hit-react event is sent separately, so "it reacted" does not prove damage landed. Type log LogXenoDamage Verbose in the console to see every hit's breakdown.

The hit roll reads its settings (Agility Hit Per Point, Hit Chance Floor, Hit Chance Cap, Miss Colour) from the execution class the attack's damage effect actually runs, so edits on BP_XenoCoreDamageExecution take effect like every other setting there. A damage effect that runs no XenoCore damage execution falls back to the C++ defaults, and a warning naming the effect is logged once under LogXenoDamage.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
• Spawn and level-up. The character applies its Stats Effect at its level; every modifier is an Override, so re-applying replaces rather than stacks. The same effect also overrides Health, which is why a level-up fully heals. See Progression.
  • Equip. Equipping runs GA_XenoCore_EquipmentStats, which applies GE_XenoCore_EquipmentStats with each XenoCore.Stat.* magnitude filled from the item's own stat tags. Unequipping removes it. See Equipment.
  • Statuses such as GE_XenoCore_Status_StrengthDown or _Slow modify attributes for their duration. See Reactions and statuses.

docs.title: What you can change
docs.text:
Setting Where it lives What it does Base stat curves CT_XenoCore_BaseStats, CT_XenoCore_EnemyStats Stat value at each level. Which rows a character reads That character's GE_XenoCore_BaseStats_* modifiers The curve row and a scale per stat. Level Difference Curve BP_XenoCoreDamageExecution › XenoCore › Damage The level-gap multiplier table. Max Defence Fraction same Defence cap on the party formula (0.9). Minimum Modifiers same Floor of the modifiers bucket (0.1). Critical Multiplier, Critical Multiplier Vs Reacting same 1.25 and 1.5. Block Multiplier same Damage a blocked hit keeps: 0 (XC1 is 0.5). Agility Hit Per Point, Hit Chance Floor, Hit Chance Cap same The hit roll: 0.01, 5% and 100%. Physical Hit By Level Gap, Ether Hit By Level Gap same › XenoCore › Damage › Level Difference Hit-chance change per level of gap, 0 to 10+. Block Rate Per Level, Block Level Dead Zone, Block Level Modifier Cap same Block-chance change per level of gap: 5%, 0 and 100%. Miss Colour, Critical Colour, Blocked Colour same › XenoCore › Damage › Notifications Battle-text colours. Critical Hit Text, Critical Hit Scale, Critical Hit Punch, Critical Hit Stop Seconds, Critical Hit Stop Dilation Project Settings › Game › XenoCore Content › Critical Hit The critical line's wording, size and punch, and an optional hit-stop (0 s, off, by default). Max Character Level DefaultGame.ini, section above Level cap.

The shipped BP_XenoCoreDamageExecution changes only Level Difference Curve; every other value above is the class default. CT_XenoCore_DamageLevelDiff multiplies damage by the gap (attacker level − target level):

Gap −6 or less −5 to −3 −2 −1 to +2 +3 +4 to +9 +10 or more Damage.LevelDiff.Physical 0.5 0.75 0.875 1.0 1.125 1.25 2.0 Damage.LevelDiff.Ether 0.625 0.875 0.9375 1.0 1.125 1.25 1.5

Every statline modifier must be Override

A statline is re-applied on every level-up. A modifier using Add stacks on the previous application and the numbers climb with each level. Use Override on every modifier of a GE_XenoCore_BaseStats_* effect.

Enemy types are one curve times a multiplier

The minion's rows are anchored on XC1's Hand Bunnit: Minion_Melee.MaxHealth is 900 + 100 per level and Minion_Melee.Strength 69 + 10 per level. The other minion types read the same rows, and their GE_XenoCore_BaseStats_Minion_* effects scale them on each modifier: Melee 1.0, Brute 1.45, Bulwark 1.15, Skirmisher 0.9. So the number the game uses is not always the number in the table. Check the scale on every modifier of an effect you duplicate.

Every character has its own statline

Each sample character's GE_XenoCore_BaseStats_<Name> reads its own rows of CT_XenoCore_PartyStatlines at a scale of 1.0, so the table number is the game number. To give a new character its own growth, add rows for it and point its effect at them. See Give a character its own statline.

docs.title: Extending it
docs.text:
• A new stat: needs C++, because attributes are reflected properties. Add it to a subclass of UXenoCoreStatSet or a new set, grant that set in your ability sets, and read it in a damage execution subclass. See Add a stat to the damage formula.
  • A different formula: subclass UXenoCoreDamageExecution in C++ and point a duplicate of GE_XenoCore_Damage at it. Keep the team check.
  • Tuning only: make a child Blueprint of BP_XenoCoreDamageExecution in Content/MyGame/ and point your damage effect at the child, rather than editing the shipped one.

docs.title: Why it's built this way
docs.text:
For programmers: the design reasons
  • Curve tables, not per-level data assets. One row per stat covers every level, and a statline effect sampled at a level is plain GAS: nothing custom stores numbers.
  • Level set by the pawn, not a curve row. An earlier design read level from a curve whose input was also level, which could silently disagree with the badge.
  • The hit and block rolls live in the attacking ability. An execution can only output attribute changes; it cannot tell the ability "you missed" or "you were blocked". Rolling first lets a miss cancel the whole hit, and lets a block stop a Topple and the rest of a multi-hit art.
  • Its own execution instead of Lyra's. Lyra's formula is a shooter's. Lyra's team check is kept, because without it arts would damage allies.

docs.title: Targeting
docs.text:
All · 15 min read · No code

Target mode is a gameplay ability, Battle/Targeting/GA_XenoCore_TargetMode, built on the C++ class UXenoCoreGameplayAbility_TargetMode. While it is active it holds the selected enemy, shows the battle HUD (diamond over the target, target badge, player plate, arts palette), and drives the battle facing. There is no targeting component. The one idea: the lock and its target are one object. The ability is instanced once per pawn, so when the ability ends the target is gone, and anything that wants "what am I fighting?" asks the ability through one function, Get Current Target.

At a glance

In play: RB (Tab) locks on to the enemy nearest the centre of the screen and steps through the others; a diamond marks the target and arrows point to it off screen.

What you can change, no code: lock range, when the character faces the target, the diamond, arrows and sound, and how far an enemy chases before it gives up. See Tune targeting and What you can change.

docs.title: How it fits together
docs.text:
Piece Asset or class Job Target mode GA_XenoCore_TargetMode (UXenoCoreGameplayAbility_TargetMode) Holds the target; owns the indicator, off-screen arrows, HUD plates, palette and strafe facing. Holds Status.XenoCore.TargetMode while active. Resolver and selection UXenoCoreTargetingStatics Get Current Target, candidate gathering, screen-order sorting, stepping. Next / previous Input/Abilities/GA_XenoCore_TargetNext, GA_XenoCore_TargetPrev Send XenoCore.Event.SwitchTarget with a direction. Exit Input/Abilities/GA_XenoCore_TargetModeExit Ends target mode on the B input: it cancels the ability tagged Ability.XenoCore.TargetMode (Cancel Abilities With Tag), and can only run while Status.XenoCore.TargetMode is on. Off-screen arrows UXenoCoreOffscreenArrowComponent Chevrons at the screen edge pointing back at a target that left the view. Indicator materials Battle/Targeting/M_XenoCore_TargetIndicator, M_XenoCore_TargetArrows The diamond and the arrows. Target changed Message XenoCore.Targeting.Message.TargetChanged Seeker, new target, old target. Sent only by Set Current Target.

Enemies do not use this system. An enemy's target is decided by its AI controller (Get Aggro Target), and a companion fights the leader's current target.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
1. Acquire. Pressing Target Next or Target Prev sends XenoCore.Event.SwitchTarget. If target mode is idle, the event starts it; the ability picks the candidate nearest the centre of the screen, horizontally, within Lock Acquire Range.
  2. Cycle. While active, the same event steps through candidates left to right as they appear on screen, wrapping at both ends. Only on-screen candidates can be cycled to.
  3. Keep. Every poll the lock is validated: the target must be alive and within Lock Keep Range, which is never less than Lock Acquire Range. A target that walks off screen is kept; the off-screen arrows point at it.
  4. Fight. Choosing an entry on the palette draws the weapon and starts the auto-attack or an art. See The combat loop.
  5. Kill. When the locked enemy dies and another enemy is still fighting the party, the lock moves to it instead of ending: one in view first, then the one with the most aggro on the leader, then the nearest. Enemies that are not part of the fight are never picked. The weapon stays drawn, so the party does not disarm mid-battle. Only when no enemy is left fighting does the kill end target mode.
  6. Exit. Target mode ends when you press Target Mode Exit, the last fighting enemy dies, or the lock becomes invalid. Every exit goes through one path, which sheathes the weapon, cancels the auto-attack, cancels any ally selection still open (the Art is not spent), clears the target (so listeners hear it) and removes the HUD.
  7. Hand over. When the player switches to another party member in battle, target mode is not exited. The old leader's target mode ends without sheathing or stopping its swing, and the new leader's target mode starts already locked on the same enemy, even if that enemy is off screen. The camera then eases onto the lock, as at the start of a fight. If the new leader's weapon is sheathed, it is drawn first. See Switching the controlled character.

A lost lock is logged, with the reason

When target mode ends because the target was lost, a warning target lock LOST (was ...: reason) is logged. The reason is one of dead, out of range (...), not on a different team or line of sight blocked by ..., naming the blocking actor (that reason only occurs while the lock check requires line of sight; see Require Line Of Sight in the settings below). A deliberate exit (B, a won fight, a switch) logs nothing. If the auto-attack seems to stop for no reason, look for this line first.

docs.title: Facing while locked
docs.text:
Out of battle a character turns to face where it runs. In battle, target mode switches facing to the target, but only when that is what the player means:

  • The weapon must be drawn and the target within Strafe Max Range (400). It releases a little further out (Strafe Range Release Scale, 1.2×) so standing on the boundary does not flicker.
  • Standing still faces the target.
  • Moving straight away from the target (within Retreat Dot Threshold, about 25° either side) backpedals while facing it.
  • Moving forwards or sideways turns and runs normally.

This is re-evaluated every Strafe Evaluate Interval seconds rather than on target change, because the weapon is usually drawn after the target is picked.

Rotation settings always return to the Blueprint's authored values

Target mode, the auto-attack and arts each take control of a character's facing flags (Orient Rotation To Movement, Use Controller Rotation Yaw, Use Controller Desired Rotation) and give it back afterwards. They restore the values authored on the pawn's Blueprint class, not whatever was there before. So if you change facing at runtime from your own graph, the next fight will put it back. Change the defaults on the Blueprint instead. And if you write a new ability that turns the character, use Suppress Self Rotation and Restore Self Rotation from UXenoCoreLocomotionStatics, never save and restore the flags yourself.

docs.title: Choosing an ally
docs.text:
An Art whose Target Type is One ally (Light Heal in the samples) does not cast at once. Confirming it opens the party cursor, the same cursor the battle switch uses:

  1. The cursor starts on the caster: a highlight on their HUD row and a small white ring on the floor under their body.
  2. D-pad up and down (arrow keys) move it through the party, wrapping. Any active member can be chosen, downed ones included.
  3. A (Space) casts the Art on the chosen member. B (leave target mode) cancels, and the Art is not spent.

Only one party cursor can be up at a time. While it is choosing an ally, the party switch is refused, and while the switch cursor is held, an ally Art cannot open it. The cursor's look is set on the party component; see Party.

docs.title: Camera
docs.text: When the fight starts (the weapon is drawn), the camera eases towards the target once, over Camera Focus Duration (0.3 s), and then the player owns the camera again. Nothing re-aims it afterwards. Set the duration to 0 to disable the ease.

docs.title: The enemy side: engage and disengage
docs.text:
Enemies choose what to fight on their AI controller, AXenoCoreEnemyController (Characters/Enemies/Core/BP_AIC_XenoCore_Enemy), through Get Aggro Target. Each poll it answers, in order:

  1. Leash. If the enemy is engaged and more than Leash Radius (7,000) from where it started, it gives up completely and walks home.
  2. Provoked? An enemy that has not been provoked has no target, however close you stand. Being hit (any health loss) provokes it, and so does detecting the leader by its Detection (Sight, Sound or Ether; None waits to be attacked). In a spawner squad, provoking one member provokes the rest (link aggro). You can also call Notify Provoked yourself to start a fight.
  3. Who. The party member with the most aggro on this enemy; the nearest player pawn it may damage if it has no aggro yet.
  4. Distance. It engages inside Engage Radius (1,600) and stays engaged out to Engage Radius × Disengage Radius Scale (2.5). Two radii stop an enemy on the boundary from engaging and disengaging on alternate frames. An engaged enemy left behind beyond that gives up, heals and walks home.

Level gap. An enemy Ignore When Levels Below (6) or more levels below the leader does not detect it, unless Always Aggro is ticked or it is a Unique Monster. It still fights back if you attack it.

Is Engaged is the signal the enemy's health bar and AI use for "in a fight". All of these settings are on the enemy controller Blueprint under XenoCore › AI. See Enemies and AI.

Who it attacks is decided by aggro, not by who you are driving: a companion that deals damage or heals can draw the enemy away from the leader, and switching the controlled character does not move the enemy's attention. See Companion AI and aggro.

docs.title: Why not Find Ability Spec From Class
docs.text:
Get Current Target finds the target-mode ability on the pawn by its ability tag, Ability.XenoCore.TargetMode, not by class.

Fails silently: looking an ability up by class

The ability system's Find Ability Spec From Class only matches the exact class. Every ability XenoCore grants is a Blueprint child of a C++ class, so passing the C++ class finds nothing, returns none and logs nothing. Use Get Target Mode Ability or Get Current Target, and in your own code find abilities by their ability tag.

Grant target mode once

A second grant of GA_XenoCore_TargetMode is a second instance with its own target, and Get Current Target returns whichever it finds first. The sample grants it only through each character's own ability set. Do not add it to a second set that the same character receives.

docs.title: What you can change
docs.text:

Default 3000; kept at or above Lock Acquire Range by the editor, the data validator and its getter Require Line Of Sight, Require On Screen Tick boxes on the Step Target From node (both) and the Is Target Still Valid node (Require Line Of Sight only) inside GA_XenoCore_TargetMode (open it, press Ctrl+F to find each node, and tick or untick the pin; then Compile and Save) Which enemies can be acquired and cycled Strafe While Locked GA_XenoCore_TargetMode › XenoCore › TargetMode Turn facing-the-target on or off entirely. See Tune targeting.

docs.title: Extending it
docs.text:
• To read the target from anything (a widget, an art, an anim Blueprint), call Get Current Target with the pawn, or listen for XenoCore.Targeting.Message.TargetChanged.
  • To change how far lock-on reaches, set Lock Acquire Range and Lock Keep Range in Class Defaults. The graph reads them through Get Lock Acquire Range and Get Lock Keep Range.
  • To change who can be targeted otherwise (line of sight, on screen), duplicate GA_XenoCore_TargetMode into Content/MyGame/, change the node pins, and grant your copy in place of the original in your characters' ability sets.
  • Only Set Current Target may change the target. A target written any other way is invisible to the reticle, the HUD and the anim instance.
  • To change how the party AI picks targets, change the party StateTree rather than target mode. See Party.

docs.title: Why it's built this way
docs.text:
For programmers: the design reasons
  • An ability, not a component. The lock has a start and an end, input, a HUD and a per-tick poll. A gameplay ability already has all of those, and instancing it per pawn makes "one target per pawn" true by construction.
  • Sorting in C++. Blueprint has no general sort node. Ordering candidates left to right on screen is the one piece that needed code; everything else is Blueprint-callable and used by the graph.
  • Horizontal angle, not screen distance. The camera looks slightly down, so a nearer enemy sits lower on screen. Scoring by full screen distance would favour a distant enemy near the horizon.
  • A switch hands the lock over. Ending the fight on a switch would sheathe both characters and reset the HUD every time the player changes who they drive; handing the lock over keeps the switch a free action, as in XC3.
  • Keep off-screen targets, cycle only on-screen ones. Dropping a lock when the enemy leaves the frame would make the arrows useless; cycling to an enemy you cannot see would be confusing.

docs.title: UI shell and HUD
docs.text:
All · 15 min read · No code

The main menu: entries on the left, one card per active party member.

What the player sees: during play, a HUD with the party's health plates, the minimap, the quest tracker, pickup badges and banners; in battle, the target plate and the Arts palette. The menu button opens an XC1-style main menu (entries on the left, a full-height card per party member) from which every other screen opens. Menus pause the game.

XenoCore's interface is built on Lyra's UI framework, CommonUI, and follows Lyra's look: clean, dark and restrained. Everything on screen falls into two groups. HUD plates sit over gameplay, take no input, and fade in and out. Screens are full menus; while one is up the game pauses and gameplay input switches off. The idea that makes the rest make sense: a HUD plate hides by fading its opacity, never by collapsing, and a screen owns the input while it is on top. Nearly every UI trap in this project is one of those two rules broken.

docs.title: What you can change
docs.text:
• Restyle the menus: Restyle the menus.
  • Add, reorder or hide a main-menu entry, or add a screen: Add a menu screen.
  • Add something to the HUD: Add a HUD element.
  • A yes/no question in a menu: Add a confirm popup.
  • A button prompt on a screen: Add an input action with a button prompt.
  • Replace any screen or HUD widget the game opens by itself: The two settings pages.

docs.title: How it fits together
docs.text:
Lyra's root layout, W_OverallUILayout, holds a stack per layer tag. XenoCore uses three of them:

Layer What goes there UI.Layer.Game The HUD: UserInterface/HUD/W_XenoCore_HUDLayout UI.Layer.Menu Every XenoCore screen: the menu shell and its screens, quest offer, shop, trade, save, title, boot cards, tutorial cards UI.Layer.Modal Lyra's own full-screen confirmation dialog. XenoCore's popups deliberately do not use it

A layer stack shows only its top widget, so pushing a screen onto the menu layer hides the one under it until the new one closes.

docs.title: The HUD
docs.text:
Experiences/LAS_XenoCore_HUD, an action set used by B_XenoCore_Experience, adds:

  • W_XenoCore_HUDLayout to UI.Layer.Game. It derives from Lyra's LyraHUDLayout and places the party member plates, the item pickup badges, the quest tracker, the quest reward banner, the level-up banner, the party join banner and the autosave badge.
  • B_XenoCore_NumberPopComponent to the player controller, for damage numbers.

The layout also carries five empty extension points (Lyra's UIExtensionPointWidget), each named by a tag. Lyra's Add Widgets action puts your own widget into one, so a new HUD element needs no edit to the layout:

Slot tag Position Stacking HUD.Slot.XenoCore.TopCenter Top centre, 48 px down Column, centred HUD.Slot.XenoCore.TopRight Top right, below the minimap and its prompt Column, right-aligned HUD.Slot.XenoCore.Center Screen centre Overlaid HUD.Slot.XenoCore.BottomCenter Bottom centre, 48 px up Column, centred HUD.Slot.XenoCore.FullScreen Whole screen, behind the rest of the HUD Overlaid

They are empty and let clicks through until something is added. See Add a HUD element.

The top-right corner holds the minimap (Minimap), and the full-screen L3 view (MinimapOverlay) sits behind everything else. Both are widgets in the layout, not extension points. See Minimap.

Other HUD elements are created by the systems that own them. The ones C++ creates by itself take their widget class from Project Settings › Game › XenoCore UI (see The two settings pages):

Element Created by Class from Target plate, player plate, Arts palette The target mode ability, Battle/Targeting/GA_XenoCore_TargetMode The ability's Class Defaults "A Talk" prompt (W_XenoCore_InteractPrompt) The interaction system, drawn under the menu layers Interact Prompt Dialogue box (W_XenoCore_DialogueBox) The dialogue anchor, a widget component drawn in screen space The anchor's Box Widget Class, else Dialogue Box NPC name plates, enemy and party overhead bars Widget components on actors, drawn in screen space The actor's Class Defaults Battle notifications (W_XenoCore_BattleNotify) The battle system Battle Notify Loot panel (W_XenoCore_LootPopup) Opening a chest Loot Popup Damage-taken and heal numbers The damage system Damage Taken Numbers, Heal Numbers (Niagara systems)

docs.title: The menu
docs.text:
Input/Abilities/GA_XenoCore_ToggleMenu (the menu button, see Controls) pushes UserInterface/W_XenoCore_MenuShell onto the menu layer. The shell holds no hand-placed buttons: its Construct calls Build Menu In Panel on its ButtonsBox, which makes one button per menu entry from Project Settings › Game › XenoCore UI › Menu Entries (plus any Additional Menu Entry Sets), sorted by Sort Order, and focuses the first. It rebuilds every time the menu opens, which is what re-asks each entry's Visible If condition.

The shell is laid out as Xenoblade Chronicles' main menu. Its parent class, XenoCoreMainMenuBase, fills in everything except the buttons each time the menu opens:

  • Party cards. One full-height card per active party member (up to seven), in party order with the leader first. The row is divided into Card Slots (7) equal slots, so a full party fills the screen and a smaller one keeps the same card width. A card shows the slot number, "Leader" on the first, the member's full-body portrait, the skill tree they are learning, their name, a divider, then Lv and HP. The cards come from Card Class on the shell's Class Defaults; the default, XenoCorePartyCardBase, builds its own look. To restyle it, make a Widget Blueprint child of XenoCorePartyCardBase and name its parts PortraitImage, SlotText, LeaderText, BranchText, NameText, LevelValueText and HealthValueText. A part you leave out is not drawn.
  • Portraits. The card draws the member definition's Menu Portrait, a full-body texture, and falls back to Portrait (the HUD bust) when it is empty. The seven sample members ship with one each. The card shows the top of it, from the crown down, filling the card's height: Portrait Crop on the card class (0.55, crown to hips) sets how much; 1.0 shows the whole body.
  • Entries are XenoCoreMenuEntryButton rows, styled like the Party Tactics list. Change Menu Button Class in the settings to use your own button. Cards, entries and the shell share the tactics panel's colours (navy panel, blue rim, Orbitron), so the menu matches the HUD.
  • Gold and play time, top right (GoldText, PlayTimeText).
  • Description, along the bottom (DescriptionText): the highlighted entry's Description.
  • Intro. Each time the menu opens it fades in, the entry list slides in from the left and the cards rise in one after another. Timings and distances are under XenoCore > Intro on the shell's Class Defaults; untick Play Intro to turn it off.
  • Groups. An entry with Starts Group set has a gap above it (Menu Group Gap in the settings, 20 px). The shipped list starts one at Save.
Sort Entry Opens 100 Equipment W_XenoCore_EquipmentScreen 200 Arts Open Arts Screen action: the Arts Screen setting 300 Skills Open Skills Screen action: the Skills Screen setting 400 Collectables W_XenoCore_ItemMenu 500 Party W_XenoCore_PartyManager 600 Quest Log Open Quest Log action: the Quest Log Screen setting 700 Change Time The C++ screen XenoCoreChangeTimeScreen: pick an hour, the screen fades and the clock jumps. See Time of day and weather 800, 900 Save, Load Open Save Screen / Open Load Screen actions: the Save Screen setting, in Save or Load mode 1000 Tutorials The C++ screen XenoCoreTutorialLogBase: every tutorial card seen so far, and the Tips on/off switch. An entry either pushes its Screen onto its Layer (empty means UI.Layer.Menu) and focuses that screen's desired target, or runs its Action (a small Blueprint you make with XenoCoreMenuAction as its parent). Entries with an Id are merged: a later entry with the same Id replaces the earlier one. See Add a menu screen.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
Opening a screen. A screen is a Common Activatable Widget pushed onto UI.Layer.Menu. When the menu layer shows anything, the game pauses and CommonUI switches to Menu input mode. The project's input config then filters every gameplay mapping context out, so A cannot also jump behind a menu. See Input and camera. The title screen opts out of the pause so its scene keeps moving.

Back. B or Escape deactivates the top screen, but only if that screen sets Is Back Handler. Screens that must be answered (the loot panel, a quest that cannot be declined) take the back action and ignore it.

Closing. Deactivating pops the screen off its layer. When the menu layer is empty the game unpauses and gameplay input returns.

Pooling. CommonUI keeps a pushed screen and reuses the same instance next time. Anything that must be fresh per visit is reset every time the screen is shown, never once when it is built.

HUD plates (widgets whose parent class is XenoCoreHudPlateBase) are created once and stay. They slide and fade in when created, Set Shown fades them in or out without removing them, and Play Outro fades out and removes. A plate that must start hidden calls Begin Hidden from its own Construct. Set Shown Immediate, Set Show Delay, Collapse All Except, Begin Hidden and Skip Intro are all Blueprint-callable.

Plates built on XenoCoreHudPlateBase: player plate, target plate, Arts palette, battle notification, quest tracker, quest reward banner, level-up banner, autosave badge.

Celebration bursts. The quest reward banner and the level-up banner each have a Celebration, and the party join banner a Joined Effect: a UI Niagara burst (UserInterface/HUD/NS_XenoCore_QuestComplete, NS_XenoCore_LevelUp, NS_XenoCore_PartyJoin) played behind the card, with its own System, Size, Scale and Duration. Clear System for no burst. A paused game does not freeze a burst. Unreal's shot screenshot command does not capture these bursts at all, so check them by eye, or with a screenshot of the whole desktop.

The stat block (W_XenoCore_StatBlock) draws a list of stat rows. Show Lines and Show Header draw what you pass; Show Character and Show Item make the block fill itself from a party member or an equipped slot and redraw when equipment changes.

Wrapping lists. Menu lists wrap from bottom to top. Ordinary panels wrap through their navigation rules. A List View cannot, so call Wrap List View once from the screen's Construct.

docs.title: The two settings pages
docs.text:
Anything C++ opens or spawns by itself (a world subsystem or a static function has no asset of its own to hold a class reference) is named on one of two pages in Edit › Project Settings › Game. Both are saved to Config/DefaultGame.ini, and every entry starts at the shipped asset, so nothing changes until you edit one.

XenoCore UI

Category Setting Must derive from Shipped Screens Save Screen XenoCoreSaveScreenBase W_XenoCore_SaveScreen Screens Quest Log Screen XenoCoreQuestLogBase W_XenoCore_QuestLog Screens Quest Offer Screen XenoCoreQuestOfferBase HUD/W_XenoCore_QuestOffer Screens Shop Screen XenoCoreShopScreenBase HUD/W_XenoCore_ShopScreen Screens Trade Screen XenoCoreTradeScreenBase HUD/W_XenoCore_TradeScreen Screens Arts Screen XenoCoreArtsScreenBase Arts/W_XenoCore_ArtsScreen Screens Skills Screen XenoCoreSkillsScreenBase Skills/W_XenoCore_SkillsScreen Screens Gem Popup XenoCoreGemPopupBase W_XenoCore_GemPopup HUD Interact Prompt XenoCoreInteractPromptBase HUD/W_XenoCore_InteractPrompt HUD Loot Popup XenoCoreLootPopupBase HUD/W_XenoCore_LootPopup HUD Battle Notify XenoCoreBattleNotifyBase HUD/W_XenoCore_BattleNotify HUD Dialogue Box should be XenoCoreDialogueBoxBase HUD/W_XenoCore_DialogueBox HUD Damage Taken Numbers, Damage Dealt Numbers, Heal Numbers Niagara systems HUD/NS_XenoCore_DamageNumbers_Taken, HUD/NS_XenoCore_DamageNumbers, HUD/NS_XenoCore_HealNumbers HUD Keyboard Key Icons Lyra's keyboard controller data Input/CommonInput_XenoCore_Keyboard Items Item Rarity Table, Rarity Pip Size, gem socket icons, tint, size and spacing A XenoCoreItemRarityRow Data Table; textures Items/DT_XenoCore_ItemRarities, Items/T_XenoCore_GemSocketFilled, _Empty. See Tutorial cards Menu Menu Entries, Additional Menu Entry Sets Entries, and XenoCoreMenuEntrySet assets The thirteen entries above Menu Menu Button Class, Menu Button Padding, Menu Group Gap A CommonUI button XenoCoreMenuEntryButton, 4 px below each, 20 px before a group

XenoCore Content

Category Setting Shipped Dialogue Dialogue Anchor (must derive from XenoCoreDialogueAnchor) Characters/NPC/BP_XenoCore_DialogueAnchor Feedback Beam Material (the heal and buff light shaft) Effects/Loot/M_XenoCore_LootBeam Debug Reaction Break / Topple / Daze Effect (for the XenoCore.Reaction command) GE_XenoCore_Reaction_Break, _Topple, _Daze

The same page also holds Startup (starting roster and New Game map overrides, title music, fallback field and battle music), Dialogue Camera Rig, Battle (victory fanfare, the sounds an AI ally plays when hit), Voice, Items (the gem registry) and Critical Hit. Each is described on the page for its system.

The widget paths in the first table are under UserInterface/.

The fallback. If a setting is cleared, fails to load, or names an asset of the wrong class, XenoCore logs a warning and uses the shipped asset. A mistake costs the replacement, never the feature. The dialogue anchor falls back one step further, to the C++ anchor.

Fails silently in a packaged build: a replacement outside the cooked folders

A setting holds a soft reference, and the cooker does not follow soft references in project settings. The shipped assets are cooked because Config/DefaultGame.ini always cooks /XenoCore/UserInterface and /XenoCore/Characters/NPC, or because other cooked assets reference them. Your replacement works in the editor, and in a packaged build it is missing, so the game falls back to the shipped asset with nothing on screen to say so. Add your folder to Project Settings › Packaging › Additional Asset Directories to Cook (DirectoriesToAlwaysCook).

docs.title: Silent traps
docs.text:
Fails silently: a plate that hides itself by collapsing never comes back

A Collapsed widget stops ticking, so it can never notice the condition that should show it again. HUD plates must hide with opacity: use Set Shown, never Set Visibility to Collapsed.

Fails silently: a popup without Is Back Handler closes the screen under it

Back falls through to the screen that asked the question, which closes and takes the popup with it. It looks exactly like "No" was pressed. Every popup must tick Is Back Handler.

Fails silently: text over a button swallows the pad's A

With the project's settings a pad's A is a simulated click at the centre of the focused widget. A text block or image drawn on top of a button, and hit-testable, takes that click instead. Set every widget layered over a button to Hit Test Invisible.

Fails silently: a Common Text Block with a style ignores its font

If a Style is set, it overrides Font and Color and Opacity. Clear Style before setting a font by hand, or set the font in a text style.

Enter and Space press the focused button

Config/DefaultGame.ini sets CommonUI's CommonButtonAcceptKeyHandling to TriggerClick, so the keyboard's accept keys click the focused button, just as the pad's A does. A pad A press is never handled twice: CommonUI's analog cursor takes it first, and only a press nothing handled reaches the button.

Hovering is not focus

A button's On Hovered does not fire for keyboard or pad navigation. Anything that acts on "the selected row" must track On Focus Received as well.

docs.title: Extending it
docs.text:
• Restyle: duplicate the styles you want into Content/MyGame/UI/ and point widgets at them. See Restyle the menus.
  • A new menu screen: make a Widget Blueprint whose parent is Common Activatable Widget (or a XenoCore screen base), set its input config to Menu, tick Is Back Handler, and add a Menu Entries row that names it. See Add a menu screen.
  • Replace a shipped screen or HUD widget: duplicate it, keep its parent class, and point the matching XenoCore UI setting at your copy. See Restyle the menus.
  • A yes/no popup: push it into the asking screen's own OverlayStack, never onto the menu layer (that would replace the screen). From Blueprint, the Ask Confirm node does the whole thing with W_XenoCore_ConfirmPopup and continues on On Yes or On No. When a popup closes, give focus back to the row that asked. See Add a confirm popup.
  • A new HUD element over gameplay: add it to a HUD.Slot.XenoCore.* slot with an Add Widgets action; give it the parent class XenoCoreHudPlateBase if it should fade in and out. See Add a HUD element.
  • A button prompt on a screen: add a row to your own action table and bind it; see Add an input action with a button prompt.

Never edit Lyra's UI assets; copy what you need.

For programmers: classes

Plates derive from UXenoCoreHudPlateBase; the stat block is UXenoCoreStatBlockBase; menu actions UXenoCoreMenuAction; the settings pages are UXenoCoreUISettings and UXenoCoreContentSettings. The game pauses through AXenoCorePlayerController whenever UI.Layer.Menu is non-empty. Widgets opened by systems with no asset of their own come from UXenoCoreBattleNotifySubsystem, UXenoCoreLootPopupSubsystem, UXenoCoreDamageNumberSubsystem and UXenoCoreInteractionSubsystem. From C++, a confirm popup is UXenoCoreConfirmPopupBase::AskWithAnswer.

docs.title: Why it's built this way
docs.text:
For programmers
  • Lyra's look, not an imitation of a console RPG. XenoCore ships as a Lyra template, so a buyer expects an interface that belongs to Lyra. The layouts and information follow the genre; the chrome is Lyra's. XenoCore authors its own style assets in Lyra's idiom rather than pointing at Lyra's, apart from the font.
  • Opacity, not visibility. HUD plates have two opacity drivers, the entrance/exit and the show/hide fade. They are multiplied through one function, so neither can erase the other.
  • Pause by the layer, not by a screen. Pushing a sub-screen deactivates the shell, so a shell-scoped pause would resume the game under an open screen. "Is anything on the menu layer" is the question that matters.
  • Menu input filtering, not ability blocking. Stopping gameplay input at the mapping-context level stops every action at once, including ones added later.
  • Settings, not asset paths. A subsystem has no asset of its own to hold a class reference, so the widgets C++ opens used to be paths typed into the code, and swapping one meant editing the plugin. They are now project settings with a shipped default and a logged fallback, so a buyer swaps a screen without touching XenoCore, and a bad value cannot break the feature.
  • Data-driven menu. Eleven hand-wired buttons meant every new screen was an edit to a shipped asset. An entry list merged by Id lets a plugin add, reword or hide entries from its own content.
  • Rows built in C++. Lyra's list view drops null items without warning, so several XenoCore screens build their rows into a vertical box from C++, where what was built can be logged.

Next: Input and camera · Events you can listen to

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
All · under 2 hours · No code

One path, in order. Each page ends with what you now have, and links to the next.

# Page Time You finish with 1 Requirements 5 min The engine and tools installed 2 Install and first launch 20 min The project open in the editor 3 Play the sample 15 min A feel for every system, in play 4 Tour of the project 15 min Knowing where everything lives 5 Your first change 10 min A character changed by you 6 Your first art 30 min Your own Art, used in combat 7 Your first enemy 30 min Your own enemy, placed and fought 8 Where next 2 min The next section for the way you work

Keep the Glossary and Controls open alongside.

All · reference
