docs.title: Where the bindings live
docs.text:
Asset Contains Input/Mappings/IMC_XenoCore XenoCore's actions: targeting, interact, palette, party switch, menu, camera, quest tracker /Game/Input/Mappings/IMC_Default Lyra's movement, look and jump Input/InputData_XenoCore Which input tag each action sends to the ability system

To rebind a key, open the mapping context, find the action's row and change its key. To add a new action with its own button prompt, see Add an input action with a button prompt.

Fails silently: a rebound key and its on-screen prompt

Some prompts (the Party Tactics hint, the quest tracker toggle, tutorial cards) draw their glyph from a row of UserInterface/Foundation/DT_XenoCore_Actions, not from the mapping context. Rebinding the key in IMC_XenoCore alone leaves those prompts showing the old key. Change the matching row's keyboard and gamepad keys in DT_XenoCore_Actions as well.

docs.title: Your first art
docs.text:
Designer · 30 min · No code

Result: a new Art called Stone Cleave. It hits hard, Breaks the enemy, and has its own cooldown. It sits on the palette and you use it on a minion in the gym.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Your first change. You should know the member definition and pawn Blueprint.
  • Glossary: Art, palette, Break.

docs.title: How an Art is put together
docs.text:
An Art is one data asset. Everything that makes it different from another Art lives there: name, power, cooldown, range, area, reactions, animation, palette look. The shared Art ability reads it and does the rest, so a standard Art needs no Blueprint and no code.

Piece Sample Needed? Art definition Battle/Arts/DA_XenoCore_AirSlash Always Art ability Blueprint GA_XenoCore_BackSlash Only for custom behaviour. Leave Ability Class empty to use the shared one. Montage AM_XenoCore_BackSlash Optional; reuse an existing one to start Cooldown tag Cooldown.XenoCore.Art.AirSlash Always, and unique to this Art

DA_XenoCore_AirSlash is the data-only example: it has no ability Blueprint of its own. Keep it open beside yours for reference, but do not duplicate it. A copy brings Air Slash's Break and side-Slow effects along with it; start every new Art blank.

docs.title: 1. Create a blank Art
docs.text:
1. In the Content Browser, right-click Content and choose New Folder. Name it MyGame, and inside it make a folder Arts.
  2. In MyGame/Arts, right-click empty space and choose Data › Data Asset. In the class picker, search for and pick XenoCoreArtDefinition, click Select, and name the new asset DA_StoneCleave.

DA_XenoCore_SlitEdge and DA_XenoCore_StreamEdge in Battle/Arts were made this way, if you want finished examples to compare against. No character learns them in the shipped tables.

docs.title: 2. Give it its own cooldown tag
docs.text:
Every Art needs a cooldown tag no other Art uses.

  1. Double-click DA_StoneCleave to open it. Under Art, find Cooldown Tag and click its drop-down to open the tag picker.
  2. Click the + button at the top of the picker (its tooltip reads Add New Gameplay Tag). In Name, type Cooldown.MyGame.Art.StoneCleave. For Source, pick a tag file of your own project rather than XenoCore's: a template update replaces XenoCore's tag file. If the list offers only XenoCore's and Lyra's, first make one in Project Settings › GameplayTags with Add new Gameplay Tag source... (for example MyGameTags.ini). Click Add New Tag.
  3. Tick the new tag so it is selected.

Two Arts sharing a tag share a cooldown

If Stone Cleave used Air Slash's tag, using either Art would put both on cooldown. Saving DA_StoneCleave catches it: the editor reports an error, "Cooldown Tag ... is also used by DA_XenoCore_AirSlash". Leaving the tag empty is an error too, because the Art has a cooldown.

docs.title: 3. Set what it does
docs.text:
Still in DA_StoneCleave:

  1. Display Name: Stone Cleave. Description: A heavy blow that Breaks the target. The palette shows name: description.
  2. Category: Break. Attribute: Physical. Effect Type: Damage. Target Type: Enemy.
  3. Power: expand it and set Value. Open Battle/Arts/DA_XenoCore_AirSlash beside yours to see its Power › Value, and set yours to about double that. Leave Curve empty. Value multiplies everything, so it must never be 0.
  4. Cooldown Duration: 12. This is in seconds. 0 means no cooldown, which is only for Talent Arts.
  5. Effects (under Art › Effects): this list is what the Art inflicts. Click + to add one entry, expand it, and set Effect GE_XenoCore_Reaction_Break, Chance 1, Condition Always. Leave Duration at 0: a reaction carries its own duration.
  6. Montage (under Art › Animation): AM_XenoCore_BackSlash, to reuse an existing strike for now.
  7. Under Art › Palette, set Palette Glyph to the one Air Slash uses and Glyph Colour to something distinct.
  8. Leave Ability Class empty.
  9. Save.

Other settings worth knowing, all on the same asset:

Setting What it does Distance How close the user must be. Used out of range, the character runs in and strikes on arrival. 0 = no limit. Area, Area Radius, Cone Angle Single target, a circle around you or the target, or a cone Target Type Enemy, yourself, one ally, or the whole party Effect Type, Attribute Damage or heal or neither; physical or ether stats Positional Bonuses Extra power from behind or the side Montage Play Rate, Impact Fraction Animation speed, and when in the animation the hit lands

docs.title: 4. Teach it to the party
docs.text:
Which Arts a character learns lives in a learnset: a Data Table the character's pawn Blueprint names as its Art Learn Table.

  1. Open your leader's learnset, Characters/Party/Learnsets/DT_XenoCore_ArtLearnset_Kael for Kael. (To find any character's table, open their pawn Blueprint, click Class Defaults, and look at XenoCore › Arts › Art Learn Table.) (DT_XenoCore_ArtLearnset_Default is the table on B_XenoCore_PartyMember_Base, used by the colour-mannequin sample members, not by the VRoid party.)
  2. Click Add in the Data Table editor's toolbar to add a row. Right-click the new row, choose Rename, and name it Lv01_StoneCleave (the name is free text; this form sorts by level). With the row selected, set in the Row Editor below:
    • Art: DA_StoneCleave
    • Unlock Level: 1
    • Default Slot: -1. This means learned but not placed on the palette; you'll place it yourself in the next step.
  3. Save.

Each sample character has their own table

Kael, Mira, Nia, Dorran, Isolde, Sabine and Tamsin each point at their own learnset in the same folder: DT_XenoCore_ArtLearnset_Kael, _Mira, _Nia, _Dorran, _Isolde, _Sabine and _Tamsin. Add the same row to each one you want to learn Stone Cleave, or it will not reach them.

docs.title: Test it
docs.text:
1. Open Maps/L_XenoCore_Gym and press Play.
  2. Open the menu (pad Y, keyboard I) and go to Arts. With your leader selected, put Stone Cleave in an empty palette slot.
  3. Close the menu and engage a minion. Stone Cleave is on the palette in its colour.
  4. Use it. The minion shows Break, and Stone Cleave greys out for 12 seconds.

docs.title: If it doesn't work
docs.text:
The Art greys out and won't fire

It is on cooldown. (A Talent Art also greys while the Talent Gauge is not full.) Range and position never grey an Art: out of range, the character runs in to reach the target first, and a side or back position only adds its bonus.

It fires but does nothing

Power is 0, or the Effects list is empty and Effect Type is "no damage or healing".

Stone Cleave isn't in the Arts menu

The row is in a learnset that character's pawn does not use as its Art Learn Table (the seven sample characters each have their own), or its Unlock Level is above the character's level.

Saving DA_StoneCleave reports an error

The Message Log names the problem: an empty Display Name, an empty Cooldown Tag, or a Cooldown Tag another Art already uses. Fix it and save again. See What saving an Art definition checks.

docs.title: You now have
docs.text:
Your own Art, used in combat, and the knowledge that an Art is data.

Next: Your first enemy

docs.title: Your first change
docs.text:
Designer · 10 min · No code

Result: your party leader has a new name and portrait and starts at a higher level. You'll see it on the HUD and in the Party menu the moment you press Play.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text: • Tour of the project

docs.title: How a party member is put together
docs.text:
Each party member is two assets:

Asset Example Decides Member definition Characters/VRoid/Kael/PartyMember_VRoid_L Name, portrait, battle role, and which pawn Blueprint to spawn Pawn Blueprint named in the definition's Member Class Mesh, abilities, stats, starting level, the Arts they can learn

The definition is who the character is; the pawn Blueprint is the body they fight in. A reserve member has no body in the world at all, only a definition, which is why the name and portrait live there.

docs.title: 1. Find your leader
docs.text:
1. In the Content Browser, open XenoCore Content › Characters › Party and double-click BP_XenoCore_Party. It is the party component: it holds the roster.
  2. Click Class Defaults in the toolbar. In the Details panel, under XenoCore › Party, look at Starting Roster. The members are fielded in this order until Max Active Members is reached; the rest start in reserve. Leader Slot says which of the active members you control, 0 being the first.
  3. In the sample, the roster is two VRoid characters, Kael (PartyMember_VRoid_L, the leader) and Mira (PartyMember_VRoid_K). The other five sample characters join later, recruited from NPCs on Gaur Plain. Click the Browse arrow (the magnifying glass) beside Kael's entry: the Content Browser jumps to Characters/VRoid/Kael/PartyMember_VRoid_L. Double-click it to open it.

docs.title: 2. Rename them and change their portrait
docs.text:
In the member definition, under XenoCore › Party:

  1. Set Display Name to a name of your own.
  2. Set Portrait to a different texture from Characters/Party/Portraits, for example T_XenoCore_Portrait_Orange. Portrait is the head-and-shoulders picture on the HUD and in most menus.
  3. Save.

The main menu uses a second picture

The main menu's character cards draw Menu Portrait, a full-body picture, from the same asset. Kael has one, so his main-menu card keeps showing him until you change Menu Portrait too, or clear it (an empty Menu Portrait falls back to Portrait).

docs.title: 3. Start them at a higher level
docs.text:
1. In the same definition, find Member Class (under XenoCore › Party). Click the magnifying glass beside it to find the Blueprint it names (B_XenoCore_Party_VRoid_L for Kael) in the Content Browser, and double-click it.
  2. Click Class Defaults. In the Details panel, under XenoCore › Combatant, set Combatant Level to 20.
  3. Compile and Save.

Combatant Level is the level a character starts at. After that the progression system owns their level, and it is saved with the game. Every stat is read from a curve at that level, so HP, Strength, Ether and Agility all rise together.

docs.title: Test it
docs.text:
1. Open Maps/L_XenoCore_Gym and press Play.
  2. The leader's HUD plate shows the new name and portrait.
  3. Open the menu (pad Y, keyboard I) and go to the Party screen. The leader reads Lv 20, with higher HP and stats than before.

Starting from the title screen instead

Continue on the title screen loads your newest save, and a save remembers each character's level. A changed starting level shows up in a New Game, or in a map started directly with Play, as above.

docs.title: If it doesn't work
docs.text:
The character never appears

Member Class is empty, or its pawn has no Combatant Pawn Data. The party cannot spawn that character. To check, right-click the member definition and choose Asset Actions › Validate Assets: the Message Log names the missing setting. Set both.

The old name or level still shows

You started from Continue on the title screen, which loads a save, or you edited a different character than the leader. Start from the gym as above, and check that the Starting Roster entry at Leader Slot is the definition you edited.

The level changed but the stats did not

The pawn's Stats Effect is empty. The character then runs on default stats, and an error naming the pawn is logged on every Play. Set it back to the stats effect it had.

docs.title: Child or duplicate?
docs.text:
Every new thing you make starts from something XenoCore ships. Which way you start depends on what kind of asset it is:

You are making Do this Why A Blueprint: a party member, enemy, weapon actor, Art ability, NPC, AI controller Right-click the base and choose Create Child Blueprint Class (for example from B_XenoCore_Party_VRoid_Base, B_XenoCore_Enemy_Base, B_XenoCore_Sword_Base, GA_XenoCore_Art_Base, GA_XenoCore_TalentArt_Base) The child keeps everything the base does, and picks up fixes when XenoCore updates. A duplicate is frozen at the day you copied it, and carries the sample's own settings with it. A data asset or table row: an Art definition, drop table, quest, member definition, stats effect, curve row Right-click a sample and choose Duplicate, then change it These hold only numbers and references, so there is nothing to inherit. An item definition: a weapon, armour piece or gem item Duplicate an item of the same kind. Never create one blank An item definition cannot have a Blueprint parent, and a blank one has no equipment settings, so it cannot be equipped. A menu or HUD widget you want to restyle Duplicate the shipped widget into your own folder A child widget cannot change the layout it inherits; the duplicate keeps the same C++ parent, so its behaviour is unchanged.

Not sure which kind it is?

Open the asset. If the editor shows a Graph or Viewport tab, it is a Blueprint: make a child. If it opens straight to a Details panel or a table, it is data: duplicate it.

docs.title: You now have
docs.text:
A character changed by you, and the two-asset shape every party member shares.

Next: Your first art

docs.title: Your first enemy
docs.text:
Designer · 30 min · No code

Result: a new enemy with its own name and level. It fights with a Break and a Topple Art and always drops a gold chest. You place it in the gym map and fight it.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text: • Tour of the project. You should know where the XenoCore content folder is.

docs.title: How an enemy is put together
docs.text:
An enemy is one Blueprint plus a few assets it points at:

Piece Sample asset What it decides Enemy Blueprint Characters/Enemies/Minion/B_XenoCore_Minion_Melee Name, level, rewards, loot, death, mesh Pawn data PawnData_XenoCore_Minion_Melee Which abilities it has: attack, hit reaction, knock-downs, death Arts Minion/Arts/DA_XenoCore_Minion_Rend, DA_XenoCore_Minion_Sweep The Arts it uses in a fight, listed on the Blueprint's Arts Stats effect Battle/Attributes/GE_XenoCore_BaseStats_Minion_Melee Its stats at its level, read from a curve table Drop table Inventory/Loot/DA_XenoCore_Drops_Minion What its chests can hold AI BP_AIC_XenoCore_Enemy + ST_XenoCore_EnemyFreeroam How it patrols, engages, chases, gives up, and picks Arts

The AI is shared by every enemy, so a new enemy needs none of its own. You will make a child of the minion Blueprint and change only what makes this enemy different.

docs.title: 1. Make a folder for your own content
docs.text:
Put your assets in your own folder, not inside XenoCore's. Template updates replace XenoCore's folders, and your work should survive them.

  1. In the Content Browser, go to Content and create a folder, for example MyGame/Enemies.

docs.title: 2. Make a child of the minion
docs.text:
1. In the Content Browser, go to XenoCore Content › Characters › Enemies › Minion (under Plugins; the folder may read just XenoCore). If it is missing, tick Plugin Content in the Content Browser's Settings; see Tour of the project.
  2. Right-click B_XenoCore_Minion_Melee and choose Create Child Blueprint Class. Name it B_MyEnemy.
  3. Drag B_MyEnemy into MyGame/Enemies and choose Move Here.

A child starts identical to its parent and keeps up with it: anything you do not change still comes from the minion. The seven sample enemy types in Minion/Variants are made exactly this way.

A child of the melee minion, not of the enemy base

B_XenoCore_Enemy_Base is the parent every enemy shares, and it has no mesh, stats or abilities. The melee minion is the complete working example. Duplicate data assets (pawn data, ability sets, stats effects) when you need your own; make Blueprints as children.

docs.title: 3. Give it a name and a level
docs.text:
1. Open B_MyEnemy and click Class Defaults.
  2. Under XenoCore › Enemy, set:
    • Display Name to Stonejaw. This appears on the target badge when you lock on.
    • Enemy Level to 8. The level scales every stat through the curve table, so this alone makes it tougher than the low-level sample minions.
    • Experience Reward to 30, double the melee minion's 15. This is the base amount: the inherited Experience Level Scale row multiplies it by the enemy's level, and the level-difference adjustment is applied after that.
  3. Compile and Save.

Keep enemies within reach of the party's level

An enemy far below the party's level never notices the party: it does not start a fight by sight, sound or ether, though it still fights back when attacked. That is the Ignore When Levels Below setting (6 levels by default) on the AI controller every enemy shares, Characters/Enemies/Core/BP_AIC_XenoCore_Enemy › Class Defaults › XenoCore › AI, and it is intended. If your enemy won't start a fight, check its level first.

docs.title: 4. Make it drop a gold chest
docs.text:
1. In Class Defaults, under XenoCore › Loot, tick Always Gold Chest.
  2. Leave Drop Table as the minion's DA_XenoCore_Drops_Minion for now. The seven sample enemy types each use their family's table instead (DA_XenoCore_Drops_Grunt, _Skirmisher, _Bulwark, _Brute), with level bands on their entries.
  3. Compile and Save.

Chests hold a drop-table reference and a tier, and roll their contents when they are opened, not when they drop. Designing your own drop table is covered in a recipe.

docs.title: 5. Place it
docs.text:
1. Open the map Maps/L_XenoCore_Gym. The sample minions are already placed here.
  2. Drag B_MyEnemy from the Content Browser into the level, on the floor, away from the other minions so you can fight it alone.
  3. Save the level.

Click the placed enemy in the viewport: its Details panel shows the same XenoCore settings, and a value changed there affects only that one placement. Display Name, Enemy Level, Experience Reward and Always Gold Chest are among them, and so are its Patrol Points (XenoCore › AI › Patrol), which you can drag in the viewport. That is how one enemy Blueprint becomes many different monsters in a map. For a squad that wanders, fights together and comes back after you defeat it, place a XenoCore Enemy Spawner instead: see Place enemies.

docs.title: Test it
docs.text:
1. Press Play.
  2. Walk up to your enemy and lock on to it (pad RB, keyboard Tab). The target badge reads Stonejaw.
  3. Attack it. Whether an enemy attacks first depends on its Detection (XenoCore › AI › Detection): None (passive) waits to be hit, Sight, Sound and Ether start the fight themselves. Try changing it on the placed enemy.
  4. Fight it. It auto-attacks and uses its Arts: Rend, which Breaks, then Sweep, which Topples the Broken target. If a companion hits it harder than you, it turns on the companion: the red ring under its target moves with it.
  5. Defeat it. After about two seconds a gold chest appears where it fell. Open it.

docs.title: If it doesn't work
docs.text:
It takes no damage and cannot die

Enemy Pawn Data is empty. Death and damage come from the abilities that pawn data grants, so without it the enemy is invulnerable. An error naming the enemy is logged. Set it back to PawnData_XenoCore_Minion_Melee.

Its stats double up after a level change

If you make your own stats effect, every modifier in it must use Override, not Add. Otherwise re-applying the effect stacks the numbers on top of the old ones.

The chest opens empty

The drop table has no pool for that chest tier (Wooden, Silver or Gold). Every tier a chest can roll needs its own pool. A warning is logged.

Fails silently: it never uses its Arts

An enemy uses only the Arts on its Blueprint's Arts list (XenoCore › Enemy › Arts). A child of the minion keeps Rend and Sweep; if the list is empty, the enemy only auto-attacks and nothing is logged.

It never starts a fight on its own

Its Detection is None (passive), or it is 6 or more levels below your party leader (see the tip in step 3). Hit it first, or change Detection on the placed enemy.

docs.title: You now have
docs.text:
Your own enemy, placed in a map and fought. You also know which settings make one Blueprint into many monsters.

Next: Where next

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: All · reference

docs.title: About this manual
docs.text: XC1 Short for Xenoblade Chronicles (2010), the real-time party RPG whose combat rules XenoCore's defaults follow. The manual says "XC1's value" or "XC1-style" when a default copies that game's number or rule, so you know where it came from and that changing it is a design choice, not a fix. XenoCore is an independent project, not affiliated with or endorsed by the game's makers, and you need no knowledge of the game to use it.

docs.title: Combat
docs.text: Art A special move a character chooses from the palette. Each has its own cooldown. Defined by an Art definition asset; see Your first art. Talent Art A character's signature Art. It has no cooldown; instead it spends the Talent gauge. Talent gauge A per-character meter that fills as the character auto-attacks. The Talent Art can be used once the gauge covers its Gauge Cost (a full gauge, unless the Art says otherwise). Auto-attack The basic attack a character repeats on its own while engaged. You don't press a button for it. Palette The row of Arts on the combat HUD. Move the selection with the D-pad and confirm to use one. Learnset A Data Table, named on a character's pawn Blueprint as Art Learn Table, listing which Arts the character learns and at what level. See Arts. Art Points (AP) What raising an Art's level costs. Each character earns them from kills and spends them in the Arts menu. Cooldown tag The gameplay tag an Art's cooldown is recorded under. Every Art needs its own; two Arts with the same tag share one cooldown. Party cursor The highlight on a party member's HUD row (and a white ring under their body) used to pick an ally: by an Art that targets one ally, or by holding a trigger to switch characters. Break, Topple, Daze A chain of reactions. Break staggers the enemy's guard. A Broken enemy can be Toppled, knocked down and unable to act. A Toppled enemy can be Dazed, which keeps it down longer. Each step only works on the one before, so chaining Arts in the right order is the core of combat. Status effect A timed effect on a character, such as Slow, shown as an icon on the HUD and a popup over the character's head. Target mode, lock on Selecting one enemy to fight. The camera and your attacks follow it. Engage, disengage An enemy starts fighting (engage) or gives up and returns home (disengage). An enemy engages once it is attacked, or when it notices the party by its Detection (sight, sound or ether). An enemy chased too far from its home, or outrun, gives up and recovers its health. Detection How an enemy notices the party before being hit: None (passive), Sight, Sound (hears the leader running) or Ether (feels an ether art). An enemy 6 or more levels below the party leader notices nothing, but still fights back when attacked. Squad, spawner A XenoCore Enemy Spawner keeps a squad of enemies alive in one place. When one is provoked the rest join in, only the last one killed drops a chest, and fallen members come back after a while, out of sight. Aggro Which party member an enemy is attacking. Party Gauge A party-wide meter of three bars, filled by critical hits and other battle events. One bar revives a downed member. See Party Gauge and revive. Downed A party member at 0 HP kneels and waits to be revived instead of dying. The battle is lost when everyone is down, or the member you control is down and the gauge has less than one bar. Party tactics Standing orders for the whole party or one member, such as who to attack and which Arts to use. Tap X to switch focus, hold X for the list. See Party tactics. Skill A passive upgrade a character learns by spending SP. It raises a stat, adds a bonus another system asks for (such as more healing), or reacts to something (a buff at the start of a battle). See Skills. Skill tree, branch A character's skills, as up to five branches of five skills each. Skills in a branch are learnt top to bottom. One branch is selected at a time; SP goes only into that one. SP (skill points) What skills cost. Every party member earns SP from each kill; benched members earn the Reserve Skill Point Rate, which the sample sets to 0 (XC1 uses 90%). SP earned after the selected branch is complete is lost. Trait The stat bonus the selected branch gives, such as Agility +8. It grows as more of the branch's skills are learnt, and moves to another branch when you select it. Gem A stat bonus set into a socket on a weapon or armour piece. Its strength is rolled when it is found, and each stat's total from gems is capped per character. Rarity Common, Rare or Legendary, shown as a name colour and pips in every menu. It belongs to the item definition, so a rarer copy is a separate item. Weapon type What kind of weapon an item is, such as Greatsword. Each character can wield only the types listed on them, and the type holds the weapon's stances, draw, sheathe and attack animations, reach and gem sockets. Drawn, sheathed Weapon in hand for battle, or stowed for exploring. Characters draw automatically when a fight starts.

docs.title: Party
docs.text: Party, roster The roster is every character you have. The party is the ones currently fielded. Active member, reserve member Active members are in the world and fight. Reserve members are on the bench, with no body in the world. They gain experience at the Reserve Experience Rate on Game/BP_XenoCore_Progression, which the sample sets to 0 (XC1 uses 90%). The sample fields up to seven, so a member is benched only by your choice. Leader The active member you control. Tap LT or RT to switch to the previous or next member, in or out of battle, or pick one in the Party menu. Member definition The data asset that says who a character is: name, portrait, role, and which pawn to use. Pawn Blueprint The character Blueprint a member definition spawns (its Member Class): the body, with its mesh, abilities, stats and starting level. Anim profile A data asset holding one character's own combat clips (reactions, death, victory emote) and idle personality. Any empty slot uses the shared default.

docs.title: Stats
docs.text: Strength, Ether Physical and ether attack power. Agility Chance to hit and to evade. Weight Total weight of worn equipment. It is subtracted from Agility. Physical defence, Ether defence Damage reduction. On party members these are points from equipment; on enemies, a percentage. Statline, stats effect The gameplay effect (GE_XenoCore_BaseStats_*) that sets a character's base stats at its level, read from a curve table. It is named on the character Blueprint as Stats Effect and re-applied on every level-up. Curve table A table of values by level. Stats and level-difference modifiers are curve tables. Experience to the next level is a Data Table instead, Game/DT_XenoCore_ExperienceCurves, with one row per character.

docs.title: Unreal and Lyra terms
docs.text: Experience (Lyra) The set of rules a map runs: which pawn, which HUD, which features. Not related to character XP. Game Feature plugin A plugin that switches its content on only when an Experience asks for it. XenoCore is one. Pawn data The asset that says which abilities and input a pawn gets. Ability set A Lyra data asset listing abilities, effects and attribute sets to grant together. Pawn data names the ability sets a character gets; a weapon's ability set grants its Talent Art. Class Defaults The button in a Blueprint editor's toolbar that shows the Blueprint's own settings in the Details panel. Most XenoCore settings are there, grouped under XenoCore › .... Data Asset, Data Table Unreal's two ways of holding plain data. A Data Asset is one record (an Art, a member definition); a Data Table is many rows of one shape (a learnset, a skill tree). Neither needs code. StateTree Unreal's state machine asset for AI. Companions and enemies each run one; the numbers on its tasks are what you tune. EQS (Environment Query System) Unreal's tool for scoring places in the world. Companions use it to pick where to stand round an enemy. Game Feature Data The asset named after a Game Feature plugin (XenoCore, at the top of XenoCore Content). Its Actions add XenoCore's components and input to the game while the plugin is active. Tag relationships Game/TagRelationships_XenoCore, a table of "while a character has this tag, these abilities cannot start". How XenoCore stops jumping in a menu or acting while downed, as data. Gameplay tag A hierarchical name such as Status.XenoCore.Reaction.Break, used to label states and abilities. Gameplay ability, gameplay effect From Unreal's ability system: an ability is something a character does; an effect changes stats or applies tags, for a moment or for a duration.

docs.title: Install and first launch
docs.text:
All · 20 min · No code · Last tested: 2026-10-10 (stock Lyra 5.8, UE 5.8.1, VRM4U_5_8_20260912)

XenoCore is a Game Feature plugin for Lyra, delivered as C++ source plus content. You add it and the free VRM4U plugin to a Lyra project, open the project (Unreal compiles XenoCore the first time), and click Apply once. Nothing in Lyra is edited by hand.

Before you start, install Visual Studio 2022 with the Game development with C++ workload; see Requirements. The first open cannot finish without it.

docs.title: 1. Create a Lyra project
docs.text:
1. In the Epic Games Launcher, open Fab Library, find Lyra Starter Game (free), and create a project from it for Unreal Engine 5.8.
  2. Put it on a short path, such as C:\Projects\MyRPG. Long paths can break the C++ build on Windows.

You can also use a Lyra project you already have. XenoCore only adds settings; see What Apply changes for the list.

docs.title: 2. Add the plugin
docs.text:
From Fab: in the Epic Games Launcher's Fab Library, click Install to Engine on XenoCore and choose 5.8. The launcher puts it in the engine's plugin folder, C:\Program Files\Epic Games\UE_5.8\Engine\Plugins\Marketplace\XenoCore. XenoCore cannot run from there, because it is built on Lyra's own game code, so move (cut, not copy) that XenoCore folder into your project as below. Leaving a second copy in the engine folder makes Unreal find the plugin twice.

From a zip download: unzip it and copy its XenoCore folder into the project.

Either way, it goes in the project's Plugins/GameFeatures folder, so you have:

MyRPG/
  Lyra.uproject
  Plugins/
    GameFeatures/
      ShooterCore/
      XenoCore/          <- here
        XenoCore.uplugin

It must be in Plugins/GameFeatures of the project, not in the engine's plugin folder: XenoCore is C++ built on Lyra's own game module, so it compiles with the project.

You do not need to edit Lyra.uproject; the plugin switches itself on.

docs.title: Add VRM4U (the VRoid party needs it)
docs.text:
The sample party is seven VRoid characters, and their skeletons, faces, toon materials and hair physics run on VRM4U, a free plugin by ruyo (MIT licence). XenoCore lists it as a dependency, so the project will not open without it.

  1. Download the VRM4U release for Unreal Engine 5.8 from its GitHub releases page (github.com/ruyo/VRM4U): the file named VRM4U_5_8_<date>.zip. XenoCore is tested with VRM4U_5_8_20260912.zip (last full install test: 2026-10-14, stock Lyra 5.8, UE 5.8.1).
  2. Unzip it into the project folder (where Lyra.uproject is). The zip already contains a Plugins/VRM4U folder, so it lands in the right place:
MyRPG/
  Plugins/
    VRM4U/             <- here
    GameFeatures/
      XenoCore/

docs.title: Let Lyra's editor build compile VRM4U
docs.text:
VRM4U is compiled from source with your project, and stock Lyra's editor target refuses the raw object pointers VRM4U's headers use, so the first build fails with dozens of "Native pointer usage in member declaration" errors unless you change one line first. Open Source/LyraEditor.Target.cs in your project folder (any text editor) and change

NativePointerMemberBehaviorOverride = PointerMemberBehavior.Disallow;

to

NativePointerMemberBehaviorOverride = PointerMemberBehavior.AllowAndLog;

This relaxes a code-style check for the editor build only; it changes no behaviour and no data, and packaged games are not affected. XenoCore's own C++ passes the strict setting.

docs.title: 3. Open the project
docs.text:
Double-click Lyra.uproject. If Windows asks which engine to use, pick 5.8.

Unreal then says that modules are missing or built with a different engine version (it names XenoCoreRuntime, XenoCoreEditor, and possibly VRM4U's modules) and asks whether to rebuild them. Click Yes. This compiles XenoCore's C++ inside your project and takes several minutes the first time; it is expected, because the plugin is delivered as source. If the build fails, Unreal offers to open the log; see Troubleshooting > Build and editor. If you would rather watch the build, right-click Lyra.uproject, choose Generate Visual Studio project files, open the solution and build the LyraEditor target in Development Editor.

After the build, the first open compiles shaders and builds cached data, and can take a long time once (10 minutes or more); later opens take under a minute. Several things you may see on the way are Unreal's, Lyra's or Windows', not XenoCore's, and are harmless:

  • "Wait for ZenServer?": Unreal's shared cache is doing maintenance. Click Yes.
  • "New plugins are available": Unreal noticing VRM4U and XenoCore. Click Dismiss; both are already enabled.
  • A Windows Firewall prompt for "Lyra": Windows asking about a program it has not seen before. XenoCore is single-player and needs no network; either answer is fine. While it is open, the editor behind it does not respond to clicks.
  • Red and yellow AutomationTool text over the viewport ending in Build FAILED and error CS0579: Duplicate 'System.Reflection...': Lyra's own build scripts failing a platform-SDK check. It does not affect the editor or play.
  • "Project file is out of date. Would you like to update it?": stock Lyra's Lyra.uproject lists three platform plugins (PlayFabParty, XInputDevice, GameInputWindows) slightly differently from the engine. Update or Not Now are both fine.

docs.title: 4. Apply the project settings
docs.text:
A few seconds after the editor opens, a notification appears in the bottom-right:

XenoCore needs N project setting(s) to run in this project. [Apply] [Not now]

  1. Click Apply.
  2. Click Restart Now on the notification that follows. If anything is unsaved, Unreal offers to save it first.

After the restart the editor opens on XenoCore's title screen map, L_XenoCore_FrontEnd.

If you clicked Not now, or the notification has gone, use Tools > XenoCore > Apply XenoCore Project Settings. It is safe to run any number of times.

docs.title: 5. Press Play
docs.text: Press Play. The boot screens run, then the title screen. Choose New Game: you start on Gaur Plain with Kael and Mira. See Play the sample.

docs.title: What Apply changes
docs.text:
Apply writes to the project's own Config/Default*.ini files, so every change is visible and yours to edit. A setting you have already changed yourself is left alone and listed in the Output Log under LogXenoSetup, with the value XenoCore expected.

File Setting Why DefaultEngine.ini Game default map and editor startup map: L_XenoCore_FrontEnd Boot into XenoCore's title screen, not Lyra's. Changed only while they still name Lyra's maps DefaultEngine.ini Physical surface SurfaceType4 = Grass Grass footstep sounds and effects DefaultEngine.ini r.TSR.16BitVALU*=0 Avoids an engine warning when the editor opens DefaultEngine.ini CommonUI.SyncCursorToFocusedWidgetOnInputMethodChange=0 Gamepad focus in menus does not jump back and forth DefaultGame.ini Loading screen widget: W_XenoCore_LoadingScreen XenoCore's loading screen DefaultGame.ini CommonButtonAcceptKeyHandling=TriggerClick Enter and Space press the focused menu button DefaultGame.ini Footstep context map: SurfaceType4 -> SurfaceType.Grass Grass footsteps DefaultGame.ini Maps and folders to cook (title screen, Gym, Gaur Plain), boot movies to stage A packaged game includes XenoCore's maps, UI and movies DefaultGame.ini Save-screen location names and story line Save files name the place they were made DefaultInput.ini Input mode query and default input mode (InputMode.Game) Gameplay input stops while a menu is open DefaultInput.ini Gamepad View button removed from Back View opens the quest tracker DefaultGameplayTags.ini Tag SurfaceType.Grass Grass footsteps

To see what is still pending without changing anything, type XenoCore.ProjectSetup in the editor's console (the Output Log's Cmd box); XenoCore.ProjectSetup apply writes the steps, the same as the menu entry.

docs.title: You now have
docs.text:
The plugin installed, the project set up, and the sample running.

Next: Play the sample

docs.title: Play the sample
docs.text:
All · 15 min · No code

Gaur Plain, the sample region, at the New Game start.

Fifteen minutes of play shows you every system you will build with. Keep Controls open the first time.

New Game starts you with Kael and Mira at Ragrinar Canyon Path, the canyon mouth at Gaur Plain's west tip. Gaur Plain is a 30 to 60 minute slice with seven quests and three hubs:

Where Who is there The canyon mouth (start) Save point; the Field Cook (quest Field Rations) The camp, about 180 m north-east Save point; Camp Captain (Clear the Road), Jeweller (Gem Cutter), Ranger (Lost Scout), Camp Quartermaster (shop), Wandering Trader (trade); Tamsin, who joins when you talk to her Out on the plain Hunter (Jade Hunt); Dorran and Sabine, who join; Nia, at the scout's camp the Ranger sends you to Kamos Outpost, far east Save point; Outpost Elder (The Unbroken), Outpost Smith (shop); Isolde, who joins once you finish her quest, Storm Supplies

Some quests open only at a party level or after another quest: Clear the Road follows Field Rations.

docs.title: Two ways in
docs.text: Start from How Good for The title screen Open L_XenoCore_FrontEnd, press Play, choose New Game The whole game: boot, title, save and load The gym Open L_XenoCore_Gym, press Play Combat, straight away. Use this when testing your own changes

docs.title: A guided route
docs.text:
1. Look around. Move, look, jump. Notice the party following you.
  2. Talk to someone. Walk up to an NPC and press Interact. Conversations advance with the same button.
  3. Take a quest. An NPC with a marker over their head has a quest. Accept it; the tracker appears on the HUD.
  4. Start a fight. New Game starts you at the west tip of Gaur Plain. Head out across the plain: the enemies come in squads that get stronger the further you go, from a lone level 1 Plains Grunt about 55 m from the start to a level 12 unique monster, Gorvath the Unbroken, about 760 m out. Each enemy shows its lvl.N above it. Grunts hear you run (walk past to avoid them), Rust Grunts and Brutes see you, and Bulwarks wait to be hit. Lock on and attack; your party draws their weapons and starts auto-attacking, and the rest of a squad joins in. The first time an enemy comes near, and the first time a fight starts, a tutorial card pauses the game to explain it; A pages through, B skips the rest. Tips can be switched off from the menu's Tutorials entry.
  5. Lock on and use Arts. Lock on to the enemy, move along the palette with the D-pad, and use an Art. Watch its cooldown.
  6. Chain a reaction. Use a Break Art, then a Topple Art while the enemy is Broken. The enemy shows Topple, is knocked down and stops attacking for a few seconds. If a party member's HP hits zero, they kneel, downed. Walk over them and press Interact to revive them for one bar of the Party Gauge (the bars under the leader's HP).
  7. Win and loot. Killing one enemy of several moves your lock to the next; when the last one falls, the party sheathes and celebrates. Out of battle, HP recovers on its own. The last enemy of a squad leaves a chest. Open it and take its contents. Squads come back a minute or so after you leave them, so you can keep levelling.
  8. Level up. Enough experience brings a level-up banner for the party.
  9. Change equipment. Open the menu, go to Equipment, and change a weapon or armour piece. Watch the stats compare before you confirm.
  10. Swap the leader. Tap LT or RT (keyboard Z / C) to take control of the previous or next party member, in or out of battle. The Party screen in the menu does the same.
  11. Save. Use a save point, or check the autosave from the title screen.

docs.title: You now have
docs.text:
Seen every system once, in play.

Next: Tour of the project

docs.title: Tour of the project
docs.text:
All · 15 min · No code

The project is Epic's Lyra sample with XenoCore added as a Game Feature plugin. Lyra is the host: it provides the game framework, the menu toolkit and the ability-system plumbing. XenoCore is everything RPG, and it all lives in one plugin.

The one rule: change XenoCore and your own content, never Lyra

Everything XenoCore does is added to Lyra, not edited into it. Keep it that way. Your changes then stay separate from both Lyra and XenoCore, and you can take template updates.

docs.title: Where things are
docs.text:
In the Content Browser, click Settings (top right of the Content Browser) and tick Plugin Content (Show Plugin Content in the older Content Browser layout). XenoCore then appears in the folder tree under Plugins. With 5.8's default settings the folder reads XenoCore; this manual calls it XenoCore Content, which is what it reads if you turn on Display Content Folder Suffix in Editor Preferences › Content Editors › Content Browser.

How to read paths in this manual

A path such as Characters/Party/BP_XenoCore_Party is inside XenoCore Content: open XenoCore Content › Characters › Party and the asset is there. A path that starts with /Game/ is Lyra's own content, under Content. To find any asset by name, type the name into the Content Browser's search box with XenoCore Content selected.

If you see a Dev folder, it holds development-only test content: it is never cooked into a packaged build, nothing outside it depends on it, and you can ignore it. XenoCore ships no music: the title screen, Gaur Plain's field and battle slots and the fallback tracks in Project Settings › XenoCore Content are empty, so the game is silent until you add your own. See Area music.

docs.title: The maps
docs.text: Map What it's for L_XenoCore_FrontEnd Boot screens and the title screen. The project opens here. L_XenoCore_GaurPlain The sample world. New Game starts here. L_XenoCore_Gym A small test arena with enemies placed. Best for trying changes quickly.

docs.title: How it starts
docs.text:
1. The project opens L_XenoCore_FrontEnd, which runs the front-end Experience: boot screens, then the title screen.
  2. New Game loads the sample map. Continue loads your newest save.
  3. The sample map and the gym run B_XenoCore_Experience. It sets the player pawn data, the HUD, the interaction abilities and the teams, and it switches the XenoCore plugin's features on.

An Experience is Lyra's way of saying "in this map, the game is this". XenoCore ships its own, which is why none of Lyra's shooter rules apply in XenoCore's maps.

docs.title: Source code
docs.text: XenoCore's C++ is in Plugins/GameFeatures/XenoCore/Source: XenoCoreRuntime for the game and XenoCoreEditor for editor-only tools. You don't need to open it to use the template: every setting this manual names is in the editor's Details panel, a Data Table or Project Settings. When a programmer wants to extend a system, the Concepts page for that system says which class to subclass.

docs.title: You now have
docs.text:
A map of the project, and the one rule that keeps your work safe through updates.

Next: Your first change

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
All · 5 min · No code

XenoCore is a Game Feature plugin for Epic's Lyra Starter Game on Unreal Engine 5.8. You need the engine, Lyra, the free VRM4U plugin, Visual Studio 2022 and room on disk. A gamepad is strongly recommended.

docs.title: Windows 64-bit
docs.text: XenoCore supports Windows 10 or 11, 64-bit, with a DirectX 12 graphics card. Its modules are built for Win64 only; macOS, Linux, consoles and mobile are not supported.

docs.title: Unreal Engine 5.8
docs.text: Install Unreal Engine 5.8 from the Epic Games Launcher. The project is built and tested against 5.8.1. Other versions are not supported: 5.7 will not open it, and a later version may need changes.

docs.title: Lyra Starter Game 5.8
docs.text: XenoCore runs inside a Lyra project. Lyra Starter Game is free in the Epic Games Launcher's Fab Library; create a project from it for 5.8. An unmodified Lyra 5.8 is what XenoCore is tested against.

docs.title: VRM4U
docs.text: The sample party are VRoid characters, and XenoCore lists the free VRM4U plugin (by ruyo, MIT licence) as a dependency: the project will not open without it. Get the release built for UE 5.8; Install has the steps and the tested version.

docs.title: A C++ compiler (Visual Studio 2022)
docs.text:
XenoCore is a code plugin delivered as source. It is built on Lyra's own C++ game module, so it compiles inside your project: the first time you open the project, Unreal compiles XenoCore's C++ (Lyra itself is a C++ project too). You do not need to write any C++, but you do need the compiler. Install Visual Studio 2022 (version 17.14 or later) with these workloads:

  • Game development with C++
  • Desktop development with C++

and the Windows 11 SDK (10.0.22621). UE 5.8 refuses some older MSVC toolsets outright, so update Visual Studio rather than pinning an old one. Install it before you first open the project.

docs.title: Disk space
docs.text:
Measured on the development machine, 2026-10-14:

Item Size Stock Lyra Starter Game 5.8 (the Fab download) about 5 GB The XenoCore plugin folder (content plus C++ source) about 1.7 GB Compiled C++ (Binaries and Intermediate) up to about 11 GB (measured on a copy that also builds the packaged game; the editor alone needs less) Unreal's shader and derived-data cache, filled by the first open and the first play about 12 GB measured, shared between projects

That adds up to roughly 25 to 30 GB. Allow at least 40 GB free, ideally on an SSD. This is an estimate: the cache grows with every map and quality level you open, and a packaged build needs room of its own.

docs.title: A gamepad
docs.text: XenoCore is designed for a controller first, like the games it takes after. Keyboard and mouse work throughout, and every prompt shows the right glyph for whichever you last used. An Xbox-style pad gives the intended feel.

docs.title: How-to recipes
docs.text:
Designer and Programmer

Each recipe does one task from start to finish. It lists what you need, gives one action per step, and ends with Test it (what to press in Play and what you should see) and If it doesn't work (the symptom and the fix, including the failures that happen without any error).

Find your task in the tables below. What you get is what you will see in Play when you finish. Code says whether you need anything beyond the editor: No means the Details panel, Data Assets, Data Tables and, at most, a few simple Blueprint nodes. C++ means a programmer.

New to the template? Do the Getting Started tutorials first: Your first change, Your first art and Your first enemy. They cover the most common tasks with more explanation than a recipe gives. Unfamiliar words are in the Glossary.

Work in your own folder

Every recipe puts new assets under Content/MyGame/… and duplicates shipped assets rather than editing them. Where a recipe has to edit a shipped asset, it says so; note those changes so you can reapply them after a template update.

Times are for a first attempt with the editor already open.

docs.title: Add a gem
docs.text:
Designer · 15 min · No code · Last tested: 2026-10-05

Result: a new gem the party can find, carry, and fit into weapons and armour from the Equipment screen. Its strength is rolled when it is found, and it raises one stat on whoever wears it.

docs.title: How gems work
docs.text:
• A gem is an item in the Gems tab. One item per kind and rank: Strength Up I, Strength Up II.
  • Strength is rolled per gem. The item gives a range (Strength Up I: 5-10); every copy found rolls its own number inside it, so two Strength Up I can read +6 and +9.
  • Gems sit in the equipment, not the character. Hand a gemmed sword to someone else and the gems go with it. A weapon has up to 3 sockets, an armour piece up to 1 - so 8 gems per character at most.
  • Each kind has a cap per character. Strength Up stops adding at +150 however many are worn.
  • Permanent gems are fitted to an item when it is made and can never be removed.

docs.title: Make a new gem
docs.text:
1. In the Content Browser, open Plugins › XenoCore Content › Inventory › Gems. Right-click ID_XenoCore_Gem_StrengthUp_I and choose Duplicate. Move the copy into your own folder (for example Content/MyGame/Gems) and name it, e.g. ID_MyGame_Gem_EtherUp_IV.

    Fails silently: never create an item from blank

    A blank item definition has none of the fragments below. It appears in the bag and can never be socketed. Always duplicate a shipped gem.

  2. Open it and click Class Defaults. Set Display Name, including the rank: Ether Up IV.

  3. In Fragments, expand Xeno Core Fragment Gem (XenoCore › Gems) and set:
    • Gem Id - a number no other gem uses. The shipped ones are kind x 10 + rank (Strength Up I is 101). Never change an id once players have socketed the gem - the socket stores the number.
    • Rank, Stat Tag (the XenoCore.Stat.* gameplay tag it raises), Min Value / Max Value, and Cap (the most this kind can add to one character).
    • A percent stat (Critical Rate) is entered as whole percent: 4 means +4%.
  4. Expand Xeno Core Fragment Item Category (XenoCore › Item). Set Sell Value and Rarity (rarity); keep Category on Gems.
  5. Expand Xeno Core Fragment Item Display (XenoCore › Display). Symbol Colour is the gem's colour on the Equipment screen. The shipped gems use their XC1 element: Strength Up red, Ether Up yellow, Agility Up green, Ether Def Up cyan, Muscle Up and Critical Up orange.
  6. Compile and Save.

  7. Open Inventory/Gems/DA_XenoCore_GemRegistry. Under XenoCore › Gems, add your gem to the Gems array. Save.

    A gem missing from the registry cannot be socketed

    It can be carried and sold, but the game refuses to put it in a socket and logs why. Every gem must be in Gems.

  8. Put it where the player can get it: a quest reward (Create a collection quest) or a shop (Open a shop). The shipped game keeps gems out of chests, as XC1 does; a chest pool in a drop table works if you want them there.

docs.title: Give equipment sockets
docs.text:
• Weapons get sockets from their weapon type. Every weapon type asset (e.g. Weapons/Types/DA_XenoCore_WeaponType_Greatsword) has Gems › Default Gem Slots = 2, so a new weapon has two sockets with nothing to set. Change it there to change every weapon of that type.
  • One weapon different? On the weapon item's Class Defaults, expand Xeno Core Fragment Equip Slots (XenoCore › Equipment), tick Override Gem Slots and set Gem Slots (0-3).
  • Armour sets Gem Slots on its own Equip Slots fragment: 0 or 1.
  • Fixed Gems (same fragment) are permanent gems, filling sockets 1, 2, 3 in order. Each entry names a Gem and its Value.

docs.title: Look and feel
docs.text:
• The socket icons are in Edit › Project Settings › Game › XenoCore UI › Items (Gem Socket Filled Icon, Gem Socket Empty Icon). Clear them and the column draws text instead.
  • The popup that lists gems is UserInterface/W_XenoCore_GemPopup, chosen in XenoCore UI › Screens › Gem Popup. Restyle that widget, or point the setting at your own.

docs.title: Test it
docs.text:
1. Validate the registry: right-click DA_XenoCore_GemRegistry in the Content Browser and choose Asset Actions › Validate Assets. No errors.
  2. To carry the gem from the start, open Characters/VRoid/Kael/B_XenoCore_Party_VRoid_L, select Equipment Component in Components, and add your gem to XenoCore › Equipment › Starting Inventory (Item Definition your gem, Count 1). Compile and Save.
  3. Open Maps/L_XenoCore_Gym and press Play (not Continue: a save remembers the old bag).
  4. Open the menu (pad Y, keyboard I), go to Equipment, and move right onto the Gems column beside the weapon. Press A, pick an empty socket, and highlight your gem: the character's stats preview the change.
  5. Pick it. The column shows one icon in your gem's Symbol Colour, the gem's name appears on the line under the weapon, and the stat rises by the rolled amount.
  6. Remove step 2's entry from Kael when you are done.

docs.title: If it doesn't work
docs.text: What you see Fix Picking the gem does nothing; the Output Log (LogXenoCoreGems) says "Refused to socket ... the gem is not in the gem registry" Add it to Gems on DA_XenoCore_GemRegistry (step 7). If you made your own registry, check Project Settings › XenoCore Content › Items › Gem Registry points at it. A permanent gem is missing; the log says "it was not fitted" Fixed Gems lists more gems than the item has sockets. Raise Gem Slots. Validation: "has Gem Id 0" or "share Gem Id" Give it a unique Gem Id above 0. Validation: "raises no stat" Set Stat Tag. Validation: "Max Value is below Min Value" Swap them. It sockets, but the stat does not move; the Output Log warns the gem adds nothing The Stat Tag is one the equipment stats effect has no channel for. That is a programmer job: Add a stat to equipment. The stat stops rising after a few gems That is the Cap: per character, across every socket. No socket to put it in The weapon's type has Default Gem Slots 0, or the item ticks Override Gem Slots with Gem Slots 0. It never appears in the bag It is not in any quest reward, shop or drop table; or you pressed Continue on an old save.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: • Gems that do something other than add to a stat (Aggro Up, HP Steal, EXP Up) are not supported yet.

docs.title: Add armour
docs.text:
Designer · 20 min · No code

Result: a new chest piece, Hide Vest, that raises physical defence, costs some Agility through its weight, and shows as Light on the item details.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Add a weapon explains item definitions and fragments in more detail.
  • Equipment.

docs.title: How armour is put together
docs.text:
Armour is simpler than a weapon. Every piece of armour shares one equipment definition, Inventory/Armour/ED_XenoCore_Armour. It spawns nothing and grants one ability set, Inventory/AbilitySet_XenoCore_EquipmentStats, whose only job is to apply the piece's stats while it is worn. So a new piece of armour is one asset: its item definition.

Armour changes numbers only. It does not change how the character looks.

The sixteen shipped pieces are in Inventory/Armour, several per slot:

Slot Example Head ID_XenoCore_PrototypeHelm Chest ID_XenoCore_BattleArmour Arms ID_XenoCore_BattleGauntlets Legs ID_XenoCore_BattleLeggings Feet ID_XenoCore_BattleBoots

docs.title: 1. Duplicate a piece for the same slot
docs.text:
1. Create MyGame/Armour under Content.
  2. In Plugins › XenoCore Content › Inventory › Armour, right-click ID_XenoCore_BattleArmour, choose Duplicate, and move the copy into MyGame/Armour. Name it ID_MyGame_HideVest.

Fails silently: never create an item definition from blank

A new, empty item definition has no Equipment Definition. It appears in the Chest list and does nothing when chosen. Duplicate a shipped piece every time.

docs.title: 2. Name and describe it
docs.text:
1. Open ID_MyGame_HideVest and click Class Defaults.
  2. Set Display Name to Hide Vest.
  3. In Fragments, open Xeno Core Fragment Item Display and, under XenoCore › Display, set Description and Icon.
  4. Open Xeno Core Fragment Item Category and, under XenoCore › Item, set Sell Value and Rarity (rarity). Leave Category as Equipment.

Leave Inventory Fragment Equippable Item › Equipment Definition on ED_XenoCore_Armour.

docs.title: 3. Choose the slot and weight class
docs.text:
In Xeno Core Fragment Equip Slots (XenoCore › Equipment):

  1. Allowed Slots: exactly one of Head, Chest, Arms, Legs, Feet. Keep Chest.
  2. Equip Type: Light, Medium or Heavy. This is the "Type" line on the details pane. It is a label; the gameplay cost comes from Weight below. Set Light.
  3. Gem Slots: 0 or 1, the number of gem sockets. See Add a gem.

docs.title: 4. Set its stats
docs.text:
In Inventory Fragment Set Stats, edit Initial Item Stats. Armour normally carries three:

Tag Hide Vest What it does XenoCore.Stat.PhysicalDefence 8 Flat points taken off physical hits from enemies XenoCore.Stat.EtherDefence 4 Flat points taken off ether hits from enemies XenoCore.Stat.Weight 1 Subtracted from the wearer's Agility for hit and evade rolls

Values are whole numbers. Every equipped piece adds up, so a full set of five pieces gives five times these numbers. Any other XenoCore.Stat.* tag works on armour too; see Add a stat to equipment.

Pitch defence against your enemies' Strength

Enemy damage is Strength − defence, so defence that is large compared with an enemy's Strength makes that enemy harmless. Early-game pieces in the shipped set carry single-digit defence per slot. Tune armour and enemy statlines together.

Weight shows as its own row

Weight does not lower the Agility number on the character sheet. The sheet shows Agility and Weight as two rows, and the subtraction happens when a hit is rolled. More Weight shows in red on the comparison block, because for this one stat, more is worse.

Compile and Save.

docs.title: 5. Put it in the bag
docs.text:
1. Open a starting party member's pawn, for example Kael, Characters/VRoid/Kael/B_XenoCore_Party_VRoid_L. A member's Starting Inventory reaches the party bag when its body first spawns, so a member who joins later brings it only then.
  2. In Components, select Equipment Component. Add an entry to XenoCore › Equipment › Starting Inventory: Item Definition ID_MyGame_HideVest, Count 1.
  3. Compile and Save.

docs.title: Test it
docs.text:
1. Open Maps/L_XenoCore_Gym and press Play (not Continue: a save remembers the old bag).
  2. Open the menu (pad Y, keyboard I), go to Equipment, choose a character and the Chest slot.
  3. Hide Vest is listed. Its comparison block shows Physical Def +8, Ether Def +4, Weight +1.
  4. Equip it. The character's totals rise by those amounts.
  5. With the Chest row focused, the unequip prompt appears in the bottom bar. Use it: the totals drop back.

docs.title: If it doesn't work
docs.text:
Fails silently: it equips and adds nothing

The piece's Equipment Definition points somewhere other than ED_XenoCore_Armour, or that definition's ability set was changed. Armour's stats come only from AbilitySet_XenoCore_EquipmentStats on ED_XenoCore_Armour. If you make your own armour equipment definition, grant that set, and do not grant GA_XenoCore_WeaponDrawSync, or the armour tries to draw itself like a weapon.

Hide Vest is not in the list at all

You pressed Continue on a save made before the change, or the Starting Inventory entry is on a member who is not in the starting party. Start with Play in the editor or New Game, and add it to Kael.

Fails silently: the item is listed but choosing it does nothing

The item definition was created blank instead of duplicated, so it has no Equipment Definition (step 1).

It appears under the wrong slot, or under several

Allowed Slots lists more than one slot, or the wrong one. The item is offered in every slot it lists.

docs.text:

docs.title: Add an enemy type
docs.text:
Designer · 90 min · No code

Result: a new enemy type with its own body, animations, gameplay abilities, stats and loot, built from its own assets rather than borrowing the melee minion's. You can then place as many as you like.

docs.title: Before you start

docs.title: 1. Make the Golem from the minion's set
docs.text:
1. Create MyGame/Enemies/Golem.
  2. Right-click Characters/Enemies/Minion/B_XenoCore_Minion_Melee, choose Create Child Blueprint Class, and save it in your folder as B_MyGame_Golem. A child keeps every component and setting that already works, and picks up fixes to the minion.
  3. Duplicate into your folder: PawnData_XenoCore_Minion_Melee, AbilitySet_XenoCore_Minion_Melee, GA_XenoCore_Minion_Attack, GA_XenoCore_Minion_HitReact, GA_XenoCore_Minion_Topple, GA_XenoCore_Minion_Daze, GA_XenoCore_Minion_Guard, GA_XenoCore_Minion_Recoil, GA_XenoCore_Minion_Evade. Rename each with MyGame in place of XenoCore and Golem in place of Minion_Melee (or Minion), for example PawnData_MyGame_Golem and AbilitySet_MyGame_Golem.
  4. Duplicate Battle/Attributes/GE_XenoCore_BaseStats_Minion_Melee → GE_MyGame_BaseStats_Golem.

The seven sample enemy types in Characters/Enemies/Minion/Variants/ are made the same way: each is an empty child of B_XenoCore_Minion_Melee. If your enemy shares the minion's skeleton (or a compatible one), the child alone is enough: keep the minion's pawn data and abilities and change only its class defaults.

docs.title: 2. Give it its body
docs.text:
1. Open B_MyGame_Golem and select the Mesh component.
  2. Set Skeletal Mesh Asset to your mesh and adjust its location so the feet sit at the bottom of the capsule.
  3. Set Anim Class. For a new skeleton, create an Animation Blueprint for it whose parent class is XenoCoreAnimInstance, and copy the shape of ABP_XenoCore_Minion_Melee:
    • A 2D blend space on your skeleton: Direction from -180 to 180 across, speed up the side. Put idle along the bottom, a forward walk and jog at their own speeds at direction 0, a left jog at -90, a right jog at 90, and a back jog at both -180 and 180. BS_XenoCore_Minion_Locomotion2D is the worked example.
    • An Idle and a Move state. Move plays the blend space, its two axes driven by the Direction and Ground Speed variables the parent class provides.
    • Transitions on Ground Speed with a gap between them: Idle to Move above 20, Move to Idle below 8. Play Idle at a play rate of 1.
  4. On B_MyGame_Golem, set Patrol Speed (XenoCore › AI › Patrol) to the speed your walk clip covers the ground at, so a patrol plays the walk without sliding.
  5. Resize the Capsule Component to fit.
  6. Under XenoCore › Death, set Death Montages to one or more death montages on your skeleton.

Fails silently: a forward-only blend space

A blend space with speed but no direction has nothing to play when the enemy strafes round its attackers or backs away. The legs run forward, or half-idle, while the body slides sideways, and nothing is logged. Give it side and back clips.

Fails silently: transitions that read the pawn's velocity

Read Ground Speed and Direction from the parent class, never the pawn's own velocity. The parent class treats a hit's knockback as standing still, so a shove slides the body under a held pose. Velocity read directly turns every hit into a burst of forward running while the body moves backwards.

Anim Blueprints: parent to the C++ class, never to another ABP

An Anim Blueprint made as a child of another Anim Blueprint loses its own AnimGraph. Always parent a new one to XenoCoreAnimInstance.

docs.title: 3. Give it its moves
docs.text:
1. Open GA_MyGame_Golem_Attack. Under XenoCore › AutoAttack:
    • Attack Montages: your attack montages. One is picked per swing.
    • Attack Range: how far the swing reaches, in centimetres.
    • Leave Target Source on Nearest Hostile, Requires Arming off and Damage Effect on GE_XenoCore_Damage.
  2. Open GA_MyGame_Golem_HitReact. Under XenoCore › Reaction, set Directional Montages to your flinch montages, in the order Front, Back, Left, Right. An empty entry means no flinch from that side. A flinch must layer over the Golem's swing, not replace it, so:
    • Make each flinch clip additive: duplicate the animation sequence, open the copy, and in its Asset Details set Additive Settings › Additive Anim Type to Local Space and Base Pose Type to Selected animation frame, with the original clip and frame 0.
    • Make a montage from each additive clip and set its slot to AdditiveHitReact.
    • Register that slot on the Golem's skeleton in its own slot group. Open the skeleton, choose Window › Anim Slot Manager, click Add Group and name it AdditiveGroup, then Add Slot AdditiveHitReact and right-click it › Set Slot AdditiveHitReact Group to › AdditiveGroup.
    • Give the Golem's Animation Blueprint an additive branch just before Output Pose: open ABP_XenoCore_Minion_Melee's AnimGraph and copy its last three nodes into yours: Additive Identity Pose feeds the AdditiveHitReact Slot's Source, the Slot feeds Apply Additive's Additive pin, your existing pose goes into its Base, and Apply Additive feeds Output Pose. Apply Additive's Alpha sets how hard the jolt reads.

Under XenoCore › HitReact › Push, lower Push Distance for a heavy enemy, or set it to 0 so it is never knocked back.

!!! warning "Fails silently: the flinch slot in DefaultGroup"
    Compiling the anim Blueprint registers `AdditiveHitReact` in `DefaultGroup`, beside the
    attack slots. Montages in one group stop each other: every hit cuts the Golem's swing short
    and its next swing cuts the flinch off, so you rarely see a flinch at all. Nothing is logged. Check the slot's group in the **Anim Slot
    Manager** after compiling, and move it back to `AdditiveGroup` if it changed.
  1. Open GA_MyGame_Golem_Topple and GA_MyGame_Golem_Daze. Under XenoCore › Reaction, set Directional Montages to your knock-down montage (one entry is enough). Leave Hold While Trigger Tag Present on, so the Golem stays down for exactly as long as the reaction lasts. Add a get-up as Follow Up Montage if you have one. The trigger and the hold come from the parent class; there is nothing else to set.
  2. Open GA_MyGame_Golem_Guard, _Recoil and _Evade (copies of the minion's). Under XenoCore › Reaction, set Directional Montages to your block, recoil and dodge clips. See Blocks and dodges for which side each slot means. No clips for one of them? Leave it out of the ability set: the Golem still blocks, recoils and dodges in the rules, just without an animation.

!!! tip "Same skeleton as an existing enemy? Skip the copies" If the Golem shares a skeleton with an enemy you already have, keep that enemy's reaction abilities in the set and give the Golem its own clips through an Anim Profile instead (XenoCore › Animation › Anim Profile on B_MyGame_Golem). See Give a character its own combat animations. 5. Open AbilitySet_MyGame_Golem. Replace the attack, hit-react, Topple, Daze, guard, recoil and evade entries with yours. Arts are not in the ability set; they come in step 5. 6. Compile and Save each.

Fails silently: Requires Arming on an enemy

Requires Arming must be off. Enemies have no draw animation, so an enemy auto-attack waiting to be armed waits forever and never swings.

docs.title: 4. Wire the pawn data
docs.text:
1. Open PawnData_MyGame_Golem.
  2. Set Pawn Class to B_MyGame_Golem.
  3. Ability Sets: keep AbilitySet_XenoCore_Enemy_Common and replace the minion's set with AbilitySet_MyGame_Golem.
  4. Save.

docs.title: 5. Wire the Blueprint
docs.text:
1. Open B_MyGame_Golem, Class Defaults.
  2. Under XenoCore › Enemy: Enemy Pawn Data PawnData_MyGame_Golem, Stats Effect GE_MyGame_BaseStats_Golem, Display Name Golem, Enemy Level, Experience Reward. Experience Reward is the type's weight; Experience Level Scale (a curve row, the minion's is Minion.ExperienceScale in CT_XenoCore_EnemyStats) scales it by the enemy's level. Leave that row empty for a flat reward.
  3. Under XenoCore › Enemy › Arts: the Arts it should use. A child of the minion keeps Rend and Sweep, which play the minion's montages; replace them with your own. See Give an enemy Arts.
  4. Under XenoCore › Loot: your Drop Table.
  5. Under XenoCore › Enemy, adjust Health Bar Height and Chevron Height so both clear the new mesh's head.
  6. Compile and Save.

docs.title: Test it
docs.text:
1. Place B_MyGame_Golem in Maps/L_XenoCore_Gym, on the navigation mesh, and press Play. (In a real level, put it on an enemy spawner instead: Place enemies.)
  2. Walk up to it. Whether it attacks first depends on its Detection (XenoCore › AI › Detection): with None (passive) it waits to be hit. Set Sight to have it charge when it sees you.
  3. Hit it. It turns, chases you if you back off, and swings with your montages. Circle round it while it fights: its legs step sideways and backwards to follow you, never running forward.
  4. Lock on: the badge shows Golem. Defeat it: it plays your death montage, dissolves, and drops a chest.

docs.title: If it doesn't work
docs.text:
It cannot be damaged and cannot die

Enemy Pawn Data is empty, or its ability sets do not include AbilitySet_XenoCore_Enemy_Common. An error naming the enemy is logged.

It stands still when hit

There is no navigation mesh where it stands, or AI Controller Class is no longer BP_AIC_XenoCore_Enemy. Press P in the editor viewport to show the nav mesh.

Its stats are the attribute defaults

Stats Effect is empty. The log says the enemy "will run on attribute defaults, not its statline".

Its Arts play no animation, or do nothing

The Arts list still holds the minion's Rend and Sweep, whose montages are on the minion's skeleton. Replace them with Arts that play montages on the Golem's skeleton.

Toppled, it stands still instead of falling

Its ability set has no Topple or Daze ability, or they still point at the minion's montages on another skeleton. The Golem still cannot act while Toppled (that rule is on the auto-attack), so the only symptom is the missing animation.

It is friendly

The team comes only from the AI controller. A Blueprint AI controller of your own cannot carry a team; always use BP_AIC_XenoCore_Enemy or a child of it.

docs.title: Going further
docs.text:
• Give an enemy Arts, Set an enemy's statline, Place enemies.
  • Enemies and AI, Animation.

docs.title: Add a HUD element
docs.text:
Designer · 20 min · No code

Result: your own widget (here, an in-game clock) on the HUD in play, placed in one of the HUD's named slots, without editing W_XenoCore_HUDLayout or any other XenoCore asset.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• UI shell and HUD: layers, HUD plates, and why a HUD element hides by opacity.
  • Glossary: Experience, Game Feature plugin.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The HUD layout, UserInterface/HUD/W_XenoCore_HUDLayout, carries five empty extension points: Lyra's UIExtensionPointWidget, each named by a gameplay tag. Lyra's Add Widgets action puts a widget into the point whose tag matches. The points are empty and do not take clicks until something is added.

Slot tag Where on screen How several widgets stack HUD.Slot.XenoCore.TopCenter Top centre, 48 px down In a column, centred HUD.Slot.XenoCore.TopRight Top right, 48 px in, 330 px down (below the minimap and its prompt) In a column, right-aligned HUD.Slot.XenoCore.Center Screen centre On top of each other HUD.Slot.XenoCore.BottomCenter Bottom centre, 48 px up In a column, centred HUD.Slot.XenoCore.FullScreen Fills the screen, behind the rest of the HUD On top of each other

All five tags come with XenoCore, so they appear in every tag picker.

docs.title: 1. Make the widget
docs.text:
1. In Content/MyGame/UI, right-click and choose User Interface › Widget Blueprint, parent User Widget. Name it W_MyGame_Clock.
  2. Lay it out small: the slot sizes itself to your widget (except FullScreen).
  3. Set anything that must not catch clicks to Hit Test Invisible.

For a widget that fades in and out

Parent it to XenoCoreHudPlateBase instead. It then has Set Shown (fade in or out without removing it), Set Shown Immediate, Set Show Delay and, from its own graph, Begin Hidden and Skip Intro, all callable from Blueprint. Never hide a HUD element by collapsing it: a collapsed widget stops ticking and cannot notice when to come back.

docs.title: 2. Add it with an action set
docs.text:
Keep the addition in your own asset, so a template update cannot remove it.

  1. In Content/MyGame/Experiences, right-click and choose Data › Data Asset, class LyraExperienceActionSet. Name it LAS_MyGame_HUD.
  2. Open it. Under Actions to Perform, add an entry and choose Add Widgets.
  3. Under Widgets, add a row:
    • Widget Class: W_MyGame_Clock
    • Slot ID: HUD.Slot.XenoCore.TopCenter
  4. Leave Layout empty. That list is for whole HUD layouts, such as the one Experiences/LAS_XenoCore_HUD adds.
  5. Save.

docs.title: 3. Use the action set in your experience
docs.text:
An Experience decides what a map loads, HUD included.

  1. In Plugins › XenoCore Content › Experiences, duplicate B_XenoCore_Experience into Content/MyGame/Experiences if you have not already, and point your maps' World Settings › Default Gameplay Experience at the copy.
  2. Open the copy, click Class Defaults, and add LAS_MyGame_HUD to Action Sets, beside LAS_XenoCore_HUD.
  3. Save.

From your own Game Feature plugin instead

If your content lives in its own Game Feature plugin, you can put the same Add Widgets action in that plugin's Game Feature Data (Actions). It applies whenever that feature is active.

docs.title: Test it
docs.text:
1. Open a map that uses your experience and press Play.
  2. The clock appears at the top centre when the HUD appears.
  3. Open the menu: the HUD, clock included, stays under the menu; close it and the clock is still there.
  4. Stop and remove the row: nothing else on the HUD changed.

docs.title: If it doesn't work
docs.text:
Fails silently: the widget never appears

Nothing is logged when a widget goes to a slot tag no extension point carries. Check, in order: the Slot ID is one of the five HUD.Slot.XenoCore.* tags exactly; the action set is in the Action Sets of the experience the map actually uses (Window › World Settings › Default Gameplay Experience); Widget Class is set. An ExperienceOverride line in your project's Saved/Config files also outranks World Settings; delete it if you find one.

The widget appears behind everything

FullScreen is deliberately behind the rest of the HUD. Use Center for an overlay that must be on top.

The widget blocks clicks on a menu

It cannot: the HUD is on the game layer, under the menus. If it blocks clicks in play, a child widget is Visible; set it to Hit Test Invisible.

docs.title: Going further
docs.text:
• UI shell and HUD
  • Add an input action with a prompt: put its glyph on the HUD through one of these slots.
  • Restyle the menus: the XenoCore UI settings replace whole HUD widgets such as the interact prompt and the battle notifications.

docs.title: Add an interactable object
docs.text:
Designer · 30 min · No code

Result: a lever in the level. Walk up to it and the prompt reads A Pull; press A and the lever does its thing, then stops offering itself. A second action, X Inspect, prints a line instead. No C++.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Interaction, NPCs and dialogue: how the prompt picks the one thing it offers, and why the button does exactly what the prompt shows.
  • People and chests already have their own classes. Use this recipe for anything else: a door, a lever, a sign, a pickup, a switch.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
XenoCoreInteractableActor is a parent class built for Blueprint children. It already does the parts you would otherwise have to write:

It does You do Tells the prompt it exists at Begin Play, and stops at End Play Nothing. Your own Event BeginPlay cannot skip it Offers its Interact Verb on A and its Secondary Interact Verb on X Type the two words Checks Interact Enabled and Can Interact before offering itself Switch it off with Set Interact Enabled, or override Can Interact Calls On Interact with the verb that was pressed Put the behaviour there Calls On Focused / On Unfocused when the prompt starts or stops offering it Optional: a highlight

Two actions, not more. Only A (IA_XenoCore_Interact) and X (IA_XenoCore_InteractSecondary) have inputs. The base has exactly two verb fields, so it cannot offer a button nothing presses.

docs.title: 1. Create the Blueprint
docs.text:
1. In Content/MyGame/World, right-click and choose Blueprint Class. Under All Classes, search for XenoCoreInteractableActor and pick it. Name it BP_MyGame_Lever.
  2. Open it. In Components, the root is Scene Root. Add a Static Mesh under it for the lever (and a collider if the player should bump into it).
  3. Place the root where the player should stand near. Range is measured from the actor's origin to the player character's location (the middle of its capsule), in 3D, so a root buried in the floor or on a high shelf shortens the effective range.

docs.title: 2. Set the verbs and range
docs.text:
Click Class Defaults. Under XenoCore › Interaction:

Setting Value What it does Interact Verb Pull The word beside A. Default Use Secondary Interact Verb Inspect The word beside X. Leave empty for no second action Interact Range 200 How close the player must be, in cm Interact Enabled ticked Whether the prompt offers this actor at all

All four are per instance too, so one placed lever can say Push and reach further.

An empty Interact Verb draws a bare button

With Interact Verb empty the prompt shows an A chip with no word, which looks like a broken widget. The actor logs a warning at Begin Play (LogXenoInteractable: "has an empty Interact Verb").

docs.title: 3. Handle the press
docs.text:
1. In the Event Graph, right-click and add Event On Interact. It gives you Interactor (the character that pressed) and Verb Index.
  2. From Verb Index, call Is Secondary Verb and add a Branch.
  3. False (A, Pull): do the lever's work (play a timeline, open a door you reference, set a variable), then call Set Interact Enabled with Enabled unticked.
  4. True (X, Inspect): call Print String with A rusty lever., or start a conversation with the dialogue nodes (see Write an NPC conversation).
  5. Compile and Save.

Branch on Is Secondary Verb, not on the number

Verb Index is 0 for A and 1 for X today. Is Secondary Verb also returns false when Secondary Interact Verb is empty, so it stays right if you remove the second action later.

Set Interact Enabled makes the prompt re-decide at once rather than on its next 0.2 s check, so the "A Pull" prompt disappears the moment the lever is pulled.

docs.title: 4. Optional: a condition
docs.text:
To offer the lever only sometimes (a key in the bag, a quest step), override Can Interact: Functions › Override › Can Interact. Return true to allow.

Keep Can Interact cheap

The prompt asks every interactable in the level five times a second. Read a variable or a tag; do not trace, spawn or search the level from here.

When Can Interact returns false the lever is skipped, not greyed out: a live interactable standing behind it still gets the prompt.

docs.title: 5. Optional: a highlight
docs.text:
