Kind Counted from Target field Collect Item The party's bag, re-read on every change Item Target Defeat Enemy Every enemy death while the quest is active Enemy Target Talk To NPC Talking to a placed NPC whose Quest Id matches Target Id Reach Location The leader walking into a placed XenoCore Quest Location whose Location Id matches Target Id

A quest asset cannot point at an actor placed in a level, so Talk To NPC and Reach Location match by name: type the same word into the objective's Target Id and into the NPC or the location. Names are not case-sensitive.

docs.title: Part 1: defeat enemies (no code)
docs.text:
The sample Quests/DA_XenoCore_Quest_Monster01 is exactly this: defeat melee minions, with a party level gate.

  1. In the Content Browser, right-click Quests/DA_XenoCore_Quest_Monster01 and choose Duplicate. Move the copy to MyGame/Quests and name it DA_MyGame_Quest_Golems.
  2. Open it. Under XenoCore › Quest, set Title, Area, Summary and Kind (Monster, a label only).
  3. In Objectives, expand entry 0 and set:
Setting Value Description Drive the golems out of the quarry. Kind Defeat Enemy Enemy Target B_MyGame_Golem Required Count 5 Counter Label Golem: the tracker reads "Golem 0/5". Needed, because an enemy has no item name to fall back on. Icon Source From Category, with an Icon Category of your choice
  1. Set Reward and Gates. The sample's gate is Party Level At Least.
  2. Save, and give it to an NPC's Quest as in Offer a collection quest.

Enemy Target matches the class and everything derived from it. Name Characters/Enemies/Core/B_XenoCore_Enemy_Base to count any enemy at all, or your own parent Blueprint to count a whole family. It is a soft reference, so the quest does not load the enemy's mesh, animations and abilities; a kill is matched against enemies that are already in the world.

Kills before accepting do not count

Only enemies defeated while the quest is active count. Unlike collection quests, nothing is counted retroactively. A kill after the count is full does not push it past the total.

Test it: accept the quest, defeat five golems, and watch the tracker count up. At 5/5 the NPC's marker returns; talk to hand it in.

docs.title: Part 2: talk to someone
docs.text:
1. In your quest, add an objective:
Setting Value Description Ask the ferryman about the crossing. Kind Talk To NPC Target Id Ferryman Required Count 1 Counter Label Speak to the ferryman
  1. Select the placed ferryman NPC (B_XenoCore_Npc). Under XenoCore › NPC, set Quest Id to Ferryman.

That is all. Talking to the ferryman, with any verb, counts the objective before the conversation plays, so if it is the last step and the ferryman also gave the quest, it hands in during the same talk. While the quest is tracked, the ferryman shows as a quest target on the minimap.

Set Quest Id on the placed NPC, not the Blueprint

On B_XenoCore_Npc's defaults it would make every NPC in the game the ferryman.

docs.title: Part 3: go somewhere
docs.text:
1. Add an objective with Kind Reach Location, Target Id OldGate, Required Count 1 and a Counter Label such as Old Gate.
  2. Open the Place Actors panel (Window › Place Actors), search for Quest Location, and drag XenoCore Quest Location into the level.
  3. Move and scale its blue box over the place.
  4. In its Details, set XenoCore › Quest › Location Id to OldGate.

When the leader walks into the box, the objective counts. Companions walking in first do not. If the quest is accepted while the leader is already standing inside, it counts at once. While the quest is tracked, the box shows as a quest target on the minimap; the rest of the time nothing is drawn.

  • "Visit three times": set Required Count 3. Each walk-in counts once; walk out and back in for the next.
  • "Any of these places": give several boxes the same Location Id.

docs.title: Part 4: count a step from any Blueprint
docs.text:
For a step that is neither a talk nor a place (a lever pulled, a cutscene watched):

  1. Give the objective Kind Reach Location (or Talk To NPC) and a Target Id, for example GateLever.
  2. In the Blueprint where the step happens (the lever's On Interact, say), right-click and add Get Party Quests.
  3. Drag off its return value and add Notify Objective. Set Kind to Reach Location and Target Id to GateLever.

It counts every active quest that wants that name, exactly as the box and the NPC do.

docs.title: Test it
docs.text:
1. Put the quest on a placed NPC's Quest, as in Offer a collection quest, and place the ferryman and the Old Gate box in the same map.
  2. Press Play, walk to the giver, and accept the quest. The HUD tracker shows each step at 0.
  3. Defeat a golem: the tracker reads "Golem 1/5".
  4. Open the minimap view: the ferryman and the Old Gate box are marked as quest targets.
  5. Talk to the ferryman: "Speak to the ferryman" completes. Walk the leader into the box: "Old Gate" completes.
  6. When every step is full, the giver's marker returns. Talk to them to hand the quest in.

docs.title: If it doesn't work
docs.text:
Fails silently: a Defeat Enemy objective that never counts

Enemy Target is empty, or names a class the enemy does not derive from. Only enemies built on XenoCore's enemy class announce their defeat. The training dummy B_XenoCore_Dummy is one, so naming the enemy base counts dummies too.

A talk or location step that never counts

The names do not match. Compare the objective's Target Id with the NPC's Quest Id or the box's Location Id. A box with no Location Id logs an error when play starts. Saving a quest whose talk or location objective has an empty Target Id reports a validation error.

The step counted nothing because the quest was not active

Like kills, talks and visits only count while the quest is active. Talking to the ferryman before accepting does not count; talk again afterwards.

docs.title: Going further
docs.text:
• Quests, Events.
  • Recruit a party member by talking to them: Recruit After Quest joins a character once such a quest is handed in.

docs.title: Megascans at shipping size
docs.text:
Level designer · 1 h · No code

Result: the rocks, cliffs and surfaces you placed from a large asset pack (Megascans, Fab environment packs, Epic sample environments) are in your project at a sensible size, with nothing missing on a fresh copy of the project, and look the same in game.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• The pack is added to a separate project, or to this one in a folder you can remove later.
  • Package a build explains why download size matters.

docs.title: Why this needs a process
docs.text:
Scan-quality assets are huge and most of the size is invisible in play: 4K textures, and cliff meshes of several million triangles. A full environment pack is tens of gigabytes; a map uses a sliver of it. Three things go wrong if you just drag assets in:

  1. You ship the whole pack. Everything in the project's Content folder that is referenced gets cooked, and packs bring far more than you use.
  2. Pieces go missing on another machine. If you keep the pack folder out of source control to save space, every asset your map uses from it is on your disk only. A teammate's copy shows holes where the cliffs were. Nothing warns: Unreal loads from disk, not from source control.
  3. You ship full-resolution sources. A cliff at 25 % of its triangles and 1K textures is usually indistinguishable at gameplay distance.

The XenoCore sample map went from a 40 GB pack to about 180 assets and under 1 GB this way.

The sample's pack assets live in the plugin, under ThirdParty/ElectricDreams/, keeping the pack's own sub-folders (Megascans, SmartAssets, PCG and the rest), so they travel with XenoCore.

docs.title: 1. Place what you want, then list what it needs
docs.text:
1. Build your map using the pack assets.
  2. Right-click the map in the Content Browser and open Reference Viewer or Size Map. Size Map shows the total and which assets dominate it.
  3. The set you must keep is the map's dependency closure: every asset it uses, and everything those use (materials, material functions, textures).

docs.title: 2. Bring in exactly that set
docs.text:
If the pack is in a separate project, open it there, select the assets your map uses, and use Asset Actions › Migrate. Migrate copies an asset and everything it depends on into another project's Content folder, at the same paths, so all references resolve with no redirectors.

Never copy a whole pack folder \"to be safe\"

That is how 40 GB ends up in a template. Migrate the map's closure and nothing else.

Check nothing comes from outside the pack

If Migrate wants to bring assets from another plugin or pack, stop and decide whether you want that dependency.

If the pack is already in this project, you don't need to copy anything, but you must make sure every asset in the closure is under source control (next step).

Fails silently: moving pack content that PCG assemblies use

Some packs (Electric Dreams among them) build cliffs and scatter from PCG assemblies that name their meshes and materials as text in point attributes, not as asset references. Moving or renaming those assets fixes every real reference and leaves the text pointing at the old path, so the next time the PCG graph generates, it spawns nothing there. Nothing warns. Decide where pack content lives before you place it; if you must move it, regenerate every PCG component afterwards and compare the instance counts before and after.

docs.title: 3. Make sure the set is in source control
docs.text:
If your repository ignores the pack folders, force-add each asset in the closure. Then clone the project somewhere else, or ask a teammate to, and open the map. Any hole is an asset you missed.

Fails silently: an ignored pack folder

The map works on the machine that built it and is missing geometry everywhere else. Do this check after every edit that places new pack content.

docs.title: 4. Cap texture sources at 1K
docs.text:
1. In the Content Browser, open the pack folder and filter by Texture. Select the textures in the set (you can select many at once).
  2. Right-click and choose Texture Source Actions › Reduce Size. In the dialog, set Texture size threshold to 1024 and click OK. Textures already at or under 1024 are left alone.
  3. Spot-check one: its Imported size in the texture editor now reads 1024 or less.

Resizing the source is what shrinks the project and the package. Maximum Texture Size and LOD Bias in a texture's Details shrink only the cooked output, and the full-size source still sits in source control.

The sample went from 1.77 GB to 191 MB of textures with no visible change up against a cliff.

docs.title: 5. Reduce rock meshes
docs.text:
For each large rock or cliff mesh:

  1. Open it in the Static Mesh editor. Under Nanite Settings, lower Keep Triangle Percent (the sample used 25 %), and click Apply Changes. This reduces what is cooked.
  2. Or, to reduce the source itself, use the Simplify tool in Modeling Mode. Leave Preserve Sharp Edges on and Discard Attributes off, which keeps the UV seams, then click Accept.

Leave foliage alone

Trees and plants use leaf cards that can collapse when simplified. Reduce rocks and cliffs; check any foliage up close before touching it.

docs.title: 6. Look at it
docs.text:
Take the same screenshots before and after, from the player's usual viewpoints and one right up against a cliff. They should match.

The first open after importing is slow

Nanite data for every new mesh is built on first open, which can take a long time and a lot of memory. Screenshots taken during that build are wrong; wait and shoot again.

docs.title: 7. Shrink before you commit
docs.text: If you use Git LFS, do the size pass before the first push. LFS uploads every version you push, so pushing full-size assets and then reduced ones stores both, forever.

docs.title: Test it
docs.text:
1. Open Size Map on your map. The pack's share is a fraction of what it was.
  2. On a fresh clone, open the map. No missing meshes, no default grey materials, no warnings about missing packages in the Output Log.
  3. Play and compare with your before screenshots.

docs.title: If it doesn't work
docs.text:
Grey checkerboard materials or missing meshes on another machine

Part of the closure isn't in source control. Re-run step 3.

The Output Log lists missing packages at load

An asset references something you didn't bring in. The warning names the path; migrate it.

A texture looks blurry up close

It is one the player sees very close (a hero rock, a surface the camera rests against). Give that one 2K.

docs.title: Going further
docs.text:
• Build a world-partition map
  • Package a build
  • Check the licence of every pack you ship. Fab and Epic sample content each have their own terms for use in a product you sell.

docs.title: Show something on the minimap
docs.text:
Designer · 15 min · No code

Result: an actor of yours, such as a treasure chest, a landmark or a camp, shows on the minimap with its own icon. Or one of the shipped markers looks different.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Read Minimap.
  • An icon image, white on transparent, around 32–64 px. White icons take their colour from the row's Tint; a coloured icon (like the quest !) uses a white tint.

docs.title: How markers work
docs.text:
Every marker is an actor that has registered with the minimap as a kind, which is a XenoCore.Map.Marker.* gameplay tag. What a kind looks like is one row of UserInterface/HUD/Minimap/DT_XenoCore_MapMarkers. XenoCore's enemies and NPCs register themselves.

Kind Who uses it XenoCore.Map.Marker.Monster Every living XenoCore enemy XenoCore.Map.Marker.UniqueMonster A living enemy with Unique Monster ticked XenoCore.Map.Marker.QuestGiver An NPC whose quest is offerable or ready to hand in XenoCore.Map.Marker.Shop An NPC with a Shop Table XenoCore.Map.Marker.QuestTarget Whatever the tracked quest still needs, including the NPC a Talk To NPC step names and the XenoCore Quest Location a Reach Location step names (set by the minimap, never registered)

docs.title: Change how a shipped marker looks
docs.text:
1. Open UserInterface/HUD/Minimap/DT_XenoCore_MapMarkers.
  2. Select the row and change:
Column What it does Icon The image. Its own size is ignored Tint Multiplies the icon's colour Size Size on the minimap. The shipped sizes were measured on XC1 against the circle's width: a monster 8, a quest tag 30 (it draws about 20 × 28, being portrait inside its square icon), the arrow 24 Rotate With Actor Turn with the actor's facing (an arrow), or stay upright (a dot, a sign) Clamp To Rim Stay pinned to the edge, pointing the way, when out of range. For objectives Draw Order Higher draws on top Pulse When Engaged For enemies: pulse while the enemy is fighting the party Label On Full Map On the L3 view, print the actor's name beside the icon (an NPC's Display Name) Label This kind's line in the L3 view's legend - the only marker text the player reads (the shipped enemy rows say Enemy and Unique Enemy). Empty = not in the legend Tint By Enemy Danger For enemies: multiply Tint by the enemy's level colour against the party leader, the same ladder as its lvl.N label (Project Settings › XenoCore Enemies › Level Label › Level Colour Bands). Leave Tint white so the ladder's colours show true
  1. Save. Play to see it.

docs.title: Add a new kind of marker
1. Add the tag
docs.text:
1. Open Project Settings › Project › Gameplay Tags and click Add New Gameplay Tag.
  2. Name it XenoCore.Map.Marker.<YourKind>, for example XenoCore.Map.Marker.Chest, add a comment saying what it marks, and set Source to your own tag source (for example MyGameTags.ini), not XenoCore's, so a template update cannot remove it.
  3. Click Add New Tag.

docs.title: 2. Add its row
docs.text:
1. Drag your icon file into your own folder, for example MyGame/UI/Minimap. Open it and set Level Of Detail › Texture Group to UI and Mip Gen Settings to NoMipmaps. Save.
  2. In DT_XenoCore_MapMarkers, click Add, and name the row after the kind (e.g. Chest).
  3. Set Kind to your tag. Expand Icon and set its Image to your texture. Then set Tint, Size and the rest as above.
  4. Save. DT_XenoCore_MapMarkers is a shipped asset: note your row for template updates.

docs.title: 3. Make your actor register
docs.text:
In your actor's Blueprint, open the Event Graph:

  1. From Event BeginPlay, add Get Map Markers (category XenoCore › Map), then Register Marker with Actor = Self and Kind = your tag.
  2. From Event End Play, add Get Map Markers, then Unregister Marker with Actor = Self.

The marker now follows the actor wherever it goes. To stop showing it, for example once a chest is opened, call Unregister Marker at that moment. To change what it shows as, call Register Marker again with the new kind.

A kind with no row draws nothing

If no row in DT_XenoCore_MapMarkers has your tag as its Kind, the actor is not drawn. The Output Log says so once, naming the actor and the tag: Minimap: <actor> is registered as <tag>, but DT_XenoCore_MapMarkers has no row for that kind.

For programmers: a kind that changes every frame

XenoCore's enemies and NPCs implement IXenoCoreMapMarkerSource and answer which kind to show each frame, or none: a dead enemy, an NPC whose quest is taken. A Blueprint actor cannot implement that interface, so it registers a fixed kind and re-registers when that changes.

docs.title: Test it
docs.text:
1. Place your actor a few metres from the player start in Maps/L_XenoCore_Gym and press Play.
  2. It appears on the minimap (top right) where it stands, with your icon, tint and size.
  3. Walk away from it: it slides to the edge and leaves the circle (or stays pinned to the rim, if Clamp To Rim is on).
  4. Press L3 (or M): it appears on the full-screen map too, and in the legend if the row has a Label.

docs.title: If it doesn't work
docs.text: What you see Cause Fix Nothing, and a Minimap: ... has no row line in the log The row's Kind is not your tag Set Kind exactly. Row names do not matter, the Kind does Nothing, and no log line The actor never registered Check Register Marker runs (BeginPlay) and Actor is Self A blank square The row has no Icon, or the icon's alpha is solid Set Icon; use a white-on-transparent image The marker stays after the actor is gone No Unregister Marker on End Play Add it. The minimap drops destroyed actors on its own, but a hidden one stays

docs.title: Give a map its minimap
docs.text:
Level designer · 30 min · No code

Result: your map's minimap shows its own XC1-style image under the party, lined up with the world, and the L3 overlay shows the same image large.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• A map that runs the XenoCore experience. See Build a world-partition map.
  • Read Minimap for what the minimap shows and where its settings live.
  • An image of your map, top-down, painted in any paint program (step 3 shows how to start from a screenshot of the map).

docs.title: How the image lines up
docs.text:
An Area Definition holds two things that must agree: the Map Texture and the rectangle of the world it covers, Map World Min (the image's top-left corner) and Map World Max (its bottom-right corner), in world centimetres.

The image is read with +X to the right and +Y downwards, so north (up on the map) is −Y. The sample maps are built that way, and your image must be drawn in that orientation. Do not assume the editor's Top viewport shows the world the same way round; check a known landmark against the world X and Y it sits at.

docs.title: 1. Create the Area Definition
docs.text:
1. In the Content Browser, go to Maps/Areas.
  2. Right-click DA_XenoCore_Area_GaurPlain and choose Duplicate. Name it DA_XenoCore_Area_<YourArea>.
  3. Open it and set Display Name: it shows under the minimap and as the L3 view's header. Clear Map Texture for now.
  4. The copy keeps Gaur Plain's Weather Table (its rain and storm odds). Clear it for an area that is always clear, or point it at your own; see Set an area's weather.
  5. Save.

docs.title: 2. Place the XenoCore Map Area
docs.text:
1. In Place Actors, search for XenoCore Map Area and drag it into your map. Its position does not matter.
  2. In the Details panel, set Area to your new asset.

An orange box appears: the rectangle the image will cover. Right now it is Gaur Plain's.

Only one per map

The minimap uses the first XenoCore Map Area it finds. A second one is ignored, and which one counts is not guaranteed.

docs.title: 3. Make the image and set its bounds
docs.text:
1. Paint the map image, square is easiest, with north at the top. XC1's look, which Gaur Plain's Maps/Areas/T_XenoCore_Map_GaurPlain follows, is a flat plan: tan ground, darker raised ground, dark rock walls, blue water, outlines between levels. To start from the real layout, set a viewport to Top, frame the whole Landscape edge to edge, and take a High Resolution Screenshot (viewport menu). Paint over it.
  2. Drag the image file into Maps/Areas (or your own folder) in the Content Browser.
  3. Open the texture. Set Level Of Detail › Texture Group to UI, and X-axis Tiling Method and Y-axis Tiling Method to Clamp. Save.
  4. Open your Area Definition and set Map › Map Texture to it.
  5. Set the bounds:
    • If the image covers exactly your Landscape: select the XenoCore Map Area in the level and click Map › Fit Bounds To Landscape in its Details panel. Then save the Area Definition: the button changes it but does not save it. On a World Partition map it measures only the Landscape pieces that are loaded in the editor, so load the whole map first (World Partition window: drag a box over the whole map, right-click, Load Region From Selection), or the box comes out too small.
    • Otherwise type Map › Map World Min and Map World Max in the Area Definition yourself, then look down on the map in the viewport: the orange box shows the rectangle you typed.

The sample's image was baked by an internal tool

T_XenoCore_Map_GaurPlain was made by a capture-and-paint tool that is not part of the plugin. There is no editor button that bakes a map image; a buyer paints one, as above. A programmer can write a capture with a Scene Capture 2D set to Orthographic, pointed straight down over the Landscape.

docs.title: 4. Check it in the editor
docs.text:
1. Select the XenoCore Map Area. The orange box should cover the same ground as the image. If you changed the asset, nudge the actor (or reselect it) to redraw the box.
  2. Run Build › Map Check. A Map Area with no Area, or an Area with no image, is listed there.
  3. Right-click the Area Definition and choose Asset Actions › Validate Assets. Bounds that run backwards are an error.

docs.title: Test it
docs.text:
1. Open your map and press Play.
  2. Look at the minimap: the ground under the arrow should match where you are standing. Walk to a recognisable feature, such as a lake or a cliff edge, and check it sits under the arrow.
  3. Turn the camera. The pale wedge should follow it.
  4. Press L3 (keyboard M). The large overlay should show the same image, lined up. Press again to close it.
  5. Type XenoCore.Minimap.Rotate 1 in the console and turn the camera. The map should turn so the wedge always points up.

docs.title: If it doesn't work
docs.text: What you see Cause Fix A plain dark circle with markers, no map No XenoCore Map Area in the map, its Area is empty, or the Area has no Map Texture Steps 2 and 3. Map Check names which The map scrolls the wrong way, or is mirrored The image is drawn with north at another edge Redraw it with north up (−Y) Features drift away from the arrow as you walk The bounds do not match the image Click Fit Bounds To Landscape again (and save the Area), or fix Map World Min/Max The image is blurry World Radius shows too much area for the image's resolution Paint the image larger, or lower Minimap › World Radius on the Minimap widget in W_XenoCore_HUDLayout

docs.title: Give an NPC a conversation
docs.text:
Designer · 15 min · No code

Result: a townsperson standing in your map. Walk up, a name plate and a Talk prompt appear, and pressing it plays a short exchange between them and the party leader.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Tour of the project.
  • Interaction, NPCs and dialogue.
  • Glossary: Leader.

docs.title: How an NPC is put together
docs.text:
There is one NPC Blueprint, Characters/NPC/B_XenoCore_Npc. A town is many placed copies of it, each with its own settings in the Details panel. You do not need a Blueprint per NPC for a plain conversation.

When the player presses the prompt, the NPC's On Interact graph runs. The default graph handles, in order: handing in a quest, offering a quest, a quest in progress, and plain talk. Plain talk plays the NPC's Dialogue list and closes the box. At the end of plain talk it also recruits the NPC's Member To Recruit and opens its Shop Table, if either is set; both do nothing on an NPC without them. To go beyond a list, see Branch a conversation.

docs.title: 1. Place the NPC
docs.text:
1. Open your map. Drag Characters/NPC/B_XenoCore_Npc onto the floor.
  2. Select it. Everything below is set on this placed actor, in its Details panel.

A freshly placed NPC is blank: Display Name reads Townsperson, Interact Verb reads Talk, and there are no lines, no quest and no quest marker. For a finished example to copy, Characters/NPC/B_XenoCore_Npc_Sample is a child of the same Blueprint that carries the sample conversation and the sample quest.

docs.title: 2. Say who they are
docs.text:
Under XenoCore › NPC:

Setting Value What it does Display Name Elder Maren The name plate, and the name on their lines Quest (empty) No quest for this recipe Has Quest Unticked (the default) Shows the quest marker when there is no Quest set. Leave it off. Portrait optional Their face on screens that show one

Under XenoCore › NPC › Interaction:

Setting Value What it does Interact Verb Talk The prompt text Interact Range 200 How close the player must be for the name, marker and prompt. One number for all three.

Under XenoCore › NPC › Animation, set Idle Animation to a looping idle. To change how they look, select the inherited mesh component and change its mesh or materials on this placement.

docs.title: 3. Write the lines
docs.text:
Under XenoCore › NPC › Dialogue, open Dialogue and add one entry per line:

# Speaker Line Source 0 (empty) The old bridge washed out in the spring. Npc 1 (empty) If you're heading east, you'll have to go round by the cliffs. Npc 2 (empty) Thanks. We'll manage. Player 3 (empty) Safe travels, then. Npc
  • Source decides whose head the box floats over: Npc is this NPC, Player is the party leader.
  • Speaker is the name on the plate. Leave it empty to use the name of whoever the box is over: this NPC's Display Name, or the leader's own name. Type a name only when someone else is talking, for example a party member chipping in while the box stays over the NPC.
  • Keep each Line to about 165 characters. Longer lines still show in full, and a warning is logged.

docs.title: 4. Frame the conversation (optional)
docs.text:
Under XenoCore › NPC › Dialogue:

Setting Default What it does Use Dialogue Camera Ticked The camera moves in over the leader's shoulder to frame both speakers, and back out when the box closes. Untick it for an NPC visited often, such as a vendor. Dialogue Camera Rig (empty) A framing for this NPC alone, for example a giant. Empty uses Project Settings › XenoCore Content › Dialogue Camera Rig. Face Player When Talked To Ticked The NPC turns to face the leader. Untick it for someone seated or behind a counter. The leader turns to face them either way. Turn Back After Talking Ticked The NPC turns back to the way it was placed once the conversation ends.

docs.title: 5. Save the level
docs.text: Press Ctrl+S, or File › Save Current Level.

docs.title: Test it
docs.text:
1. Press Play and walk towards the NPC. Within 2 m, their name and a Talk prompt appear.
  2. Press the prompt (pad A). The first line appears over their head.
  3. Press A to advance. Line 2 appears over the leader's head, with the leader's name.
  4. After the last line the box closes and you can move again.

While a line is on screen the party cannot move, and the camera does not turn. With Use Dialogue Camera on, the camera moves in when the conversation starts and returns to exactly where it was when it ends.

docs.title: If it doesn't work
docs.text:
The NPC offers a quest you did not give them

You placed B_XenoCore_Npc_Sample, or duplicated it, rather than B_XenoCore_Npc. The sample carries the sample quest in Quest. Clear it on the placed actor, or place the blank Blueprint instead.

Fails silently: the prompt never appears

You are outside Interact Range, or another interactable (a chest) is nearer and takes the prompt. NPCs do not need any special collision; the prompt finds them by distance.

The name plate is blank

Display Name is empty, and so is the line's Speaker. For a player line, the leader's name comes from their party member definition.

An extra verb does not show

Only one extra verb can be pressed (pad X), so only the first Extra Interact Verbs entry is used, and none at all when the NPC has Trade Offers, because Trade takes that button. The rest are dropped with a warning in the Output Log.

docs.title: Going further
docs.text:
• Branch a conversation: conditions, and anything between lines.
  • Offer a collection quest.
  • Open a shop and Set up a trade: the same NPC does both.
  • Recruit a party member by talking.

docs.title: Turn on NVIDIA DLSS and Frame Generation
docs.text:
Any · 15 min · No code if your Lyra project already has the DLSS settings (see the warning below) · Last tested: 2026-10-05 (RTX 4060 Laptop, plugin v8.8.0)

Result: the game's Video settings gain an NVIDIA DLSS group: Super Resolution (including DLAA), Frame Generation and NVIDIA Reflex Low Latency, on any GeForce RTX graphics card.

XenoCore does not include NVIDIA's plugin, because NVIDIA's licence lets it ship inside a finished game but not inside a source project sold to developers. The settings are already built in. They appear the moment you install the plugin, and stay out of sight when it isn't there.

Fails silently: a stock Lyra project has no DLSS group

The NVIDIA DLSS group lives in Lyra's own settings screen, which is part of the host Lyra project's C++, not the XenoCore plugin. A stock Lyra Starter Game project does not have it, so installing NVIDIA's plugin there adds nothing to Options › Video, and nothing warns. Adding the group to a stock Lyra needs a programmer and a C++ build; see the note at the end of this page. The XenoCore download is the plugin folder only, so it does not include those Lyra files.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Windows, DirectX 12 (the project default) and a GeForce RTX card for the options to appear.
  • Frame Generation needs an RTX 40 Series or newer, and Hardware-accelerated GPU Scheduling switched on in Windows Settings > System > Display > Graphics. Multi Frame Generation (3X to 6X) and Dynamic need an RTX 50 Series.

docs.title: Install the plugin
docs.text:
1. Download DLSS 4.5 for Unreal Engine 5.8 from https://developer.nvidia.com/rtx/dlss.
  2. From the download's Plugins folder, copy DLSS, StreamlineCore, StreamlineDLSSG, StreamlineReflex and StreamlineNGXCommon into the project's Plugins folder (for example Plugins/NVIDIA/). Use either the project's Plugins folder or the engine's Engine/Plugins/Marketplace, never both.
  3. Open the project. The plugins are enabled by being there; let it rebuild when it asks.
  4. Recommended: in Edit > Plugins, disable the engine's own Reflex plugin (NVIDIA's replaces it).

docs.title: Test it
docs.text:
Play, open Options > Video, and find NVIDIA DLSS. The output log shows what was applied:

LogLyraNvidia: DLSS Super Resolution ON (Quality) at 66.7% of 1707x1067
LogLyraNvidia: DLSS Frame Generation On2X
LogLyraNvidia: NVIDIA Reflex Enabled

docs.title: How the settings behave
docs.text:
Setting Options Default Notes NVIDIA DLSS Super Resolution Off, Auto, Quality, Balanced, Performance, Ultra Performance, DLAA Auto While on, Anti-Aliasing and 3D Resolution are greyed out: DLSS sets the render resolution. Auto turns DLSS off below 1080p, as NVIDIA's own table does. Frame Generation Off, plus whatever the card supports: Auto, Dynamic, 2X to 6X Off Runs in Standalone and packaged builds, not in the editor viewport. NVIDIA Reflex Low Latency Off, On, On + Boost On Locked on while Frame Generation is on.

Only the modes your card supports are listed. Auto is missing in Play In Editor; that is the plugin's own rule.

docs.title: Shipping a game with DLSS
docs.text: Your game now redistributes NVIDIA's binaries, which carries NVIDIA's own obligations: notify NVIDIA before release, credit NVIDIA, and include their third-party notices. Read the NVIDIA RTX SDK EULA in the download. Do not use NVIDIA logos in your store page without NVIDIA's approval.

docs.title: If it doesn't work
docs.text:
• No NVIDIA DLSS group: the plugin is not enabled, the card is not an RTX card, or the driver is too old. Search the log for LogDLSS and LogStreamline.
  • Frame Generation does nothing: you are in the editor viewport. Use Standalone. Check Hardware-accelerated GPU Scheduling.
  • The editor crashes after resizing the window with Frame Generation on: a known NVIDIA plugin issue (release notes 8.8.0). Turn Frame Generation off while working in the editor.
For programmers: how it works

The settings call NVIDIA's own Blueprint libraries by name, so nothing in the project links to NVIDIA's code. They are a Lyra game-settings class, LyraNvidiaSettings (in the host project's Source/LyraGame/Settings/), registered on Lyra's Video settings page. In a stock Lyra project those files must be added to LyraGame and the project rebuilt: the new LyraNvidiaSettings.h/.cpp and LyraGameSettingRegistry_Video_NVIDIA.cpp, plus small edits to LyraGameSettingRegistry.h/.cpp and LyraSettingsLocal.h/.cpp.

docs.title: Open a shop
docs.text:
Designer · 20 min · No code

Result: a townsperson who talks to you first and then opens a shop selling your own stock. You buy an item with gold, sell one back, and leave.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Write an NPC conversation. A shopkeeper is an ordinary NPC with one extra setting.
  • Shops and trade explains how prices are worked out.
  • The items you want to sell already exist. See Add an armour piece or Add a consumable item.

docs.title: How a shop is put together
docs.text:
A shop is one data asset plus one setting on a placed NPC. There is no shop Blueprint to write.

Piece Sample What it decides Shop table Shop/DA_XenoCore_Shop_Colony9 (Gaur Plain's Kamos Outpost uses Shop/DA_XenoCore_Shop_KamosOutpost) What is for sale, in what order, and at what price NPC Characters/NPC/B_XenoCore_Npc, placed in a level Who runs the shop and what they say first Shop screen UserInterface/HUD/W_XenoCore_ShopScreen, named by Project Settings › Game › XenoCore UI › Screens › Shop Screen The screen itself. You don't touch it for this recipe.

The NPC Blueprint already contains the shop logic. When you talk to an NPC, its On Interact graph plays the NPC's dialogue. Then, if Can Shop is true, it calls the Open Shop node with that NPC's shop table. So a shopkeeper always talks first, and the shop opens at the end of the conversation. There is no separate "Shop" button on the prompt.

Prices come from the item. Every item carries a Sell Value on its XenoCoreFragment_ItemCategory fragment. A shop charges Sell Value × 10 to buy, and pays Sell Value to sell. You only type a price on the shop table when you want something different.

Stock never runs out. A shop table is a price list, not an inventory.

What the shop buys is not authored anywhere. Any shop buys anything except key items.

docs.title: 1. Check your items can be sold by a shop
docs.text:
For each item you want to stock, open its item definition and find the XenoCoreFragment_ItemCategory entry in its Fragments list. Check:

  1. Category is not Materials and not Key. A shop never sells materials or key items.
  2. Sell Value is above 0. With 0, the item has no price.

Fails silently at play time, loudly at save time

An item with no XenoCoreFragment_ItemCategory fragment has no price at all. The shop table flags this as a red error when you save it (see step 3), but if you skip that check the row is simply missing from the game.

docs.title: 2. Create the shop table
docs.text:
1. Create a folder MyGame/Shops under Content.
  2. Right-click in it and choose Data › Data Asset. In the class picker, pick Xeno Core Shop Table (search Shop Table). Name it DA_Shop_Blacksmith.
  3. Open it. Under XenoCore › Shop, add one entry to Offers per item:
    • Item: the item definition.
    • Price Override: leave at 0 to charge the item's own buy price. Type a number to charge that instead.
  4. Look at the greyed-out Resolved Price beside each row. That is exactly what the player will pay. It updates as you edit (on a table you have just opened it may take a moment to fill in while the items load). In game the items load when the shop screen opens, not with the map.
  5. The order of Offers is the order the rows appear inside each category tab.
  6. Save.

Price Override 0 means \"use the item's price\", not \"free\"

A shop never gives anything away. If you want a free item, give it as a quest reward instead.

docs.title: 3. Let the editor check the table
docs.text:
Right-click DA_Shop_Blacksmith and choose Asset Actions › Validate Assets. The table reports:

Message Meaning sells nothing Offers is empty, so the Buy list would open empty has no Item set A row has no item cannot be sold by a shop The item is a Material or Key item, or has no category fragment and Sell Value prices at 0 The resolved price is 0 same item as offer n (warning) The item is listed twice

Fix every error before you go on.

docs.title: 4. Place the shopkeeper
docs.text:
1. Open the level you want the shop in. For a first try, use Maps/L_XenoCore_Gym.
  2. Drag Characters/NPC/B_XenoCore_Npc into the level.
  3. With the placed NPC selected, in the Details panel under XenoCore › NPC:
    • Display Name: Blacksmith.
    • Shop Table: DA_Shop_Blacksmith.
  4. Under XenoCore › NPC › Dialogue, fill in Dialogue with what they say before the shop opens, for example one line: Take a look at what I've got.
  5. Save the level.

Set Shop Table on the placed NPC, never in the Blueprint's Class Defaults

Shop Table is a per-instance setting. If you set it in B_XenoCore_Npc's Class Defaults, every NPC in every level becomes a shop.

A vendor the player visits often

Untick Use Dialogue Camera under XenoCore › NPC › Dialogue, so the camera does not move in and out on every visit. Untick Face Player When Talked To for a shopkeeper behind a counter. See Give an NPC a conversation.

Fails silently: an NPC with no lines

If Dialogue is empty the conversation completes instantly and logs a warning. The shop still opens, but the NPC never speaks. Give every shopkeeper at least one line.

docs.title: Test it
docs.text:
1. Press Play in the level with your shopkeeper.
  2. Give yourself gold: open the console (`) and type XenoAwardGold 5000.
  3. Walk up to the Blacksmith. The prompt reads Talk. Press A (keyboard E).
  4. The line plays. When it ends, the shop opens on the Buy tab with your items, at the Resolved Price you saw in the table.
  5. Buy one. Your gold goes down by the price and the item is in your bag.
  6. Switch to Sell and sell something. Your gold goes up by its Sell Value.
  7. Leave with B (keyboard Escape). The conversation box does not come back.

docs.title: If it doesn't work
docs.text:
The NPC talks but no shop opens

Shop Table is empty on this placed NPC, or you set it on a different copy. Select the NPC in the level and check XenoCore › NPC › Shop Table.

The shop opens and the Buy list is empty

Every row failed its checks, or Offers is empty. Run Validate Assets on the table.

An item can't be sold back

Key items can't be sold. Equipped copies are never sold either: unequip it first. A sell count of zero shows the "in use" message instead of the confirm.

The Output Log says Open Shop could not load XenoCore UI > Shop Screen

The screen named by Project Settings › Game › XenoCore UI › Shop Screen was moved, renamed, or does not derive from XenoCoreShopScreenBase. A setting that fails to load falls back to the shipped UserInterface/HUD/W_XenoCore_ShopScreen with a warning; this error means that one is missing too. Point the setting at a valid screen, or move the shipped one back. See UI and input.

docs.title: Going further
docs.text:
• Shops and trade: buy and sell prices, carry limits, and what the screen does.
  • Set up a trade: the barter version, on the second interaction button.
  • Branch a conversation: to open the shop only after a choice, place your own Open Shop node (category XenoCore › Shop) in a conversation. It has two exits, Transacted and Nothing Changed, and exactly one always fires.

docs.title: Package a build
docs.text:
Programmer · 1–2 h (mostly waiting) · No code (editor menus; one optional command line)

Result: a Windows build of your game that boots to the title screen, starts a new game in your map, and has every menu working, checked in the packaged build rather than only in the editor.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Requirements: Visual Studio and the Windows SDK are needed to package, because the project has C++.
  • Your content is in place. See Replace the sample content.

docs.title: What packaging does here
docs.text:
The project is Lyra with XenoCore added, so it packages as Lyra does: the LyraGame target, Development configuration by default, compressed into pak files. The editor-only XenoCoreEditor module is left out automatically.

Two XenoCore specifics shape the packaging settings. The Apply step of Install and first launch writes both into your project's Config/DefaultGame.ini. If you are not sure it ran, use Tools › XenoCore › Apply XenoCore Project Settings; it changes nothing that is already set:

  • Some assets are found by path, not by reference. The shop, trade, arts, save, quest and loot screens and the dialogue anchor are loaded by a fixed path from C++. The cooker can't see those paths, so the project cooks /XenoCore/UserInterface and /XenoCore/Characters/NPC in full (Additional Asset Directories to Cook in the packaging settings). Keep them there.
  • Maps reached only by a setting must be listed. The new-game map and any map a save file names are soft references. The shipped list is L_XenoCore_FrontEnd, L_XenoCore_GaurPlain (where New Game starts) and L_XenoCore_Gym. List every map you ship.

docs.title: 1. Check the packaging settings
docs.text:
Open Project Settings › Project › Packaging:

  1. Build Configuration: Development while testing; Shipping for release.
  2. List of maps to include in a packaged build: your title map (Maps/L_XenoCore_FrontEnd unless you replaced it) and every playable map. The shipped list is the front end, L_XenoCore_GaurPlain and L_XenoCore_Gym; remove the sample maps once yours replace them.
  3. Additional Asset Directories to Cook: keep /XenoCore/UserInterface and /XenoCore/Characters/NPC. Add any folder of yours whose assets are loaded only by path.
  4. Directories to Never Cook: add your own test or scratch folders.
  5. For Distribution: tick for the build you release.

Fails silently: a map left off the list

The packaged title screen works, and New Game or Load goes nowhere, because the map was never cooked. The editor never shows this; only a packaged build does.

Fails silently: shipped content that uses a never-cooked asset

Anything that references an asset in a Directories to Never Cook folder works in the editor and arrives in the build with that asset missing (a silent level, a default material). Before packaging, open the Reference Viewer on the test assets you have used, or keep your own test content out of shipped folders altogether.

docs.title: 2. Check which plugins ship
docs.text:
Your Lyra project still carries Lyra's own sample game features (ShooterCore, ShooterMaps, ShooterExplorer, TopDownArena and others), and they cook unless you turn them off. XenoCore.uplugin declares every plugin XenoCore's content needs (Niagara, Niagara UI Renderer, Water, DataRegistry, Metasound and VRM4U among them), so they stay on whatever you disable. See Compatibility for the list.

  1. Open Edit › Plugins, filter by Enabled.
  2. Disable what your game doesn't use. Re-open the editor and play-test after each change.

VRM4U is needed at runtime

The sample party is VRoid characters, and their materials, spring bones and facial expressions use the VRM4U plugin in the game, not only at import. Keep it enabled while any VRoid character ships. It compiles from source with the rest of the project; its assimp library is in Plugins/VRM4U/ThirdParty/assimp, and a packaged build links it.

docs.title: 3. Set the version
docs.text: Set Project Settings › Project › Description › Project Version. XenoCore draws this version in the bottom-right corner of every screen, including in packaged builds, so a bug report can name the build.

docs.title: 4. Package
docs.text:
From the editor: Platforms › Windows › Package Project, and choose an output folder.

For programmers: the same from the command line

Unreal Automation Tool runs the whole package without the editor:

"<Engine>\Engine\Build\BatchFiles\RunUAT.bat" BuildCookRun -project="<project folder>\Lyra.uproject" -noP4 -target=LyraGame -platform=Win64 -clientconfig=Development -build -cook -stage -pak -iostore -archive -archivedirectory="<output folder>" -unattended

Fails silently: the exit code can say success

Build.bat and some automation steps can return exit code 0 after a failed step. Don't trust the exit code or a "finished" message. Read the end of the log for BUILD SUCCESSFUL (or Result: Succeeded from Build.bat) and search it for Error:.

docs.title: 5. Test the packaged build, not the editor
docs.text:
Run the .exe from the output folder and go through the whole path:

  1. The boot screens play, then the title screen.
  2. New Game loads your map, with your party.
  3. Open every menu screen: Items, Equipment, Arts, Party, Quests, Save.
  4. Talk to an NPC, open a shop and a trade, open a chest after a fight.
  5. Save, quit to title, Continue.

Anything that works in the editor and not here is almost always a missing cooked asset.

docs.title: Test it
docs.text: The packaged game completes step 5 with nothing missing, and its log (<output folder>/Windows/Lyra/Saved/Logs/Lyra.log) has no LoadErrors or "failed to load" lines for your assets.

docs.title: If it doesn't work
docs.text:
A menu or popup never opens in the build

It is loaded by path and its folder is not cooked. Add the folder to Additional Asset Directories to Cook, or move the asset back where XenoCore expects it.

The build fails on a plugin you don't use

Disable that plugin in Edit › Plugins rather than fixing it. Do not disable one that XenoCore.uplugin lists; XenoCore's content will fail to load without it.

The package is far bigger than expected

Sample content, pack assets or unused Lyra features are still being cooked. Right-click each of your maps in the Content Browser and choose Size Map... to see what it pulls in, and see Megascans at shipping size.

More in Build and editor troubleshooting.

docs.title: Going further
docs.text:
• Replace the sample content
  • Compatibility

docs.title: Set palette slots and unlocks
docs.text:
Designer · 20 min · No code

Result: you decide how many Art slots the palette has at each level, which Arts each character learns and when, and which slot each Art starts in. The player then rearranges them on the Arts menu.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Your first art
  • Glossary: Art, Palette, Talent Art.

docs.title: The three settings
docs.text:
What Where Setting How many slots open at which level Game/BP_XenoCore_Progression, Class Defaults › XenoCore › Arts Art Slot Unlock Levels Which Arts a character learns, and when A learnset Data Table, set as Art Learn Table on the character's pawn Blueprint, Class Defaults › XenoCore › Arts One row per Art Where a learned Art starts Each learnset row Default Slot

Art Slot Unlock Levels is one list for every character: entry i is the character level at which slot i opens. The default is 1, 1, 1, 12, 20, 28, 34, 40: three slots from the start, eight by level 40. The list's length is the palette's full width, so slots not yet open draw as locked. Eight entries of 1 give every slot from the start. Keep the list ascending.

Slots are numbered in unlock order, not left to right. The bar fills from the centre out: slot 0 sits immediately left of the Talent Art, slot 1 immediately right, slot 2 next left, slot 3 next right, and so on. So with the default list, the further a slot is from the centre, the later it opens. Default Slot counts the same way.

A learnset is a Data Table whose row structure is XenoCoreArtUnlock. Each row holds an Art, an Unlock Level (1 or more) and a Default Slot (0 to 7, or -1 for learned but not placed). The row name is free text; only the columns matter, and rows are read sorted by Unlock Level, so their order does not matter either. The shipped tables are in Characters/Party/Learnsets/: DT_XenoCore_ArtLearnset_Default on Characters/Party/B_XenoCore_PartyMember_Base, and one per sample character: _Kael, _Mira, _Nia, _Dorran, _Isolde, _Sabine and _Tamsin. Each VRoid member's pawn (Characters/VRoid/<Name>/B_XenoCore_Party_VRoid_*) points at its own table, and so does the matching colour-variant pawn. Kael's, for example, adds Stream Edge and War Swing to the Back Slash / Light Heal / Air Slash start; Isolde, Sabine and Tamsin have their own Arts entirely.

docs.title: 1. Choose the slot ladder
docs.text:
1. Open Game/BP_XenoCore_Progression and click Class Defaults.
  2. Edit Art Slot Unlock Levels. For example, 1, 1, 5, 10, 15, 20 gives two slots at the start, a sixth at level 20, and a six-wide palette.
  3. Compile and Save.

Wider than eight

Default Slot accepts 0 to 7, so a ninth slot or later can only be filled from the Arts menu. The palette widget has no hard limit: it repeats its slot art outward from the centre for every entry. XC1's bar is eight wide; keep the list to eight entries or fewer unless you have checked a wider bar fits your screen.

docs.title: 2. Choose each character's Arts
docs.text:
1. Make the character a learnset. Duplicate Characters/Party/Learnsets/DT_XenoCore_ArtLearnset_Default into your own folder as DT_Rook_ArtLearnset (it is a table, not a concrete Art, so duplicating it is fine), or create a new Data Table with row structure XenoCoreArtUnlock. Learnsets can also be CSV-imported like any Data Table.

  2. Open it. Click Add for each row, rename it, and fill in the columns in the Row Editor:

    Row Name Art Unlock Level Default Slot Lv01_FrostFan DA_FrostFan 1 0 Lv01_Mend DA_Mend 1 1 Lv08_BackSlash DA_XenoCore_BackSlash 8 -1

  3. Save.

  4. Open the character's pawn Blueprint, for example B_Party_Rook, and click Class Defaults. Under XenoCore › Arts, set Art Learn Table to DT_Rook_ArtLearnset.
  5. Compile and Save.

An Art is learned as soon as the character reaches its Unlock Level, including in reserve, and the level-up banner names it under that character. Default Slot is used only when the character's palette is first built. After that the player's arrangement is kept, and an Art learned later arrives in the Arts menu's list, not on the bar.

Fails silently: a Default Slot that isn't open yet

If Default Slot is a slot the character's level has not opened, the Art is learned but not placed. It is in the Arts menu, not on the bar. Use a slot that is open at the Unlock Level.

docs.title: 3. The player's side: the Arts menu
docs.text:
The Arts menu edits any roster member, benched ones included. Its Setting tab puts learned Arts into open slots; its Level Up tab spends Art Points. What the menu arranges is exactly what the battle palette shows, drawn from the centre out in both. The menu shows no slot numbers: a list row reads Equipped for an Art on the bar, an empty strip slot is Empty Slot, and a locked one is Locked Slot, whose detail line says This slot opens at level N.

The Arts menu cannot empty a slot yet: it can only put a different Art there, or move one. To empty a slot while testing, type XenoSetArt <slot> none in the console (it edits the character you are controlling), or call Set Art Slot with no Art from a Blueprint.

docs.title: Palette Order
docs.text: Each Art definition also has Palette Order (Art › Palette). It only matters for an Art that is granted to a character but is not in that character's stored palette: such Arts are drawn after the palette's own, sorted by Palette Order. For party members with an Art Learn Table, the slot decides and Palette Order is ignored.

docs.title: Test it
docs.text:
1. Press Play in Maps/L_XenoCore_Gym.
  2. Open the Arts menu and pick the character. The palette strip shows the open slots with your default Arts in them, and the rest locked.
  3. Type XenoAwardExp 20000 in the console. Open the Arts menu again: more slots are open and later Arts are in the list.
  4. Move an Art into a newly opened slot, close the menu and engage. The battle palette matches.

XenoArts in the console prints the controlled character's learned Arts and palette. XenoSetArt 3 Mend puts an Art whose name contains "Mend" into slot 3.

docs.title: If it doesn't work
docs.text:
Fails silently: my learnset change does nothing

The character already has a palette from a save, or from an earlier session of the same Play. Default Slot only applies to an empty palette. Test with a new game.

The character still has the base Arts

You edited DT_XenoCore_ArtLearnset_Default instead of the character's own table, or the character's Art Learn Table still points at the default. Every sample character has its own table, so a row added to the default does not reach them. The player's own pawn, Game/B_XenoCore_Player, uses Kael's table (DT_XenoCore_ArtLearnset_Kael) and also gets Back Slash and Light Heal from its ability set, Game/AbilitySet_XenoCore_Hero.

An Art is on the bar twice, or not at all

Arts granted by an ability set and Arts from a learnset are merged when the palette is built. Give each character its Arts one way: through its Art Learn Table.

docs.title: Going further
docs.text:
• Tune levelling: Art Points and art level costs.
  • Arts and Progression

docs.title: Place enemies in a map
docs.text:
Designer · 20 min · No code

Result: a squad of enemies that wanders a patch of your map at a spread of levels, fights together and comes back after you defeat it, plus a single hand-placed enemy walking a patrol and a named unique monster.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Your first enemy.
  • Glossary: Squad, spawner, Detection, Aggro.
  • Enemies and AI.

docs.title: Two ways to put enemies in a map
docs.text:
• A spawner (the usual way). Place one XenoCore Enemy Spawner (AXenoCoreEnemySpawner) and tell it what to keep alive. One spawner is one squad. The Gaur Plain sample places all of its enemies this way. Place the spawner, never its enemies: the enemies it makes are runtime actors it owns, and they do not exist in the level.
  • Hand-placed. Drag an enemy Blueprint straight into the map. Use it for a single enemy on a set patrol route, a scripted encounter, or a test. A hand-placed enemy does not respawn and is not part of a squad.

docs.title: How a field enemy behaves
docs.text:
Knowing this before you lay out a map saves a lot of confusion in play:

  • It may notice you first. Each enemy has a Detection setting (XenoCore › AI › Detection):

    Detection Starts a fight when… None (passive) never; it fights only once it is attacked Sight the party leader enters its view cone (Sight Radius, Sight Half Angle) Sound the leader runs within Sound Radius. Walking past is quiet enough Ether the party uses an ether art within Ether Radius, even a harmless one

  • It ignores a party far above it, until hit. If the party leader is 6 or more levels above the enemy, it does not notice the party. Attack it and it fights back whatever its level. A Unique Monster, or an enemy whose controller has Always Aggro ticked, skips this rule.

  • Its squad joins in. When one member of a spawner's squad is provoked, the others within Link Radius join the fight (Link Aggro).
  • It attacks whoever holds its aggro. A companion who hits harder can draw it off. A red ring under a party member shows who it is after. It fights within Engage Radius (1600 cm), and stays engaged out to 2.5 times that.
  • You can outrun it. Get far enough away and an engaged enemy gives up, walks home calm and recovers its health.
  • It is tied to its home. A spawned enemy's home is where it spawned; a hand-placed one's is where you put it. If a chase takes it farther than Leash Radius (70 m) from home, it gives up, heals and walks back.
  • A squad drops one chest. Only the last member killed drops a chest (Squad Loot Rule). It is gold at three times the usual chance (Squad Gold Multiplier), otherwise silver, and holds the leader's loot: the first enemy of the first Members entry. Put the type whose loot the squad should give at the top of the list.
  • A spawner's squad comes back; a hand-placed enemy does not. A fallen squad member returns after Respawn Delay (90 s), and only out of sight: when the leader is beyond Hidden Distance (50 m), or behind the camera and beyond Behind Camera Min Distance (18 m). Nothing respawns while its squad is fighting. A hand-placed enemy stays gone until the map loads again.
  • Its level shows above it. Every enemy wears a lvl.N label, coloured by how its level compares with the party leader's, faded out with distance and always shown in battle. A unique monster's label is gold and carries its name. The colours, the text and the distances are in Project Settings › Game › XenoCore Enemies › Level Label.

The radii and the level rule are on the AI controller, Characters/Enemies/Core/BP_AIC_XenoCore_Enemy, under XenoCore › AI. They apply to every enemy using that controller, unless an enemy sets its own Engage Radius Override, Leash Radius Override or Disengage Radius Scale Override (XenoCore › AI, -1 = use the controller's).

Respawning on a timer is a deliberate choice

The classic games bring field enemies back when you reload an area. XenoCore uses an out-of-sight timer so the party can level in one place. Untick Respawn on a spawner to keep its squad down until the spawner streams out and back in.

docs.title: 1. Make sure the map has a navigation mesh
docs.text:
Enemies move by pathfinding. Without a navigation mesh they stand still, and a spawner finds nowhere to put them.

  1. Open your map. Press P in the viewport to show navigation.
  2. If there is no green area where enemies will stand, add a Nav Mesh Bounds Volume (Place Actors › Volumes) and scale it over the play area.

Maps/L_XenoCore_Gym already has one.

docs.title: 2. Place a squad with a spawner
docs.text:
1. In Place Actors, search for XenoCore Enemy Spawner and drag it onto the green area.

  2. In its Details panel, under XenoCore › Spawner, add an entry to Members:

    Field Value Enemy Class B_XenoCore_Minion_Grunt (in Characters/Enemies/Minion/Variants) Count 3 Min Level / Max Level 6 / 8

    Each member rolls its own level in that range. Add more entries for a mixed squad. 3. Set Wander Radius (default 1200 cm) to how far the squad strolls from the spawner while nobody is fighting. The viewport draws it as a sphere. 0 makes them stand where they spawn. 4. Leave Link Aggro and Squad Loot Rule (XenoCore › Spawner › Squad) and Respawn (XenoCore › Spawner › Respawn) ticked. Change Respawn Delay if 90 s is too quick or too slow for your area.

The level drives all of an enemy's stats, so one Blueprint at different levels is already a different fight.

docs.title: 3. Hand-place one enemy on a patrol
docs.text:
1. Drag Characters/Enemies/Minion/Variants/B_XenoCore_Minion_Grunt (or your own enemy) into the map, on the green area. Under XenoCore › Enemy, set its Enemy Level.
  2. In its Details panel, under XenoCore › AI › Patrol, add two entries to Patrol Points.
  3. Each point appears in the viewport as a diamond handle (select the enemy to see them). Drag them to where the enemy should walk, on the green navigation area. They are relative to where the enemy stands, so moving the enemy moves its whole route.
  4. Leave Patrol Speed at 105 for the minion (its walk), and set Patrol Wait to how long it pauses at each point, for example 3.

The enemy walks from where you placed it, through each point to the last, and back again, until a fight starts. After a fight it walks home and starts again. With no patrol points, a hand-placed enemy whose Wander Radius is above 0 mills about its home instead.

docs.title: 4. Make a unique monster
docs.text:
The quickest way is a spawner of its own:

  1. Place a second XenoCore Enemy Spawner. Give it one Members entry with Count 1, for example B_XenoCore_Minion_Brute at level 12 to 12.
  2. Under XenoCore › Spawner › Unique, tick Unique Monster and set Unique Name to Stonejaw the Old.
  3. Under XenoCore › Spawner › Respawn, set Respawn Chance to 0.3, so it only sometimes comes back.

A unique monster ignores the six-level rule, wears a gold, named label, and always drops a gold chest. The spawner sets all three on the enemy it makes; nothing is needed on the enemy Blueprint.

You can also make a hand-placed enemy unique. Set, on that placed actor only:

Setting Category Value Display Name XenoCore › Enemy Stonejaw the Old Enemy Level XenoCore › Enemy 12 Unique Monster XenoCore › Enemy Ticked Experience Reward XenoCore › Enemy 400 Always Gold Chest XenoCore › Loot Ticked Chest Drop Delay XenoCore › Enemy › Loot 3.0

These, the patrol and wander settings, the Detection settings, the three radius overrides, and the enemy's Arts and AI Profile can all be changed per placement. Everything else (its mesh, abilities, stats curve, drop table) belongs to the Blueprint.

To make an enemy skip the level rule without making it unique, give it a controller with Always Aggro:

  1. Create a Blueprint child of BP_AIC_XenoCore_Enemy in your folder, BP_AIC_MyGame_Aggressive.
  2. In its class defaults, tick Always Aggro.
  3. Make a child Blueprint of your enemy, and set its AI Controller Class to BP_AIC_MyGame_Aggressive.

Fails silently: a controller that is not a child of the XenoCore one

An enemy's team comes from its AI controller, and only the XenoCore controller class can carry one. A plain AI Controller Blueprint leaves the enemy on no team: it cannot be damaged by the party and never fights. Always make a child of BP_AIC_XenoCore_Enemy.

docs.title: 5. Save
docs.text: Save the level.

docs.title: Test it
docs.text:
1. Press Play and approach the squad. Grunts hear by sound: walk past and they keep wandering; run near them and they attack.
  2. Hit one squad member from a distance. The others nearby join the fight.
  3. Defeat the whole squad. Only the last one drops a chest, at least silver, with the leader's loot.
  4. Walk well away (beyond 50 m) and wait 90 seconds. The squad is back when you return. XenoCore.Enemies.RespawnAll in the console brings it back at once.
  5. The hand-placed enemy walks its route and pauses at each point. Run more than 70 m from its placed position mid-fight and it turns and walks home.

docs.title: If it doesn't work
docs.text:
The enemy never notices the party

Its Detection is None (passive), the party leader is 6 or more levels above it (the level rule applies to noticing), or it hears by Sound and you are walking. Hit it, lower the level gap, change its Detection, or tick Always Aggro on a child controller.

Nothing spawns

The spawner's Members is empty, an entry has no Enemy Class, or there is no navigation mesh near the spawner. Press P and check.

The squad never comes back

Respawn is unticked, Respawn Chance is 0, its squad is still fighting, or you are standing near the spawner and facing it. Walk beyond Hidden Distance and wait.

It stands still while engaged

No navigation mesh where it stands. Press P and check.

The patrolling enemy stands still, or skips a point

A patrol point is off the navigation mesh, or Patrol Points is empty. Press P and drag the handles onto the green area.

It snaps home in the middle of a fight

The chase crossed Leash Radius, measured from its home. Place it, or its spawner, where you want it to fight.

Levels on the placed enemy seem ignored

You changed the Blueprint's default after placing. A placed enemy keeps any value you set on it directly. Reset the field on the placement (the yellow arrow) to take the Blueprint's value. A spawned enemy always takes its level from the spawner's Min Level / Max Level.

docs.title: Going further
docs.text:
• Enemies and AI.
  • Build a drop table, Set an enemy's statline.
  • Build a World Partition map.

docs.title: Recruit a party member by talking to them
docs.text:
Designer · 10 min · No code

Result: a character standing in your map. Walk up, press Talk, they say their lines, and they join the party at its current level. The NPC disappears and the new member is standing where they were.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Give an NPC a conversation. A recruit is an ordinary NPC with one extra setting.
  • The character exists as a party member definition (Characters/Party/PartyMember_*). See Add a party member. Leave them out of BP_XenoCore_Party → Starting Roster, or they are in the party before you ever meet them.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The NPC Blueprint already has the logic. Its On Interact graph calls Try Recruit in two places:

  • at the end of plain talk, before the shop check;
  • straight after a quest is handed in.

Try Recruit does nothing on an NPC with no Member To Recruit, so every other NPC is unaffected. On a recruit it adds the member to the roster, fields them if there is a free slot, and moves their body to where the NPC stood. Then the NPC leaves.

docs.title: 1. Place the NPC and give them their lines
docs.text:
Place Characters/NPC/B_XenoCore_Npc and fill in Display Name and Dialogue, as in Give an NPC a conversation. This is what the character says before joining. To make the hand-over read, give the NPC the member's own body: the NPC plays one clip, Idle Animation, straight on its mesh, so the clip must be on that mesh's skeleton.

  • A VRoid member: select the NPC's inherited mesh component and set Skeletal Mesh Asset to the member's Characters/VRoid/<Name>/Mesh/SK_AvatarSample_<X>_Lit (<X> is the letter in the member's asset names, for example L for Kael). On the actor, set Idle Animation to Characters/VRoid/<Name>/Animation/AS_XenoCore_NpcIdle_<X>, a standing idle already retargeted to that skeleton for each of the seven sample members. Set Portrait to the member's Characters/VRoid/<Name>/T_XenoCore_Portrait_VRoid_<X>. This is how the five Gaur Plain recruits are set up. For a VRoid character of your own, retarget a standing idle onto its skeleton (right-click the idle, Retarget Animations, using that character's IK Retargeter).
  • A Mannequin member: its mesh and colour materials, with Lyra's MM_Unarmed_Idle_Ready.

docs.title: 2. Pick who joins
docs.text:
On the placed NPC, under XenoCore › NPC › Recruit:

Setting Default What it does Member To Recruit empty The only field you must set. The party member definition who joins. Recruit After Quest empty Optional. They join only once this quest has been turned in. Usually the NPC's own Quest. Empty = they join the first time you talk to them. Join At Party Level on They arrive at least at the leader's level. A recruit authored above the party keeps their own level. Leave When Recruited on The NPC leaves and the member stands in their place. Turn it off for someone who stays behind (a recruiter, not the recruit).

Set it on the placed NPC, never on the Blueprint

Setting Member To Recruit on B_XenoCore_Npc's defaults makes every NPC in every level the same recruit.

docs.title: 3. Optional: "help me first"
docs.text:
1. Give the NPC a Quest (see Create a collection quest).
  2. Set Recruit After Quest to that same quest.

Talk once: they offer the quest. Hand it in: they say their Turn In Dialogue and join.

docs.title: Test it
docs.text:
1. Press Play and walk up to the NPC. Their name and a Talk prompt appear.
  2. Press A (keyboard E) and advance through the lines.
  3. When the conversation ends, the join banner plays, the NPC is gone, and the member is standing where the NPC was.
  4. Open the menu (pad Y, keyboard I) and the Party screen: they are listed, at least at the leader's level.
  5. With Recruit After Quest set: the first talk offers the quest and nobody joins. Hand the quest in, and they join after their Turn In Dialogue.

docs.title: Things to know
docs.text:
• Saves. The roster is saved, so after loading, a recruit already in the party is not standing in the world any more. The NPC checks this a few times a second and removes itself.
  • A full party. If every active slot is taken, the recruit goes to the reserve.
  • Other ways to recruit. A walk-in volume is XenoCore Party Recruit Trigger; any Blueprint can call Add To Roster on Get Party Component with Join At Party Level ticked. All three go through the same code.

docs.title: If it doesn't work
docs.text:
Fails silently: the conversation ends and nobody joins

Member To Recruit is empty on this placed NPC (you may have set it on a different copy), or Recruit After Quest names a quest that has not been turned in yet. Only accepting the quest is not enough.

The member is already in the party at the start

They are listed in Characters/Party/BP_XenoCore_Party › Starting Roster, or in Project Settings › Game › XenoCore Content › Startup › Starting Roster Override. Remove them there.

The NPC is gone when I load a save

Intended: the member is already in the loaded roster, so the NPC removes itself.

The NPC stands in a T-pose

Idle Animation is on a different skeleton from the NPC's mesh. Use an idle made for that mesh.

The member joined but is not fighting. Every active slot was full, so they went to the reserve. Swap them in from the Party screen.

docs.title: Related
docs.text: • Party · Progression

docs.title: Replace the sample content
docs.text:
Designer · 2–4 h · No code

Result: your project carries your own characters, gear, enemies and map, the sample content is gone, and the game still boots, starts a new game and plays with no missing references.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• You have your own replacements working, made with the other recipes: Add a party member, Add a weapon, Add an enemy type, Build a world-partition map.
  • Commit, or back up the project. Deleting assets cannot be undone from inside the editor.

docs.title: What is sample and what is framework
docs.text: The framework is the part other assets are built on. The sample is the part that is merely an example of something. Delete sample, keep framework.

docs.title: Framework: keep
docs.text:
Folder or asset Why XenoCore (the Game Feature Data at the plugin root) Registers the plugin, its input and its components Experiences/* The game rules every map runs, the front end and the HUD Game/* except the backup pawn (see below) Game mode, player pawn base, ability sets, progression, save point, tag relationships Characters/Party/B_XenoCore_PartyMember_Base, BP_XenoCore_Party, AbilitySet_XenoCore_PartyMember, BP_AIC_XenoCore_PartyMember, AI/ Party bases and AI Characters/Enemies/Core/* Enemy base, AI controller, common ability set, chevron Characters/NPC/* NPC and dialogue anchor Characters/Player/* The animation Blueprint, anim layers, blend spaces and clips every character uses Characters/Core/Cosmetics/* Body-type cosmetic parts Battle/* Arts ability, effects, attributes, stat curve tables, reactions, statuses, targeting Inventory/BP_XenoItemDefinition, Inventory/*EquipmentStats, Inventory/Armour/ED_XenoCore_Armour, Inventory/Loot/*, Inventory/Collectables/* Item and equipment bases, loot chests, pickup orbs Weapons/B_WeaponInstance_Base, GA_XenoCore_WeaponDrawSync, AN_XenoCore_WeaponHandoff, M_XenoCore_Weapon Weapon bases Input/*, UserInterface/*, Cameras/*, ContextEffects/*, GameplayCues/*, Effects/* Controls, every screen, camera, footsteps, hit feedback Maps/L_XenoCore_FrontEnd The title screen, unless you replace the front end too

Never move or rename these screens

The shop, trade, arts, save, quest and loot screens, the dialogue anchor and several popups are found by a fixed path, not by a reference. Moved or renamed, they simply stop opening. Keep UserInterface and Characters/NPC where they are.

docs.title: Sample: replace or delete
docs.text:
Sample Where The sample party (the shipped roster) Characters/VRoid/<Name>/ (Kael, Mira, Nia, Dorran, Isolde, Sabine, Tamsin), their Battle/Attributes/GE_XenoCore_BaseStats_<Name> and their rows in CT_XenoCore_PartyStatlines and Game/DT_XenoCore_ExperienceCurves. Keep Characters/VRoid/B_XenoCore_Party_VRoid_Base, B_XenoCore_Cosmetic_VRoid_Base and M_XenoCore_VRoidLit if your characters are VRoid models The twelve Mannequin colour members (examples, not in the shipped roster) Characters/Party/PartyMember_*, B_XenoCore_Party_*, PawnData_XenoCore_Party_*, Portraits/, Materials/ Sample weapons Weapons/AmberSword, BlueSword, GoldSword, GreatSword, GreenSword, IronBlade, IvorySword, RedSword, VioletSword. Keep the sword bases (Weapons/B_XenoCore_Sword_Base, ED_XenoCore_Sword_Base, AbilitySet_XenoCore_SwordCommon) and Weapons/Types while any weapon of yours uses them Sample armour and items Inventory/Armour/ID_*, Inventory/Items/ID_* Sample enemies Characters/Enemies/Minion (including the seven types in Minion/Variants), Characters/Enemies/Dummy, Inventory/Loot/DA_XenoCore_Drops_Minion. Gaur Plain's 15 XenoCore Enemy Spawner actors point at the variants: delete the map or repoint the spawners first Sample arts Battle/Arts/DA_*, GA_* (keep any your characters still use) Sample quests, shop, trade Quests/, Shop/, Trade/ Sample maps Maps/L_XenoCore_GaurPlain, Maps/L_XenoCore_Gym, Environment/GaurPlain The sample map's pack assets ThirdParty/ElectricDreams (the cliffs, boulders, trees and their materials, reduced) A leftover backup pawn Game/B_XenoCore_Player_XC1_Backup

Keep B_XenoCore_Player

The sample leader is Kael, a VRoid member. The colour member PartyMember_Blue uses Game/B_XenoCore_Player as its pawn, which is also the bootstrap pawn the game falls back on when the party has no starting roster. Keep B_XenoCore_Player even after you delete the colour members.

docs.title: 1. Point the framework at your content first
docs.text:
Deleting something still in use leaves a broken reference. Repoint these before deleting:

  1. Characters/Party/BP_XenoCore_Party › Class Defaults › XenoCore › Party › Starting Roster: your members only.
  2. UserInterface/W_XenoCore_TitleScreen › Class Defaults › XenoCore › Title › New Game Map: your map.
  3. Project Settings › Game › XenoCore Content › Startup: leave Starting Roster Override and New Game Map Override empty (they replace the two settings above), and set Title Music, Fallback Field Music and Fallback Battle Music to your own tracks if you want music. The plugin ships no music; these are empty until you fill them.
  4. Project Settings › Packaging › List of maps to include: remove the sample maps, add yours.
  5. Project Settings › Game › XenoCore Save › Location Names: add an entry for each of your maps, so save rows name them, and remove the sample maps' entries.
  6. Any placed NPC, chest or enemy in maps you keep that uses a sample shop table, quest or drop table.

docs.title: 2. Delete in small batches
docs.text:
1. Select one row of the sample table above in the Content Browser and press Delete.
  2. If the Delete Assets dialog lists references, read them. A reference from another sample asset in the same batch is fine. A reference from framework or from your own content means step 1 missed something: cancel, repoint, try again.
  3. When a sample asset has a like-for-like replacement of yours, use Replace References in that dialog to point everything at your asset in one go.
  4. After each batch, right-click the XenoCore content folder and choose Fix Up Redirectors.

Force Delete hides the problem until packaging

Force Delete removes the asset and leaves every reference to it pointing at nothing. The editor loads, and the cook or the first playthrough fails. Only force-delete when the dialog lists nothing but other sample assets.

docs.title: 3. Check the result
docs.text:
1. Right-click the XenoCore content folder and run Validate Assets. Fix every error.
  2. Open Window › Output Log and Build › Map Check on each map you keep.

A Reimport warning on some retargeted clips is expected

A few retargeted animations under Characters/Player/Animations record a development folder as their import source. The source files are not included. That is editor-only metadata: the clips load and cook normally, and only Reimport on those clips fails.

docs.title: 4. Remove what you don't ship from the host
docs.text: Your Lyra project still has Lyra's own sample game features (ShooterCore, ShooterMaps, TopDownArena and others). Whether to disable them is covered in Package a build.

docs.title: Test it
docs.text:
1. Close and reopen the editor. The Output Log shows no missing-package warnings on startup.
  2. Open Maps/L_XenoCore_FrontEnd, press Play, choose New Game. You arrive in your map with your party.
  3. Open every menu screen once, fight an enemy, open a chest, talk to an NPC.
  4. Save, return to the title, Continue. The save loads.
  5. Make a packaged build (Package a build) and repeat steps 2–4 in it.

docs.title: If it doesn't work
docs.text:
New Game goes nowhere

New Game Map still names a deleted map, or your map isn't in the packaging list.

The party is empty

Starting Roster still lists deleted members. Its entries show as None.

A menu screen never opens

A screen found by fixed path was moved, renamed or deleted. Restore it from your backup.

docs.title: Going further
docs.text:
• Package a build
  • Megascans at shipping size, to keep only what your own map uses.

docs.title: Restyle the menus
docs.text:
Designer · 45 min · No code

Result: the menus use your own colours and font. List rows, tab strips and headings all change together, because you edit the few shared style assets rather than each screen.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• UI shell and HUD: how screens, buttons and styles relate.
  • Import your font first if you want one (see step 4).

docs.title: Where the look lives
docs.text:
XenoCore's menus are built with Epic's CommonUI, the same toolkit Lyra uses. In CommonUI a widget does not store its own colours; it points at a style asset. Change the style and every widget using it changes.

The shared pieces are in UserInterface/Foundation:

Asset What it styles ButtonStyle_XenoCore_Menu List rows and small buttons: item rows, art rows, party member buttons, trade rows, and the Skills screen's branch headers (Selected = the selected branch). Normal, hovered, pressed and selected looks.
